reqs.text: A complete re-engineering of morm in Rust: define PostgreSQL models in code, track them with rock-solid up and down migrations, and write queries in plain SQL. There is no extra query language. This is a new design, not a port. python-morm is a reference for what real projects need, and nothing is kept just for compatibility.

There is no extra query language. This is a new design, not a port. python-morm is a reference for what real projects need, and nothing is kept just for compatibility.

reqs.text: - `morm-mgr` also runs a migration's Rust data hooks, and nothing else. Build it in CI and ship the binary with the migrations. `migrate --hooks ./morm-mgr` and `rollback --hooks ./morm-mgr` call it as `morm-mgr hook ID up` or `down`, and a migration with hooks refuses to run without it, or if that binary doesn't contain the hook, because `morm-admin` holds no project code. A hook connects with the migration role and runs as a `no-tx` step, so it must be safe to run again on `--resume`.

reqs.text: **How it fits together:** `morm-admin` holds the engine. When a command needs the models, it builds and runs `morm-mgr` to get the manifest. Commands that don't need models (`migrate`, `rollback`, `status`, `purge`) run from `morm-migrations/` alone, so a production host needs `morm-admin` and no Rust toolchain. The app binary carries no migration code or schema metadata, apart from the short per-model column list `check_schema` reads.

reqs.text: **Registration:** models, objects and `sql!` queries register themselves through a distributed static list, with no central list to maintain. Their metadata is behind `cfg(morm_mgr)`, not a cargo feature, because `cargo build --workspace` unifies features and would pull it into the app. `morm-admin` builds `morm-mgr` in its own target directory with that `cfg` set. This needs proof early, including models in several crates, where a linker can drop a crate nothing references (section 16).

reqs.text:
```toml
# An example. Every setting, at its default and with what it does, is in morm-core's shipped morm.toml
[database]
# Either a URL, or the separate fields below. Separate fields override URL parts.
url = "${DATABASE_URL}"
host = "/var/run/postgresql"     # Unix socket directory or hostname
port = 5432
name = "app"
user = "app"                     # no password needed with peer auth on a Unix socket
password = "${MORM_DB_PASSWORD}" # keep secrets in the environment
sslmode = "require"              # the default; TCP only, a Unix socket never uses TLS; disable, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full
target_session_attrs = "any"     # "read-write" finds the primary among several hosts
connect_timeout = "5s"
application_name = "auto"        # the binary's name; shows in pg_stat_activity
search_path = "public"           # pinned, so another role can't shadow objects
pooler = "none"                  # "transaction" when connecting through PgBouncer in that mode

[database.migration]             # owner role, so the app can run with fewer privileges
url = "${MORM_MIGRATION_URL}"

[server]                         # optional: the database server, which SQL can't report
ram = "8G"
cores = 4

[pool]
min = "auto"                     # 2 x [server] cores, or of this machine if unset
max = "auto"                     # 10 x min
processes = 1                    # app processes sharing this database
idle_timeout = "5m"              # shrink to 1 after this
last_idle_timeout = "1h"         # then close the last one
max_queries = 50000              # 0 = no limit
max_lifetime = "off"
hold_warn_after = "1h"
wait_timeout = "5s"              # longest wait for a connection; can't be off
max_holds = "auto"               # max / 4, at least 1
lock_timeout = "5s"              # longest wait for one lock
statement_timeout = "off"        # longest single statement
statement_cache = 256            # prepared compile-time statements per connection
shape_cache = 128                # prepared runtime-built statements per connection
shutdown_timeout = "30s"         # db.close() waits this long
plan_cache_mode = "auto"         # or force_custom_plan, force_generic_plan
transaction_timeout = "30s"      # longest db.transaction
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = "1m"
client_connection_check_interval = "5s"
tx_warn_after = "1s"
check_schema = "on"              # "off" starts against a schema that may not match: read the README first
stale_cooldown = "60s"           # one window for pool-wide stale repairs, the epoch, the pooler cool-down; 1s to 10m
stale_cooldown_max = 64          # cool-down entries per pool, behind a pooler only; 1 to 4096
stale_pending_expiry = "60s"     # how long a pending entry keeps a stale statement fresh; "off", or "0s" to 10m
stale_pending_max = 64           # pending entries per pool; 0 (off) to 4096
servers = "auto"                 # or "several" when one host reaches several servers, or "one"; read the README first

[pools.replica]                  # a read replica
host = "db-replica.internal"
read_only = true

[pools.replica.server]           # a pool on a different server describes that server
ram = "16G"
cores = 8

[pools.jobs]                     # optional named profile
user = "app_jobs"                # any [database] field can be set here
password = "${MORM_JOBS_PASSWORD}"
min = 1
max = 4

[outbox]
batch = 100                      # events claimed at once
poll_interval = "1s"
lease = "60s"                    # a crashed worker's events return after this
max_attempts = 10
retention = "7d"                 # how long delivered events are kept

[telemetry]                      # used by the tracing and metrics features
span_sample = 0.01               # share of queries that get a span: 0 = none, 1 = all
slow_query = "250ms"             # always report slower queries, pool wait included; "off"
metrics_interval = "10s"         # how often metrics are published

[migrations]
dir = "morm-migrations"
min_postgres = 15
scratch_url = "${MORM_SCRATCH_URL}"
```

password = "${MORM_JOBS_PASSWORD}"
min = 1
max = 4

[outbox]
batch = 100                      # events claimed at once
poll_interval = "1s"
lease = "60s"                    # a crashed worker's events return after this
max_attempts = 10
retention = "7d"                 # how long delivered events are kept

[telemetry]                      # used by the tracing and metrics features
span_sample = 0.01               # share of queries that get a span: 0 = none, 1 = all
slow_query = "250ms"             # always report slower queries, pool wait included; "off"
metrics_interval = "10s"         # how often metrics are published

[migrations]
dir = "morm-migrations"
min_postgres = 15
scratch_url = "${MORM_SCRATCH_URL}"
```

If `host` is a full socket file path, morm takes the directory and port from it.

reqs.text: **`morm-admin import`** is a simple starting point for any existing database. It reads the catalog only, never rows, and writes model files that match the schema exactly: types, nullability, defaults, indexes, constraints and their names. Nothing is "improved". Anything models can't express, such as exclusion constraints or partitioned tables, is listed in its output and stays unmanaged. `morm-admin mgr baseline` then records that state as migration zero. Views, hooks and validation are added by hand afterwards.

use morm::{model, Timestamp};

#[model(
    table = "products",
    base = "common",                 // adds id (identity bigint pk), created_at, updated_at
    ordering = "name, -price",       // default ORDER BY
    was = "items",                   // rename hint: table used to be called "items"
    hooks,                           // this model implements Hooks itself
    extensions = "pg_trgm",
    indexes(
        index(cols = "vendor_id, sku", unique),
        index(cols = "name", using = "gin", ops = "gin_trgm_ops"),
        index(cols = "vendor_id", filter = "deleted_at IS NULL"),
    )
)]
pub struct Product {
    #[col(fk = Vendor::id, on_delete = "cascade", index)]
    pub vendor_id: i64,

    #[col(sql = "varchar(64)", len = "1..=64")]
    pub sku: String,

    #[col(sql = "varchar(255)", was = "title", clean = "trim_name")]
    pub name: String,

    #[col(sql = "numeric(12,2)", default = "0", min = 0)]
    pub price: rust_decimal::Decimal,

    #[col(default = "0", min = 0)]
    pub stock: i32,

    #[col(default = "true")]
    pub active: bool,

    pub attrs: Option<serde_json::Value>,          // jsonb, nullable

    #[col(expr = "price * stock", sql = "numeric")]  // computed in SELECT, not stored
    pub stock_value: rust_decimal::Decimal,

    pub deleted_at: Option<Timestamp>,
}
```

reqs.text: Rules:

- **`unique` gives both a constraint and an index.** Postgres backs a UNIQUE constraint with a unique index of the same name, so morm creates one object that serves as both. This applies to `#[col(unique)]` and to `index(cols = "a, b", unique)`, and `include` is kept on the constraint. A unique index with `filter` or `expr` stays an index only, because constraints can't be partial or use expressions.

Inherited base fields are included. Indexes differing in `using`, `ops`, `filter`, `expr` or `include` are allowed, and `lint` reports the ones that look redundant.

reqs.text: - **Explicit ids:** a normal insert always leaves an identity column to Postgres, whatever the field holds. `.explicit_ids()` on `insert`, `insert_many` and `insert_stream` writes the ids you give, adds `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` to every `INSERT` that sends an identity column, and moves the sequence past them in the same transaction. Postgres needs it for `GENERATED ALWAYS` and accepts it under `BY DEFAULT`, where it changes nothing: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11 an insert with it stored the given id in a `BY DEFAULT` column. So it's sent under either kind, whichever the model was built with, and a build made while a column was `BY DEFAULT` keeps writing chosen ids after a migration makes it `GENERATED ALWAYS`. A `COPY`, on `insert_many`'s `COPY` path and in `insert_stream`, sends the key column with no clause, as R-1202 says.

reqs.text: - **Moving the sequence.** It finds the identity's sequence through `pg_depend`, as the one the identity owns, and first takes the two-argument `pg_advisory_xact_lock(<morm namespace>, <sequence oid>)`, which can't collide with the hashed keys of `tx.advisory_lock`, so two imports into one sequence run one after the other and can't overwrite each other's position. Then, inside a savepoint, it takes `LOCK TABLE <table> IN SHARE MODE`, reads the sequence's `last_value`, calls `setval(seq, max(id))` only when `max(id) >= last_value`, where `max(id)` is the highest key the call sends, taken from the rows, with no scan of the table, and rolls back to the savepoint, which releases the table lock and keeps the `setval`, because a sequence isn't transactional. `insert` and `insert_many` do this before sending any row, and with `.in_batches(n)` each batch's transaction does it for that batch's rows. It's `>=` because a sequence that was never used has `last_value = 1` with nothing taken. The table lock is what makes the read safe. A sequence can't be locked: `LOCK TABLE` refuses one with `This operation is not supported for sequences`, `FOR UPDATE` with `cannot lock rows in sequence`, and `nextval` takes only `ROW EXCLUSIVE` on it. So without the table lock a normal insert can take a value between the read and the `setval`, and the `setval` moves the sequence backwards: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with the read and the `setval` as two statements, five normal inserts between them were given 1 to 5, the `setval` put the sequence back to 3, and the next insert was given 4 again. `SHARE` conflicts with the `ROW EXCLUSIVE` lock every insert takes on its table before it draws a value, so the lock waits for inserts already running and holds new ones back until the savepoint is rolled back, and on a partitioned table it holds back inserts straight into a partition too, because `LOCK TABLE` reaches every partition. With it, on both versions, a normal insert during an import was given 101 straight after the move to 100, while the import was still open, and a second import, waiting on the advisory lock, then read 102 and moved the sequence to 150, with no key given twice. Without the advisory lock, two imports that had each written a row deadlocked on the table lock.

On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a role with only `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the table was refused the lock with `permission denied`, and `UPDATE` on the table let it in, as `MAINTAIN` does on 17 and later. On a partitioned table, grants on the parent were enough.

reqs.text: - **What the move costs, and what it doesn't stop.** The lock waits for writes already running on the table and holds new ones back while it waits, for up to `lock_timeout`, past which the call returns `LockTimeout`. For `insert` and `insert_many` that comes before any row is sent, so nothing is written, and once the sequence has moved no normal insert can be given a chosen key above where it stood. A chosen key at or below that point may already be in the table, which fails the call with `Unique`, or, on a sequence with `CACHE` above 1, may sit in another session's cache, which fails that session's later insert: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, under `CACHE 20`, a session that had taken 1 was refused with `23505` on its next insert, after an import stored 2 and left the sequence at 20. `insert_stream` moves the sequence only after its `COPY`, as R-1202 says, so a normal insert during the stream can be given a key the stream writes, and one that waits on a streamed row, over that key or any other unique column, deadlocks with the stream's table lock. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, Postgres broke it by failing the stream's lock with `deadlock detected`, over the key and over another unique column, so the stream rolls back and returns `Deadlock`, with nothing written. A `nextval` called other than by an insert into the table isn't held back: one ran while the lock was held. So run streams with chosen keys while the table is quiet.

A chosen key at or below that point may already be in the table, which fails the call with `Unique`, or, on a sequence with `CACHE` above 1, may sit in another session's cache, which fails that session's later insert: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, under `CACHE 20`, a session that had taken 1 was refused with `23505` on its next insert, after an import stored 2 and left the sequence at 20. `insert_stream` moves the sequence only after its `COPY`, as R-1202 says, so a normal insert during the stream can be given a key the stream writes, and one that waits on a streamed row, over that key or any other unique column, deadlocks with the stream's table lock. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, Postgres broke it by failing the stream's lock with `deadlock detected`, over the key and over another unique column, so the stream rolls back and returns `Deadlock`, with nothing written. A `nextval` called other than by an insert into the table isn't held back: one ran while the lock was held. So run streams with chosen keys while the table is quiet.

reqs.text: - **A second connection on the same task is refused.** Using `db` inside a transaction closure, or inside a `stream()` loop, returns `NestedConnection` immediately. This can't be a compile error, because closures can capture `db`. Inside `db.transaction`, morm runs the closure, so a task-local flag works. A `stream()` loop body is ordinary code outside any morm future, so a task-local can't wrap it: an open stream registers its `tokio::task::try_id()` in a small sharded set, and checkout consults that set only while an atomic count of open streams is above zero. A stream registers on its first poll, not at creation, because it's `Send` and can move to another task. Each later poll compares `try_id()` and re-registers if the task changed, which is one integer comparison. An app with no open streams pays one atomic load. The check is per task, so running a stream beside another query in `join!`, `select!` or `FuturesUnordered` is refused too. That really does hold two connections on one task, which is the risk this rule exists for, so such a query uses `db.extra_conn()`. This needs proof early (section 16).

reqs.text: - **Retire instead of drop.** A dropped column is renamed `_morm_retired_<migration>_<col>`, with NOT NULL and defaults removed, and with its indexes, CHECK constraints and triggers dropped, along with foreign keys going out from the retired object. Otherwise a column the app no longer knows about would keep blocking deletes, or cascade them silently. The ledger records each definition. A dropped table moves to the `_morm_retired` schema, with its migration in the name. Long names follow the 63-byte rule with the hash suffix, because Postgres would truncate them and two could collide. The ledger records each original name. Rollback restores them with their data, rebuilds indexes concurrently, and recreates foreign keys and CHECKs as `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE`. Rows changed in the meantime can fail those steps, such as a parent deleted since, or a duplicate where a unique index was, so it stops with the offending rows and offers a decision: clear those values, delete those rows, or keep the constraint `NOT VALID`.

reqs.text: - **Objects that still depend on it stop the retire.** `makemigrations` and `migrate` read `pg_depend` and refuse, showing the list, while an object that isn't being retired depends on the column or table: a foreign key from a live table, a view, a materialized view, a function, a generated column, an RLS policy, extended statistics or a publication. Functions matter because a `BEGIN ATOMIC` body has an empty `prosrc`, so the text search can't see it, but it does record its dependencies. Renaming doesn't break these, which is the danger: a view would keep serving retired data, and the purge would fail later. Dropping a foreign key would quietly remove integrity from a column the app still uses. Retire them together, change them in the same migration, or remove them first. The planner applies managed changes first, so only what still depends after them counts. A generated column's dependency is recorded through `pg_attrdef`, so the query must include it.

reqs.text: - **Code Postgres doesn't track.** A `plpgsql` function body has no recorded dependency on the columns it names, so a retire or rename can break inserts through a trigger like `NEW.note := 'x'`. Before either, morm searches `pg_proc.prosrc` in every schema for the name, whole words only, in any case, because a body in another schema can name the object too, and an unquoted `SELECT N FROM T` names `n` and `t`. Common names like `status` will give false hits, which is fine, because a hit costs a decision, a `plpgsql_check` run and at most a `proof` (steps 35 and 59). A hit on a managed function is a decision with evidence, `makemigrations` proposes the rewritten function, and step 59 proves it with a real call and `plpgsql_check`. `migrate` preflight repeats the search on the live database, which is the only way to see unmanaged functions, and a hit not yet accepted is an open decision, which stops `migrate` with exit code `3` until `--decide` answers it. `rollback` preflight does the same before an inverse that retires or renames. `makemigrations` stores the names to search for in `op_data`, for each direction, because neither command has the models and `rollback` must work from the ledger's `meta.json` when the files are gone.

Migrations carry `phase: expand | contract`, and `--phase` splits them. `contract` refuses while a required `#[col(deprecated)]` hasn't shipped. Marking a `NOT NULL` column with no default as `deprecated` generates an expand step dropping that `NOT NULL`, because the new binary stops writing it. A rename decision offers an expand/contract form for live tables: add the new column, keep both in sync with a generated trigger, backfill in batches, and drop the old column and trigger in `contract`. `check_schema` checks compatibility, not equality, at startup, where morm runs it when each pool starts, as R-1116 says, and when `db.check_schema()` is called, so an old binary restarting during an expand phase still boots. Every column the binary reads or writes must exist, with a type the field can decode in the same family as the type it was built against, so only an unrelated kind fails. These are the families, and there are no others: for a field of a Rust integer type, `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint` and `numeric(p,0)` with any `p`, and never a `numeric` with a scale or with no precision, because an integer field has no way to read a fraction; for `Decimal`, `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, because every one of their values fits in its 28 digits; for `morm::Numeric`, `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, as for `Decimal`; for `String`, `text`, and `varchar` with any length or none; for a `String` built against `char(n)`, `char` with any length; for `DateTime<Utc>` and `Timestamp`, `timestamptz` with any precision, and for `NaiveDateTime`, `timestamp` with any precision; and for an array of any of these, an array of its element's family. Every other field needs the same type, with the same length or precision, as `format_type` prints it from `atttypid` and `atttypmod`. `char` is a family of its own, apart from `text` and `varchar`, because Postgres pads a `char` value with spaces to its length and a change to `text` or `varchar` drops them, so `'ab '` would read as `'ab'`. Postgres treats those trailing spaces as insignificant, so a `String` field built against `char(n)` reads `char` of any length through a decoder that trims trailing spaces back to `n`: on `char(4)`, `'ab  '` reads as `'ab '`, as it did on `char(3)`, and `'abcd'`, with no spaces to trim, reads whole. `timestamp` and `timestamptz` are different kinds here, because a change between them converts each value through the `TimeZone` of the session that runs it, with no error, so the same stored `12:00` becomes `12:00` UTC under one session and `06:00` UTC under another, and no decoder could tell which. Any other difference fails the check, such as `text` for an integer field, `numeric(25,2)` for an integer field, or `text` or `varchar(3)` for a field built against `char(3)`. Within a family, the check also fails a field built against a type that the column's real type is one of R-1108's silent narrowings of, because Postgres would round or cut what that binary writes with no error: a field built for `numeric(6,2)` on `numeric(4,1)` or on `integer`, for `numeric` on `numeric(6,2)`, for `varchar(3)` on `varchar(2)`, for `text` on `varchar(10)`, for `char(3)` on `char(2)`, for `timestamptz` on `timestamptz(3)`, or for `numeric(6,2)[]` on `numeric(4,1)[]`. It names the column, both definitions and the silent change, such as `1.25` stored as `1.3`. A running binary never meets this, because R-1108 holds such a change for `contract`, which runs once every binary is built for the new shape, or for `--fast`, with apps stopped. So only a binary built for the old shape that starts after it, such as an older build brought back, is refused, and it fails to start loudly, with R-1116's `Error::SchemaMismatch`, rather than storing values other than the ones it writes. A narrowing that raises a real error on a write that doesn't fit still passes, such as a field built for `numeric(6,2)` on `numeric(5,2)` or for `bigint` on `integer`. Within a family, the field reads through the decoder for the column's real type, chosen once per statement when it's prepared, and chosen again when a cached statement is re-prepared because Postgres reports that its result type changed, as it does after a cutover. When the types match, the path is the one the binary always ran. A field wider than the column reads every value losslessly. A field narrower than the column checks each value's range, and only a value that can't fit errors: an integer field returns `Error::OutOfRange` naming the column, never a wrapped value, and `Decimal` returns `Error::Decimal` for a value it can't hold exactly, past its 28 significant digits, as it does on unbounded `numeric`. `morm::Numeric`, and `String` on `text` and `varchar`, read every value whole. Nothing read is rounded. A write goes as the column type the binary was built against, and Postgres converts it to the column's real type, so a value the column can't hold, such as a number with more digits before the point than it allows or a text longer than its length, gets the database's error for that write. Where Postgres would round or cut the write silently instead, R-1108 holds the change for `contract`. So a type change never stops a running binary, and one restarting after it still boots, apart from a binary built for the old shape of one of R-1108's silent narrowings, which the check above refuses. A type change has no expand and contract of its own and never waits for `contract`, apart from R-1108's silent narrowings, and `contract` still guards dropped columns and removed enum values. Extra columns and objects are fine. Two cases that would fail that binary's inserts are reported: an extra `NOT NULL` column with no default, and a column the binary may leave out that is no longer nullable and has lost its default. A column that has lost its identity counts as one that has lost its default, because a binary built while it had one never sends it, so each of its inserts would fail with `NOT NULL`.

reqs.text: The default `max` is deliberately generous. On a larger server, raise `max_connections` in Postgres to match, and `morm-admin size` suggests the value. morm can't see other apps on the same server, which is what the margin is for, and `processes` is set by hand. reqs.text: `morm::Pool` makes a pooler unnecessary for one process, but large fleets and managed Postgres often have PgBouncer in front. `pooler = "transaction"` says so:
reqs.block: **R-0669** `morm::Pool` makes a pooler unnecessary for one process, but large fleets and managed Postgres often have PgBouncer in front. `pooler = "transaction"` says so:

reqs.text: - **Only tracked startup parameters, on PgBouncer 1.20 or later.** PgBouncer refuses a startup parameter it doesn't track, by default, so of morm's settings only two go at startup: `application_name`, as its own startup parameter, and `TimeZone = 'UTC'`, the one setting sent in `options`, as `-c TimeZone=UTC`. PgBouncer tracks both per client and sets them on every server connection the client gets, in transaction mode too, even after another client's `SET` on that connection, so the binary's name shows in `pg_stat_activity` and the role's `timezone` can stay as it is. PgBouncer accepts `options` from 1.20, so morm needs PgBouncer 1.20 or later. An older one refuses every connection with `unsupported startup parameter: options`, and morm turns that into `Error::Config`, from `Db::connect`, `connect_as`, `connect_to` and a pool `db.pool(name)` adds, quoting PgBouncer's message and naming the two fixes: upgrade PgBouncer to 1.20 or later, or add `options` to its `ignore_startup_parameters` and set the role's `timezone` to `UTC`, which the startup check then checks. It does so whatever `pooler` says, and with `pooler = "none"` it first says to set `pooler = "transaction"`. Falling back to session `SET` for the rest isn't safe here, because in transaction mode that setting stays on a server connection other clients will share. So set `lock_timeout`, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, `client_connection_check_interval` and `search_path` on the role with `ALTER ROLE`. A pooler that drops `TimeZone`, such as PgBouncer 1.26.1 or later with `TimeZone` in `ignore_startup_parameters`, leaves sessions in the role's zone, and then a pool whose sessions report a zone other than UTC refuses to start, with an error naming the zone and saying to let the pooler pass `TimeZone` or to set the role's `timezone` to `UTC`. Owner decisions DJ2, DK1 and DK5.

reqs.text:
**Stale statements: the statement class.** A cached statement can go stale when a schema changes under it, and it then fails every time until it's prepared again. A statement that casts a parameter to a non-built-in type, such as an enum, a domain or a composite, survives a swap of that type made by a migration, because every migration `tx` step ends with a reset that marks every cached plan invalid, so Postgres parses it again and resolves the name again, whether or not it touches a table holding the type. Without that reset, as after a swap made by hand, one that touches no such table, such as `SELECT ($1::st)::text`, gets `XX000` `cache lookup failed for type` once the old type is dropped, or `22P02` naming the old type while it's kept, and while it's kept a label both types share runs on the old type's order with no error, which no retry can see. Each statement-class signal R-1245 lists is handled the same way whether Postgres returns it at prepare or at execute, as it does through PgBouncer. Postgres rolled the failed statement back, so running the call again is safe, and the statement parsed once, so its error comes from a schema change or the data, not a typo.

- **A fresh run:** straight to Postgres, morm evicts the statement on this connection, prepares it again and runs it; behind PgBouncer, it runs the call once unnamed through `query_typed`, which PgBouncer never shares, because a re-prepare would get the same stale server statement back. A stale statement gets one fresh run and no other retry.
- **A pending entry,** R-1270's, keeps a statement fresh while a confirmation is outstanding. reqs.text: morm has no vendor code. It emits OpenTelemetry-shaped data through `tracing` and `metrics`, so Datadog, Grafana, Honeycomb and in-house stacks work through exporters the app chooses, and morm depends on no exporter or vendor. Spans reach an agent through `tracing-opentelemetry` and OTLP. Metrics usually go through `metrics-exporter-prometheus`, scraped by the agent, because the `metrics` crate has no official OTLP exporter. Logs and database monitoring come from Postgres directly, as `app_suggestions.md` describes.

reqs.text: **No per-request SQL comments.** Trace-linking modes such as Datadog's `full` propagation add a `traceparent` comment to every statement. reqs.text: - Encode and decode go through one per-column conversion layer, so a column's Rust type can differ from its stored type. Generated code calls `ToSql` and `FromSql` directly through static dispatch, with no pointer or allocation. A field has one decoder for each column type its family accepts, as `check_schema` lists them, and which one a column uses is chosen once per statement from the column's real type when the statement is prepared, never per row. When every column has the type the binary was built against, the statement's rows go through `from_row`, and that path is unchanged: no branch, pointer, allocation or per-row state. Otherwise they go through `from_row_as`, which `#[model]` generates beside `from_row` and which reads each field through the decoder the statement chose. The choice is held by the statement, not the row, so that path adds one branch per value on the statement's choice and no per-row state. `from_row_named` and `ProductRef` work the same way. A parameter is always sent as the column type the binary was built against, and Postgres converts it to the column's real type. A benchmark against hand-written tokio-postgres decoding checks that the unchanged path adds no cost.

Types are declared once, on their Rust type. A sequence has no Rust type, so it uses a macro:

```rust
#[derive(PgDomain)]
#[pg_domain(name = "email", check = "VALUE LIKE '%@%'")]
pub struct Email(pub String);                       // base type comes from String: text

#[derive(PgComposite)]
#[pg_composite(name = "money_amount")]
pub struct MoneyAmount {
    #[col(sql = "numeric(12,2)")] pub amount: Decimal,
    pub currency: String,
}

#[derive(PgEnum)]
#[pg_enum(name = "order_state")]
pub enum OrderState { Pending, Paid }

morm::pg_sequence!(invoice_no, "START 1000 CACHE 20");
morm::pg_sequence!(order_no, file = "sql/order_no.sql");
```

reqs.text: - **Stale generation.** The pool holds a generation counter for connections, in one atomic word, and each connection remembers the value it started with. A checkout compares them with one atomic read and no lock, and replaces a connection that's behind. Step 14 raises the counter only through its gate's *replace* action, at most once per `stale_cooldown` plus once per migration, so after an enum swap the other connections don't each have to fail first. Behind a pooler, with `pooler = "transaction"`, it's never raised, because replacing a client connection can't reach the server session that holds the stale code. Owner decisions SD and MB. `pool_stats()` counts these replacements.

reqs.text:
**Stale sessions straight to Postgres: the session class and the epoch.** R-1245's session class means the session holds compiled code that no fresh statement can reach: `XX000` `cache lookup failed for type` from a fresh run or a statement that isn't cached, from a dropped type; `42804` from one of plpgsql's three parameter routines, from a plpgsql function compiled before a column or row type changed; and `22P02` from `enum_in` holding `_morm_retired_`, from a plpgsql variable compiled against an enum type a cutover kept under that name with its labels renamed. Each repeats on every call in that session, and a new session compiles the code fresh, so a connection opened after a change can't hold code compiled before it. Straight to Postgres one pool-wide **epoch**, R-1270's, decides which connections may be stale:

- **Old connection.** On a session-class failure morm reads `<n>` on the failing connection, from the `_morm` schema's comment, one catalog read, and the step that applies that read, R-1270's, starts an epoch at that step's time, `T`, if there's none, it has ended, or the pool's last-read `<n>` differs from the epoch's, which means `<n>` moved since; so a migration that commits between the failure and the read is inside the epoch. The test judges by the last-read `<n>` once the read is applied or refused: a read that overlapped the last applied read, or in a pool that reaches several servers one that finds a lower `<n>`, counts as the last-read `<n>`, so it starts an epoch only when any read would, when there's none, it has ended or the last-read `<n>` differs from the epoch's, and never under the older `<n>` it found; so a read sent before a migration or a lowering that arrives after a newer one never sets the epoch back. Inside a `tx.transaction(..)` savepoint, rows B3 and B4, morm reads nothing, and the test judges by the pool's last-read `<n>` as after a read that applies nothing, so a migration first seen there starts its epoch at the next read outside a transaction. An epoch ends `stale_cooldown` after `T`. A connection is old when it was opened before `T` and the epoch isn't suspended. An old connection is replaced on its first such failure; one opened since `T` can't hold code compiled before the change, so its failure is data, and returns as it is at no cost.
- **Replace,** outside a transaction. morm opens a new connection as the pool's one momentary extra, within the process's connection budget, which every pool in the process shares; when another replacement holds the extra, with the budget full, or when Postgres refuses the extra open with `53300`, too many connections for the server or for the role, which the budget can't see, it closes the old connection first and opens the new one in its slot. A `53300` on the extra also ends extras for the rest of that epoch: its later replacements close the old connection first and open in its slot, with no open beside it, and the next epoch tries the extra again. The step that decides the replacement decides which, R-1270's. It runs the call on the new connection as a fresh run. The new connection takes the old one's slot and the old one is closed, whatever that run returns, unless the new connection is lost. If the new connection can't be opened, the caller gets the original error, the old connection keeps its slot if it's still open, a slot already emptied is left to the pool, which reopens a connection on demand with its backoff on too many clients, and the epoch whose test decided the replacement is suspended, unless a newer one has started since. So, however many calls replace connections at once, the pool's slots never pass `max`, its connections never pass `max + 1` or the budget, and one server slot is enough for a stale session to heal.
- **Discard,** inside a transaction, built in step 20. After the whole transaction's rollback, which comes before R-0981's read, or inside a savepoint, where there's no read, after the step that decides it, morm closes the connection, and `.retry(n)`'s next attempt opens a new connection in that slot through the pool's ordinary open, with its backoff. If that open fails, `.retry(n)` returns its error and the epoch whose test decided the discard is suspended, unless a newer one has started since.

Before any row, in every mode and context:

- **The parameter test.** A `22P02` holding `_morm_retired_` can come from a client, because its message holds the input value. morm encodes every parameter itself, and no `PgEnum` label can start `_morm_`, so when a bound parameter's text holds `_morm_retired_`, the client sent it: morm returns the error as it is, with nothing done and nothing requested, at no cost.
- **The transient `XX000`.** `XX000` `could not open relation with OID`, from a caller of a `BEGIN ATOMIC` function while a cutover replaces that function or a view under it, doesn't repeat, and a new statement on the same connection works, so the connection isn't at fault: outside a transaction morm retries once on that connection, held or not; inside one it returns `Error::SchemaChanged`; nothing is replaced or requested. Tested on Postgres 15 to 18: all 3,566 such errors, with plain and cached plans, cleared on the first retry on the same connection.

| # | Signal | morm does | Caller gets | May request | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A2 | Session class, on an old connection, outside a transaction | Replace | The new connection's run | `42804` and `XX000` request *replace* at the failure, once, and the new connection's run requests nothing more; a `22P02`'s request comes from the new connection's run, if it confirms | One catalog read, one connection, one run |
| A3 | Session class, on a connection opened since `T`, or with the epoch suspended, outside a transaction | Nothing | As it is | Nothing | One catalog read |
| A4 | Session class, on a `db.hold()` connection | `Error::SchemaChanged`; an old connection is replaced on release, counted as the epoch's replacement | `Error::SchemaChanged`, or as it is if the connection isn't old | As A2 | One catalog read, which inside a transaction the app opened gets `25P02` and applies nothing, the test judging by the last-read `<n>`; one connection on release |
| B3 | Session class, on an old connection, inside a transaction | Discard | `Error::SchemaChanged` | `42804` and `XX000` request *replace* at the failure, once, and the next attempt's run requests nothing more; for a `22P02`, the next attempt's run of the same text and parameter bytes on the new connection requests it, if it confirms | One catalog read, none inside a savepoint; one connection |
| B4 | Session class, on a connection opened since `T`, or with the epoch suspended, inside a transaction | Nothing | As it is, so `.retry(n)` stops; inside a savepoint, a Postgres error the savepoint clears, so the app can catch it and carry on | Nothing | One catalog read, none inside a savepoint |

Rows B3 and B4 are built in step 20. Outside a savepoint each rolls the whole transaction back before its read. Inside `tx.transaction(..)`'s savepoint neither reads: the test judges by the pool's last-read `<n>`, B3 rolls the whole transaction back after its step and returns `Error::SchemaChanged`, and B4 rolls back nothing but the savepoint, so its error, as it is, is a Postgres error the savepoint clears, and the app can catch it there and carry on, as R-1270 says. Behind PgBouncer the session class is R-1246's rows C2 and D2: no epoch, no replacement and no discard, because a client connection can't reach a server session.

So straight to Postgres, a client's stored or transformed text costs at most the connections open at an epoch's `T`, each replaced once, then nothing until the epoch ends: at most `max` replacements per epoch, whatever it sends and however many statements. Epochs start at least `stale_cooldown` apart unless `<n>` moves, but an epoch's replacements come at each old connection's next failure, anywhere in its life, so one span of `stale_cooldown` can hold the tail of one epoch and the head of the next: at most `2 × max` replacements in any span of `stale_cooldown`, plus `max` per migration. Each repeats on every call in that session, and a new session compiles the code fresh, so a connection opened after a change can't hold code compiled before it. Straight to Postgres one pool-wide **epoch**, R-1270's, decides which connections may be stale:

The test judges by the last-read `<n>` once the read is applied or refused: a read that overlapped the last applied read, or in a pool that reaches several servers one that finds a lower `<n>`, counts as the last-read `<n>`, so it starts an epoch only when any read would, when there's none, it has ended or the last-read `<n>` differs from the epoch's, and never under the older `<n>` it found; so a read sent before a migration or a lowering that arrives after a newer one never sets the epoch back. Inside a `tx.transaction(..)` savepoint, rows B3 and B4, morm reads nothing, and the test judges by the pool's last-read `<n>` as after a read that applies nothing, so a migration first seen there starts its epoch at the next read outside a transaction. An epoch ends `stale_cooldown` after `T`. A connection is old when it was opened before `T` and the epoch isn't suspended. An old connection is replaced on its first such failure; one opened since `T` can't hold code compiled before the change, so its failure is data, and returns as it is at no cost.

A `53300` on the extra also ends extras for the rest of that epoch: its later replacements close the old connection first and open in its slot, with no open beside it, and the next epoch tries the extra again. The step that decides the replacement decides which, R-1270's. It runs the call on the new connection as a fresh run. The new connection takes the old one's slot and the old one is closed, whatever that run returns, unless the new connection is lost. **The one gate for pool-wide actions.** Three actions reach the whole pool: *clear*, which raises the statement generation, so every connection clears both statement caches at its next checkout; *salt*, behind PgBouncer only, which adds a new random 64-bit salt to the marker, replacing any earlier one, and then raises the statement generation, in that order in one step, as R-1246 says; and *replace*, straight to Postgres only, which raises step 11's connection generation, so every connection is replaced at its next checkout, which clears its caches too. Every pool-wide action, whatever asked for it, a confirmation, `0A000`, `42804` or `XX000`, passes one gate:

- **A request** is judged in the step that makes it, R-1270's, by the pool's last-read `<n>` after any read the request makes itself; a request carries no `<n>` of its own. It's taken now when the window is open, or when the last-read `<n>` differs from the window's, the one the last action or adoption was taken under. Otherwise it's remembered as due, and taken at the first checkout after the window ends; a due *replace* outranks a due *clear*. Straight to Postgres, a request whose call hasn't read `<n>`, made while the window is closed outside a transaction, or after the whole transaction's rollback as row B1's is, and not on a `db.hold()` connection, reads `<n>` on that connection, one catalog read, so a migration's stale state isn't held back there, and a read that counts as moved, by R-1270's read order, is taken as event E1 says; that, R-0981's epoch and the read when the pool starts, R-1270's, are the only reads of `<n>` straight to Postgres. A request made while its call's transaction is open, a confirming run's inside a transaction, never reads, in either mode, because a REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE transaction's catalog reads see the snapshot of its first statement, which can be older than the pool's last applied read: it's judged by the last-read `<n>`, so when such a run is the first thing in the pool to meet a migration's stale state, its action is due until the window ends or the next read outside a transaction adopts the move, and every connection's stale statements are still cleared within `stale_cooldown` of the first confirmation. A request on a `db.hold()` connection never reads either, for the same reason, because its session can be inside a transaction the app opened, and is judged the same way. Behind PgBouncer a request never reads.
- **The window** starts when an action is taken and ends `stale_cooldown` later; it's closed from its start to its end and open after. Taking an action removes every pending entry and every cool-down entry and starts a window, under the last-read `<n>`; the epoch is kept.
- **The window never changes a call's own outcome.** Inside it or outside it each signal gets its row, a statement-class signal its fresh run and the caller its result; only the pool-wide action waits.
- **A checkout** does one atomic read of the generation word, as it already does: a connection behind the connection generation is replaced, and one behind the statement generation clears both caches. While an action is due it also reads the window's end, and once that window has ended it starts the due action's take with one compare-and-swap that sets R-1270's starting bit and nothing else, so two checkouts can't both take it, and finishes it in one step under R-1270's stale lock, `finish_take`, before any other step judges the gate: a *salt*'s fresh salt, then the raised generation with the due bits cleared, then the window, under the last-read `<n>` the finishing step started with, so a take whose compare-and-swap lands while a step moves `<n>` is taken under the old `<n>`, and the move's own request still passes the closed window. No generation is raised before the marker it's raised for is set, so no connection prepares the old text under a generation raised for a new one.

So a pool takes at most one pool-wide action per `stale_cooldown`, plus one per migration, whatever clients send and however many calls run at once. Every action is taken in a step, the request's own or `finish_take` after a checkout's compare-and-swap, before any other step judges the gate, as R-1270's steps say, and only when the window is open or the last-read `<n>` differs from the window's; so two actions less than `stale_cooldown` apart have between them a change of the last-read `<n>`: a migration, or another change of `<n>` R-1270's read order adopts, such as a lowered `<n>` in a pool that reaches one server, which counts as a migration here. A read that overlapped the last applied read never changes the last-read `<n>`, so a late read lets nothing through; and in a pool that reaches several servers `<n>` only rises, so standbys replaying a migration at different times let one action through for it, and a lowered `<n>` lets none through until `<n>` passes the old value.

**The events,** the machine's other inputs:

| # | Event | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | A migration commits a `tx` step | The reset and the raised `<n>`, the relabel and the refreshes, as the migration steps say. The pool learns of it at its next read of `<n>` that counts, by R-1270's read order: the next read that doesn't overlap the last applied one, and in a pool that reaches several servers the next such read that finds `<n>` greater than the last-read one. Behind PgBouncer it adopts the marker, which drops the salt, or takes a fresh one when the `<n>` isn't above every `<n>` the pool has adopted, raises the statement generation, removes every pending and cool-down entry, and sets the window's `<n>` to the new one and starts a window, so the adoption is the one pool-wide action the migration allows and a *salt* requested after it with `<n>` unmoved waits for that window's end; straight to Postgres it removes every pending entry, its next session-class failure starts a new epoch, and its next request passes a closed window once, starting a window under the new `<n>`. A moved `<n>` is adopted wherever a read that counts finds it, outside a transaction or after the whole transaction's rollback, never inside an open one or after a rollback to a savepoint, and is never salted. Nothing is gated, because migrations pace it. `migrate` sends `RECONNECT` where PgBouncer admin URLs are listed, as step 59 says |
| E2 | A schema change made by hand | Nothing until a signal |
| E3 | `RECONNECT`, or PgBouncer's `server_lifetime` | PgBouncer replaces each server connection as it's released, which cures stale plpgsql and stale server statements alike. No morm state changes: cool-down entries run out by themselves |
| E4 | The window ends with an action due | The first checkout after it takes the action: its one compare-and-swap starts the take, and `finish_take`, one step, sets a *salt*'s salt, raises the generation and starts the window |
| E5 | A pool-wide action is taken | *clear*: the statement generation rises. *salt*: a new salt replaces any earlier one and the statement generation rises. *replace*: the connection generation rises, so every connection is replaced at checkout. Every pending and cool-down entry is removed and a window starts. The epoch is kept |
| E6 | A checkout | One atomic read of the generation word, with the window's end while an action is due, as above |
| E7 | Time | A pending entry expires `stale_pending_expiry` after it was created, a cool-down entry `stale_cooldown` after, the epoch `stale_cooldown` after `T`, the window `stale_cooldown` after its action |
| E8 | A recovery conflict on a standby | Unchanged: `Error::Serialization` inside a transaction, `Error::CommitUnknown` during `COMMIT`, `Error::ConnectionLost` on a held connection, as steps 12 and 20 say; as a fresh run's outcome it's on R-1245's no-confirm list |

The cost is the one atomic read a checkout already does, and one more while an action is due; one catalog read per request made outside an open transaction and off a `db.hold()` connection while the window is closed; one atomic add per read of `<n>`, for its ticket; and the stale lock, R-1270's, held for one step at a time and taken only on the stale-session paths. A `42883`, or a `42804` from any routine but R-1245's three, from a statement that isn't in a cache is never retried, R-0981's session-class errors are retried from any statement, on the new connection that replaces an old one, nothing is retried once a row has reached the caller, and a retry that fails again returns its error. A stale statement gets one fresh run, R-0718's, and no other retry. Owner decision SC.

- **Stale statements and sessions inside a transaction.** Postgres has already failed the transaction, so nothing is retried inside it, and morm rolls the whole of it back, savepoints included, before any read of `<n>`, as R-0441 says, so `Error::SchemaChanged` inside `tx.transaction(..)` fails the whole transaction and every read these rows make runs on a snapshot of its own; inside a savepoint rows B3 and B4 make no read, as step 14 says. This step builds the rows of step 14's stale-session machine that run inside a transaction, B1 to B4 and D1 and D2, as step 14 states them, and adds B5 and D3, below. Each signal is step 14's, recognised as it says, never by translated text. morm marks the transaction failed and returns `Error::SchemaChanged` when the next attempt may succeed: where morm repaired something for it, a statement evicted, a pending entry made, or a connection discarded or marked for replacement; behind PgBouncer, on a session-class failure's first time, D2, whose next attempt may reach another server session; on the transient `XX000`, which doesn't repeat; and behind PgBouncer with pending entries off, on D1, whose next attempt runs the statement unnamed. reqs.text: - **Retired types.** A type can be retired along with the columns that still use it. It's renamed `_morm_retired_<migration>_<type>`, following the 63-byte rule, and the ledger records its original name. An enum type's labels are renamed in the same transaction, each to `_morm_retired_<label>`, through the same 63-byte rule, because a label has the same limit, and the ledger already holds the type's labels in order. So code still compiled against the retired type, such as a plpgsql variable or a cached statement, fails with `22P02` naming it, instead of running on the old labels' order with no error. Rows keep every value, because Postgres stores a label by its OID, and read as `_morm_retired_<label>` until `purge`. Down and rollback read a retired column by mapping each placeholder back to its recorded label in their own expression, and never rename the labels back, which would make stale code silent again. Restoring a retired type to live, as a rollback of a retire does, renames the type and its labels back, which is right, because it's live again with the same OID. A second run of a migration, while an earlier run's retired objects remain, gives its own a suffix holding its run, which the ledger records, and the migration's files, which name them unsuffixed, are mapped to those names when they run, as step 52 says. `verify` doesn't report it as drift, and `purge` drops the retired columns first and the type after them, without `CASCADE`, stopping with the list if anything else depends on it. Owner decision SA.

> **Use `TextEnum` unless you have a reason not to.** Changing a `TextEnum` is an ordinary migration. - **The swap.** Postgres stores an enum value as an internal ID, so moving to a new type always rewrites the data. The one-transaction form is one `tx` step:

1. Set `lock_timeout` and lock every affected table in sorted order, so a busy table fails before anything has changed.
2. Drop column defaults on the affected columns, and anything step 53 drops.
3. For a map that keeps old values, add the retired column and fill it.
4. Rename the old type and create the new one under the real name, with the declared labels.
5. Change each column with `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING`, applying any map, with one `ALTER TABLE` per table so each is rewritten once. The cast fails if a row holds a removed label with no map, which rolls everything back.
6. Copy the owner, comment and grants from the old type, then drop it.
7. Restore defaults and anything step 53 dropped, and check the fingerprint before commit.

`ANALYZE` of each affected table then runs as its own step, because the rewrite removes the column's statistics.

reqs.text: - **Code Postgres doesn't track.** Before any op, or its inverse, that changes a column's type, length or precision, changes a composite type's attributes, drops and recreates a type or view, or renames or removes an enum label, morm walks everything that reaches what changed, of any kind, and repeats until nothing new turns up. This is one rule with no list of kinds, so a kind this text never names is found the same way, and every example here is only an example. The walk starts from what the op reports: each table and column whose type, length or precision changes, each type and view it changes or replaces, including a domain or composite type, and the text of each label that changes. Each round sends everything found so far down two routes. The first is `pg_depend`. It gives every object with a row against something found, and the object something found is part of, which is the target of its row with `deptype` `a` or `i`: a default brings in its column, a check, an index, a policy or a trigger brings in its table, a domain's check brings in its domain, and a view's stored query brings in its view. A break carries on from these: once a table's check calls a found function, whatever writes to that table fails too. From a changed column's own table, rows against that column or against the table as a whole count for any object, and rows against its other columns count for any object R-1102 calls code, because a whole row can carry the changed column while `pg_depend` holds only the column a query names. So a view, a function, a trigger, a policy, a rule, a check, a default or an index that carries code is found on that table whatever column it's on, and a plain index or a foreign key on another column isn't found, and doesn't lead on to anything. From any other table or view found, rows against any of its columns count, because what reads any of it is reached. A trigger also brings in its function, because a row reaches that function whatever it names, and that's the only call the walk follows downward. The second route is the source search. It reads `pg_proc.prosrc`, in every schema but those R-1102 leaves out, for the name of everything found, in whole words, in any case, because a body has no `pg_depend` row for what it names, and a name hits every overload of that name. A `BEGIN ATOMIC` body isn't in `prosrc`, so `pg_depend` gives it instead. An object's name is the word a body writes to use it, such as a function's, an aggregate's, a view's, a table's, a type's or a column's name, or a cast's target type. An operator has no word to match, so its symbol is matched as plain text anywhere in a body, which covers `1 ~~~ 2`, `1~~~2` and `OPERATOR(public.~~~)`, and a longer symbol holding it is a false hit. A name is searched once and an object is found once, so each round can only add to a finite set, and the walk stops at the first round that adds nothing. So it ends whatever shape it meets: a cycle of calls, a function that calls itself, or `pg_depend` rows that lead back to something already found. It has no limit on rounds. On a change to a column's type, length or precision, every function and procedure holding the word `EXECUTE`, by R-1081's search, counts as found from the start, even one that names nothing the change touches, because no tool can see what a built query reads, and whatever calls it is then found by its name. The walk follows objects, not values. A function that a found object only passes the value to as an argument, and that names nothing the change touches, isn't found, such as `pass_f` in `pass_f(max(n))`, because a value can flow through arguments, other tables, application code and other services, further than any tool can follow. That's the walk's stated limit: R-1092's fixed line says it on every widening, and the README says why. The preflight of `migrate`, `rollback` and `rehearse` repeats all of this on the live database, and `makemigrations` stores what the walk starts from in `op_data`, for each direction, because preflight doesn't have the models and `rollback` must work from the ledger's `meta.json` when the files are gone. What counts as a hit is what R-1102 keeps, and everything else found is only walked. A hit on a managed function is a decision, `makemigrations` proposes the rewritten function, and R-1066 and R-1076 prove it. A managed object of another kind that's a hit is a decision too, and it has nothing to call, so the decision is all it gets. After a change to a column's type, length or precision all of these are one decision, as R-1092 says, and after any other op, an enum swap included, each keeps its own. A `plpgsql` body can name a removed label, and a `s::text = 'old'` comparison never fails, it just stops matching.

reqs.text: - **Refreshing managed functions.** Every managed plpgsql function R-1038 finds, which includes every one an affected table's triggers call, is refreshed in that op's transaction. A trigger function needs this even when it never names the type: on Postgres 18 a trigger comparing `NEW.s` failed on every call in every open session until it was refreshed. In the same transaction, each unmanaged plpgsql function the walk finds, where the migrating role owns it or is a member of its owner, gets a no-op `ALTER FUNCTION <regprocedure> COST <its current cost>`, and each such procedure `ALTER PROCEDURE <regprocedure> SECURITY <its current setting>`, because a procedure has no cost. Either writes a new catalog row and changes nothing in the definition, so every session compiles the function again on its next call, behind PgBouncer and on a standby too, as a reconnect would. It isn't a change to the unmanaged object, and the object stays in R-1040's decision, because a refresh fixes a stale copy and not the body's logic. On Postgres 15 to 18 the `ALTER FUNCTION` cured a `DECLARE v st` function that the reset doesn't, and on 18.6 `ALTER PROCEDURE ... SECURITY INVOKER` on a procedure that was already `INVOKER` wrote a new row as `ALTER FUNCTION ... COST` does. Owner decision SB.

reqs.text:
- **The steps,** each with its own boundary:

1. `tx`: create the new type under a temporary name.
2. `tx` per table: add the shadow column and a sync trigger on every insert and update, applying the map.
3. `batch` per table: copy by key, with a resumable cursor.
4. `no-tx`: build each index on the shadow column with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, or `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for a unique one, named `_morm_new_<name>`, made from the real index's name `<name>` through the 63-byte name function, so step 14 maps a unique violation on it to the field of `<name>`, such as a write of a label the map turns into one another row holds.
5. `tx`, then a separate `tx`: for a `NOT NULL` column add `CHECK (shadow IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`. For a nullable one add `CHECK (<col> IS NULL OR shadow IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, dropped at cutover. Then `VALIDATE`. Any CHECK naming the column goes the same way.
6. `ANALYZE`, because statistics follow the column through a rename.
7. `tx` per materialized view above the column: build it beside the old one on the shadow column, as late as possible, with R-1051's text.
8. `tx`: the cutover, below.

reqs.text: - **The copy walks by key up to a bound,** the highest key read once the sync trigger has committed, and reads that bound and each batch after the trigger has committed. `CREATE TRIGGER` waits for every open write, so any row above the bound was written through the trigger, while a walk that went on until nothing was left chased new inserts for 6,283 batches under nonstop load and finished only when the load stopped, where the bounded copy took 104. A range worked out before the trigger attached misses rows inserted just before it did. `VALIDATE` is the safety net: it fails if any row was missed.

reqs.text: - **The cutover** is one short transaction across all affected tables, and it gives way to live transactions under step 39's rule, with the same settings and the same `--terminate-blockers`, because a waiting lock holds up new readers behind it, and a wait past `deadlock_timeout` lets Postgres kill a transaction. If it can't get in, it stops with nothing changed, and `--resume` carries on from there. It takes each carried view's lock with its own `DROP VIEW`, from the outside in, dropping anything carried above a view before that view, then locks the tables in sorted order and walks `pg_depend` again, because a reader locks the view first, locking the table first deadlocked every time, and `LOCK TABLE` on a view takes every table under it at once. Sorted order is each table that a foreign key from another affected table references, in name order, then the rest in name order, as step 60's cutover takes the key table first, because readers, and writers going from a parent to its children, lock the parent first, and a cutover that locked the referencing tables first got in on none of 176 attempts under nonstop traffic. It drops the sync trigger, the old indexes and the rest of step 53's dependents, apart from materialized views, renames the old column to a retired column with `NOT NULL` and its default removed, and renames the shadow column to the real name. It sets `NOT NULL` from the validated check, for a column that had it, renames each `_morm_new_<name>` index to `<name>`, re-attaches unique constraints with `ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX`, and copies the column's comment and grants. It retires the old type, renaming each of its labels to `_morm_retired_<label>` as step 38 retires an enum type, so code still compiled against it fails with `22P02` naming it instead of running on the old order, gives the new type the real name and restores defaults. Then it recreates the dependents, copies the owner, comment and grants, and refreshes functions. Owner decision SA.

reqs.text: - **Old values stay.** The retired column holds every old value and keeps the retired type alive until `purge`, which drops any retired materialized view, then the column, then the type. Its rows read as `_morm_retired_<label>`, because the cutover renames the retired type's labels, and down and rollback map each back to its recorded label. So a map's data effect here is `retires`, and down restores a value only where the row still holds what it was mapped to. A rollback of the swap doesn't move a retired copy of a materialized view back, as step 38 does for a column swap, because the copy reads the retired column, which this swap's down doesn't bring back, and its column holds the retired type. `rollback` runs `down.sql`, the one-transaction form, and in that transaction it drops the live copy before it changes the column, as it drops any managed materialized view over it, and after the change creates the copy again from its definition on the restored type, with its indexes, owner, comment and grants, populated, or `WITH NO DATA` where the retired copy was unpopulated. On Postgres 17.12 and 18.6, dropping the live copy, changing the column and creating the copy again in one transaction worked, the rebuilt copy reading the real labels and the unpopulated one staying unpopulated, while changing the column under the live copy failed with `cannot alter type of a column used by a view or rule`. The rebuilt copy's contents come from today's table, so the preflight of `rollback` opens the same decision step 39 opens for a rebuild on the way up, naming the view and saying the retired copy keeps the old rows until `purge`, with a default that refuses; an unpopulated copy opens none. The retired copy, the retired column and the retired type stay until `purge`: the rollback's row in `_morm.history` records each by name with the migration's id, and they are retired objects for every reader of the ledger, not only `purge`: `verify` and `check_schema` don't report them as drift, a later op's `pg_depend` walk passes over them, a later change Postgres refuses under the retired copy is refused with exit code `2` naming it, as step 38 says for a retired copy, and `purge` drops the copies, then the column, then the type. A second run of the migration before `purge` would collide with those names, so it names its own retired objects with a suffix holding its `_morm.history` row's id, as `_morm_retired_<migration>_<name>_<run>`, through the 63-byte rule. `up.sql` and `down.sql` stay as `makemigrations` wrote them, naming retired objects unsuffixed, byte for byte what the checksum covers: the ledger records, for each run, the actual name each retired object got, and the text sent to Postgres maps each unsuffixed name to the actual one, never the stored file. The mapping rewrites identifier tokens, bare or quoted, `"..."` and `U&"..."`, as Postgres reads them, a `U&"..."` token together with any `UESCAPE` clause after it, which it drops when it writes the name back as a plain quoted identifier, and a bare identifier as Postgres scans it, `$` included, so `x$_morm_retired_m2_s$` is one identifier and not a dollar quote, so a quoted name and a schema- or table-qualified one are mapped as `makemigrations` writes them, matched on the identifier's decoded name, a bare one folded to lower case as Postgres folds it, and written back quoted. It never touches a string, a comment or a dollar quote, and a migration file never names a retired object inside one: `makemigrations` refuses to write one, and every command that runs migration text refuses such a file with exit code `2`, naming the file and the name. Every command that executes migration text maps it: `migrate` and its `--resume`, `rollback`, each pass of `rehearse`, and the forward migration `revert` writes. An unsuffixed `_morm_retired_<migration>_<name>` in any migration's text maps to the actual name from the run of `<migration>` the ledger records as applied, or, in `rollback` and `--resume`, the run being rolled back or resumed, and a new run maps to the names it gives its own retired objects. So the second run's `rollback`, and `revert` of the migration after its second run, read the second run's retired column, not the first run's, which is still there under the unsuffixed name and would be read with no error. On 17.12 and 18.6, with files that quote every name and qualify it by schema or table as generated SQL does, mapped by a token-level mapper that skips strings, comments and dollar quotes: the second run as written failed with `type "_morm_retired_m2_st" already exists`; with its names mapped it ran; its rollback as written ran with no error but restored rows 1 and 4 from the first run's retired column, as `b`, while mapped it restored `c`, `a`, `a` and `c`, each row from its own run's retired column, a row changed and a row inserted between the runs included; a file naming the retired column inside a dollar quote, a comment or a string was refused; and the stored files' checksums still matched. reqs.text: - **Text on the shadow column.** A partial index, an expression index, a CHECK or a materialized view that names the column takes its text from Postgres by step 39's route. On its throwaway scratch, the new column, the new type and each new object are renamed to their temporary names, and morm reads `pg_get_indexdef`, `pg_get_constraintdef` or `pg_get_viewdef`. So a cast reads the temporary type's name with no text replaced, even when the column and its type share a name. The scratch proof confirms the result: after cutover, each definition must match the one built from the models, and a view whose text differs is checked for the same meaning, as step 39 says.

This differs from `PgEnum`, whose labels are snake_case. `#[model]` emits the CHECK in metadata like a range CHECK, named `__CHK_{table}_{column}_enum__`, reading labels through a trait constant on the type. `ModelMeta` and the manifest also carry these labels on the column, so step 32's with-data proof can read them.

reqs.text: - **`TextEnum` fallback.** `#[text_enum(unknown)]` on one unit variant works like `#[pg_enum(unknown)]`: any stored value the binary doesn't know decodes to that variant, as one branch on read, instead of returning `Error::UnknownEnumValue`, and writing that variant returns `Error::Validation`. It's opt-in. Without it, an unknown stored value returns `Error::UnknownEnumValue`, with the Rust type's name and the value. This variant has no label: it isn't in the CHECK list, the managed type or `check_schema`, and it can't take `value`, `was` or `deprecated`.

reqs.text: - **Changing a domain or composite type.** A changed domain `check` drops and adds the constraint `NOT VALID`, then runs `VALIDATE` in a separate step. When no column uses a composite type, directly or through an array, a range, a domain or another composite, adding an attribute at the end, dropping the last attribute and changing an attribute's type use `ALTER TYPE`. Any other shape, such as a middle attribute, a new order or a rename, drops and recreates the type in one transaction, keeping its owner, comment and grants. Each of these has an exact inverse. A changed base type, or a change to a composite a column uses, is refused with exit code `2` and changes nothing. Postgres doesn't enforce this: it runs `ADD ATTRIBUTE` and `DROP ATTRIBUTE` on a composite a column uses, and the dropped data is lost. A change that needs a dependent dropped is also refused with exit code `2` and changes nothing: a recreate when anything depends on the type, or `ALTER TYPE` on an attribute a function or view depends on. Step 37 replaces that refusal for managed dependents. `migrate` preflight repeats these checks on the live database, because scratch can't see what no model declares, and `rollback` repeats them before an inverse that drops an attribute. The with-data proof leaves out domain columns whose `check` its rows fail.

reqs.text: **A view above an online column swap.** R-0566's swap carries a managed view above the column instead of stopping at the retire. Its cutover is one short transaction that gives way to live transactions, as R-1072 says. It takes each carried view's lock with its own `DROP VIEW`, from the outside in, dropping anything carried above a view before that view, then locks the table and walks `pg_depend` again. A reader locks the view first, so the table comes last, and it never runs `LOCK TABLE` on a view, because that takes every table under the view at once and deadlocked. reqs.text: - **Retired materialized views.** An online column swap (step 39) retires the old copy of a materialized view, because a view can hold rows its table no longer has, and one may be frozen on purpose. It moves to the `_morm_retired` schema, named with its migration and following the 63-byte rule, and keeps its rows, indexes, owner, comment and grants. The ledger records its original name. A view or `BEGIN ATOMIC` function it still reads is retired with it, the same way. `verify` doesn't report any of these as drift, and a later op's `pg_depend` walk passes over them, including a retired copy, and what it reads, that a rolled-back online enum swap leaves, which the rollback's `_morm.history` row records. The old copy still reads the retired column, and it's an object being retired under R-0571, so it doesn't stop the swap. `purge` drops the copies from the outside in, then what they read, then the retired columns and type, without `CASCADE`, stopping with the list if anything else depends on them. `rollback`, and `revert` of the swap, drop the new one and move the old one back to its schema and name in the inverse's short transaction, exactly as it was: the same rows, unpopulated if it was, and with no refresh. After the copy, `VALIDATE` and `ANALYZE`, as late as possible before the cutover, a step of its own creates it under a temporary name on the shadow column, using R-1064's query, with its indexes, owner, comment and grants, and runs `ANALYZE`. reqs.text: - **Managed functions are proven by a real call.** Every managed function or procedure R-1038 finds, and every one step 38's source search finds before a retire or a rename, is proven on scratch after `up`, in the with-data proof, once its rows are written. Each call runs in its own transaction that's rolled back, with a 30-second statement timeout. A failure stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the function and the error, so a broken one never ships, and the developer fixes the definition in the same migration. A function or procedure callable with no arguments gets `SELECT * FROM f()` or `CALL p()` automatically. If it declares `proof` lines, those run instead, each in its own rolled-back transaction, in the order written, and any failure stops `makemigrations`, naming that `proof`. One that needs arguments and has no `proof` stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, asking for one. Nothing is skipped silently. A passing call can't show that a body still means what it did, such as a `s::text = 'old'` comparison, so a hit stays a decision too. A trigger function can't be called directly, so it's proven by a write that fires it: for each managed trigger on it, morm runs an insert, an update of every column or a delete, as the trigger's events need, under `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)`, after `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE`, and the plan must list that trigger. A write that doesn't fire it, such as under a `WHEN`, stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, asking for a `proof`, and each `proof` is a write checked the same way. A trigger function with no managed trigger on it, one that only a `TRUNCATE` trigger fires, and an event trigger function need a `proof` too, run as written.

reqs.text: - **What a call may touch.** A rollback undoes what a call does in the database, including volatile functions' writes, session settings and `NOTIFY`, and scratch is thrown away, so a moved sequence or an advisory lock doesn't matter. It can't undo what leaves the server, so morm's own calls and writes run as `_morm_proof`, a role morm creates on scratch if it's missing, which isn't superuser, has rights on every table, sequence and schema in that database, and has no `EXECUTE` on any function from an extension or in a language other than `sql` or `plpgsql`. The scratch user keeps those, and any it can't take from `_morm_proof` stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`. So a body that reaches `dblink`, an HTTP extension or `COPY ... PROGRAM` fails with `42501`, directly, through another function or through `EXECUTE`, and `makemigrations` stops with exit code `2`, asking for a `proof`. A `SECURITY DEFINER` function, or one in another language, gets past that role, so it always needs a `proof`. Each `proof` is one statement, and it runs with the scratch user's rights, because the developer wrote it and vouches for it: it must not reach outside Postgres, and morm can't check that. One that ends the transaction fails the same way as a failed call. A procedure that commits can't run in a transaction, so on `2D000` morm runs the same call with no transaction on a throwaway copy of that database, made with `CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE` and dropped afterwards.
