reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside the managed function rows. A migration can stop and ask you to add a `proof` line to a managed function or procedure before it goes through, because a change under a function can break it in ways Postgres only shows when it's called, and morm won't ship one it can't call. morm really runs that call, on a scratch database, in a transaction it rolls back, with a 30-second timeout, so the call has to be safe to run, and it must not reach outside Postgres. With no `proof`, morm's own call runs as a role that can't use extension functions or other languages, so a function that uses `dblink`, an HTTP extension or `COPY ... PROGRAM` stops and asks for a `proof`. With a `proof`, morm runs what you wrote with your scratch user's rights and can't check it, so write a call that takes no outside action. Unmanaged functions can't be proven, because scratch can't see them, so they become a migration decision that names each one and says it may fail until it's rewritten. morm can only see them on the live database, so `migrate`, `rollback` or `rehearse` stops with exit code `3` and prints an ID, and you answer with `--decide ID=OPT` on that same command. morm keeps the answer in `_morm.decisions` on that database, and it covers only that migration, that version of it, that direction and that ID. So an answer on `migrate` doesn't cover `rollback`, an answer on `rehearse` doesn't reach production, and editing the migration or changing the function asks again.

reqs.text: **Same meaning when the text differs.** Postgres keeps an alias once it has one, so after cutover a `USING` view reads `FROM (t t JOIN t2 USING (n))` where the models' reads `FROM (t JOIN t2 USING (n))`, and a later rename of another column on that table prints the whole column list again. The view is the same, so neither is a change. Where the text of a view or `BEGIN ATOMIC` function differs from the model's, morm checks the meaning on the database that holds it. It builds the model's definition there under a temporary name, `WITH NO DATA` for a materialized view, reads both stored query trees, `pg_rewrite.ev_action` or `pg_proc.prosqlbody`, removes every `location`, `stmt_location`, `stmt_len`, `isNatural`, `alias` and `eref` field, compares what's left, and drops the temporary object. Both trees are on one database, so tables, columns and types compare by number, and the join's `usingClause` and every output name stay in. Equal is a match. Anything else is a difference, and so is a model definition that can't be built there. In the scratch proof a difference fails the proof and writes no file. Step 30's diff runs this check before it counts a text difference as a change, so `makemigrations` proposes nothing for a matching view. A match found while a migration is made stores the two texts, the database's and the model's, in `op_data`, and `migrate` copies that pair to the ledger. `verify` can't build anything on a live database, so it treats a live view as matching when its text and the model's are a pair the ledger holds, and any other text is drift. On a `pg_major` mismatch, step 34's replay runs the check in its temporary database in place of the pair.

reqs.text: **A cutover gives way.** A cutover can deadlock with an app transaction: one that touched the table and then reads the view waits on the cutover, while the cutover waits on it. Once either has waited for `deadlock_timeout`, Postgres kills one of them. So by default a migration never kills a live app transaction. Each attempt runs with `lock_timeout` set to `[migrations] cutover_lock_timeout`, default `"50ms"`, well under `deadlock_timeout`, so the attempt rolls back before Postgres looks for a deadlock. An attempt that hits the timeout with `55P03`, or that Postgres picks as a deadlock's victim with `40P01`, changes nothing, and morm waits `cutover_pause`, default `"250ms"`, and tries again, up to `cutover_attempts`, default `600`, so a cutover that can't get in gives up after about 3 minutes. The three settings are plain values in `morm.toml`, and they hold for the cutover's inverse too. An attempt holds its first lock through every later wait, so `migrate` and `rollback` preflight read the server's `deadlock_timeout`, and each lock in that cutover waits `min(cutover_lock_timeout, deadlock_timeout / (2 × locks))`, where `locks` is the number of locks the cutover takes. So a whole attempt stays under half of `deadlock_timeout` however many locks it takes, with no setting to change, and when that wait is shorter than `cutover_lock_timeout`, the output says so, naming the three numbers and the wait. Postgres rounds `lock_timeout` to a whole millisecond and reads 0 as no timeout, so morm rounds the wait down to a whole millisecond, and when that's under 1 ms preflight refuses with exit code `2` before the swap's first step, naming the three numbers. reqs.text: - **Every path is checked statically.** A real call proves only the path it takes, and Postgres checks a plpgsql statement only when it first runs, so a column dropped from a branch the call misses passes R-1066 with no error. So every managed plpgsql function and procedure R-1066 proves is also checked by `plpgsql_check`, at the same point in the with-data proof. It needs no preload and runs nothing. morm calls `plpgsql_check_function_tb` with the function's `regprocedure`, `fatal_errors => false` and `all_warnings => true`, so overloads stay apart and every finding comes back at once. A procedure, an event trigger function and a polymorphic function need nothing more. A trigger function fails with `22023` `missing trigger relation` with no table, so it's checked once for each managed trigger on it, with that trigger's table as the second argument, plus `oldtable` and `newtable` from `pg_trigger` when the trigger has transition tables, because without them a healthy function gets `42P01`. A trigger function with no managed trigger has no table to check against, so it must declare a `proof`, as a body using `EXECUTE` must, and without one `makemigrations` stops with exit code `2`, asking for one. That `proof` is all it gets. A `language sql` function fails with `22023` here, so morm never sends one, and R-1066 alone covers it. With no managed plpgsql function in scope, none of this runs, and the extension isn't needed.

reqs.text: - **Without the extension.** With a managed plpgsql function in scope, `makemigrations` writes nothing if the check can't run: `plpgsql_check` isn't in `pg_available_extensions` on scratch, there's no template and the scratch user can't make it, or the clone fails or holds no extension. It names each function and says what to do: install the extension on the scratch server, `postgresql-NN-plpgsql-check` from PGDG, with R-1077's statements printed in full when the scratch user isn't a superuser, or add `proof` lines to the function and accept the risk. Accepting is a decision that names the function and says only the paths its `proof` lines take are proven. A function with no `proof` can't be accepted, even one R-1066 would call by itself, so `makemigrations` stops with exit code `2` while any function in scope has none. Once each has a `proof` the decision is open, its default refuses, and `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` until it's accepted. Accepted functions still get their real calls.

reqs.text: - **Findings stop `makemigrations`.** Any finding at level `error` is an open decision, so it stops `makemigrations` with exit code `3`, naming the function, the line and the message, with no file written. No other level stops it, apart from R-1080. A healthy function can get a false `error`, from a temp table, a table created in the body or by the caller, a record filled by `EXECUTE`, a record with different fields by branch, `set_config` of `search_path`, or a constant `1/0`. There are two ways past a false one. A `PERFORM 'PRAGMA:...'` line in the function stays there, so later checks pass too, and to Postgres it's only a string, so the function runs with no extension: `PRAGMA:TABLE: x (a int)` declares a table, `PRAGMA:TYPE: r (a int)` declares a record's fields, and `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK` stops checking until its block ends. Or a decision that names the function, the line and the message accepts that one finding for that migration, and its default refuses. Both can hide a real break, which is why the README says so loudly.

reqs.text: - **A narrowing is a decision.** An `int` variable reading a column now `bigint` isn't an error. It works until a value needs the new type, and with default arguments the check reports nothing. With `all_warnings` it's a finding at level `performance`, with SQLSTATE `42804` and detail `cast "bigint" value to "integer" type`. A widening looks the same, so morm reads both type names from the detail, and it's a narrowing when `pg_cast` holds that pair with a `castcontext` other than `i`. Each narrowing is a decision that names the function, the line and both types, and says the function fails once a value doesn't fit. Its default refuses, so `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` until it's accepted. Every other `all_warnings` finding is ignored. A length or precision limit doesn't show up: `varchar(3)` reading `text` is a cast `pg_cast` calls implicit, and `numeric(6,2)` reading `numeric(20,4)` gave no finding at all, so R-1092 works from the column's definitions instead. reqs.text: - **morm won't run a disabled check.** With `plpgsql_check.mode` set to `disabled`, the check returns no findings and only a `NOTICE`, so it looks like a pass. Before checking, in the session that runs the check, morm reads `current_setting('plpgsql_check.mode', true)`, which shows a role or connection setting even before the library loads, and is NULL when nothing sets it. It also reads each function's `pg_proc.proconfig`, because `SET plpgsql_check.mode = 'disabled'` on a function turns the check off for that function alone, and `current_setting` doesn't show it. Either one stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the setting and any function.

**The extension in CI.** Every job whose tests run `makemigrations` over a managed plpgsql function installs the extension into its running service, which needs no restart. These are `integration` and `pooler` in `ci.yml`, `property` and `full-chain` in `nightly.yml`, `test` in `release.yml`, and the `standby` job step 12 adds, into its primary, the job's `postgres` service, where `makemigrations` runs; the standby needs no package, because no test calls the extension there:

```yaml
- name: Install plpgsql_check
  env:
    PG_CONTAINER: ${{ job.services.postgres.id }}
  run: |
    docker exec "$PG_CONTAINER" apt-get update
    docker exec "$PG_CONTAINER" apt-get install -y "postgresql-$MORM_TEST_PG_MAJOR-plpgsql-check"
```

A new `ci.yml` job, `no-plpgsql-check`, runs the plain `postgres` image on Postgres 15–18 with no install step, because R-1078 needs a server without the extension. Its test has its own Cargo feature, `no_plpgsql_check`, with `required-features`, as `pooler` does. The feature sits on `morm-tests`, because `integration` runs `morm-migrate` with `--all-features`. The `ci` job waits for the new job, and `tests/tests/repo_policy.rs` gets its command, with `docker exec ` added to `SETUP`.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the managed function rows:

> **Silencing a check can hide a real break.** When a migration changes something a managed plpgsql function names, morm runs `plpgsql_check` on that function, and any `error` stops the migration. There are two ways past an error, and neither one fixes anything. If the finding was real, the function ships broken and fails in production the first time that line runs.
>
> **What each one does.** A `PERFORM 'PRAGMA:...'` line goes in the function. It changes what `plpgsql_check` looks at, on this migration and every later one, and when the function runs it's only a string, so it does nothing. A decision leaves the function alone and lets that one finding through on that one migration. It's recorded in the migration's `meta.json`, and the next migration that reaches the function checks it again.
>
> ```sql
> -- Tell the checker what it can't see. It still checks every other line.
> PERFORM 'PRAGMA:TABLE: report_rows (id bigint, total numeric)';
> PERFORM 'PRAGMA:TYPE: r (id bigint, total numeric)';
>
> -- Stop checking until this block ends. Keep the block as small as you can.
> BEGIN
>   PERFORM 'PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK';
>   PERFORM 1 / 0;
> END;
> ```
>
> ```
> makemigrations --decide ID=OPT     # morm prints the ID and the options
> ```
>
> **When it's right.** Only when you've read the finding and can say why it's false, such as a temp table the function creates, or a record it fills with `EXECUTE`. Prefer `PRAGMA:TABLE` and `PRAGMA:TYPE`, because the checker keeps reading every other line. Use `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK` only when those can't describe the problem. Use a decision when you won't change the function.
>
> **What you give up.** No line under `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK` is checked, on this migration or any later one, so a column dropped from one of them passes. The checker believes a `TABLE` or `TYPE` line over the database, so one that no longer matches hides a break too. An accepted finding stays unfixed, and morm won't stop that migration for it again. After that, only a `proof` that runs that line can catch a real break, and a call proves only the path it takes.
>
> **Two pragmas can hide a value that no longer fits.** A check of a function that reads a changed column reports a narrowing, such as an `int` variable reading a column that's now `bigint`, as a `performance` warning, and morm turns that into a decision. `performance_warnings` anywhere in a managed plpgsql function's source, as in `PERFORM 'PRAGMA:DISABLE:PERFORMANCE_WARNINGS';`, would hide every one of them, so it stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the function: take the line out. morm decodes escapes before it looks, so the same words spelt with escapes in an `E'...'` or `U&'...'` string, or in a plain one in a function declared with `SET standard_conforming_strings = off`, are refused too. `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK` around a read of a changed column hides it too, so that function gets a line of its own in the change's decision, saying its check is off in places, and the decision's default refuses.

reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside that notice. A call proves only the path it takes, so a passing `proof` says nothing about a branch it didn't reach, and a function can have several `proof` lines to cover the paths that matter. `plpgsql_check` reads every branch without running it, but it can only read what's in the source. A query built at run time with `EXECUTE` isn't checked, so a function using `EXECUTE` must have a `proof`. morm finds it with a word search, so the word in a comment or a string asks for a `proof` too. That `proof` proves only the query its one call builds, and any other query the body can build stays unproven until production runs it. A trigger function with no trigger on it has no table to check against, so it must have a `proof`, and that `proof` is all it gets, so any path it doesn't take stays unproven until production runs it. `plpgsql_check` can't see a length or precision limit, so `varchar(3)` reading a longer `text` column, or `numeric(6,2)` reading a wider `numeric`, gets no finding. So after any change to a column's type, length or precision, even a widening, morm walks everything that reaches that column, of any kind, and repeats until nothing new turns up. It follows `pg_depend` to every object that depends on what it has found, and it searches function source for the name of everything it has found, including operator and aggregate symbols. Everything it finds goes on one list, as one decision per migration. A function using `EXECUTE` starts the walk too, even one that doesn't name the column, because no tool can see what a built query reads, and whatever calls it is found by name. Being on the list doesn't mean something is broken. The search reads text, so a common name can bring in something that has nothing to do with the change. The list holds only what carries code or an expression: functions, procedures, views, triggers, policies, rules, expression and partial indexes, and non-constant defaults and checks. Any such object on the changed table is listed, even one on another column, because a whole row such as `to_jsonb(x)` carries the changed column without naming it. A default or a check on another column that only calls built-ins, such as `DEFAULT now()`, isn't listed, because it can't depend on the changed column. A built-in that runs query text it's given, such as `query_to_xml`, `ts_stat` or `ts_rewrite` with a query, or reads every table in a schema or the database, such as `schema_to_xml` or `database_to_xml`, or a table or a cursor it's given by name at run time, such as `table_to_xml` or `cursor_to_xml`, counts as code, so a default or a check that calls one is listed, on any column. A plain index, a `NOT NULL` or a constant default isn't listed, because it can't hold a stale type. morm walks only what it can see. On scratch that's your managed objects, so `makemigrations` lists those. Scratch can't see an unmanaged object, so that part of the walk only works in the preflight of `migrate`, `rollback` and `rehearse`, on the live database, and that's where the first warning about one comes, as a list of its own. The walk follows objects, not values, and that's its stated limit. So every widening's decision carries this line, and a widening with nothing to list still prints it in `makemigrations` output and as a comment in the migration, without stopping: `Values can now exceed the old limit anywhere that reads them, including code morm can't see.` `pass_f(max(n))` shows why. A function that only receives the column's value as an argument, and names nothing, isn't found, though what calls it is, because a value can flow through arguments, other tables, application code and other services, further than any tool can follow. So read what a listed object calls, and treat everything that reads that column as able to see a value the old limit kept out. A query built from data in a table leaves nothing in the catalog or in any source to find, so that shows up when production runs it. Your Rust code is on that side of the line too, because the walk reads nothing but the database. The compiler checks a model field only against the SQL type declared for it: `i64` on `integer` is a compile error, and `i32` on `bigint` compiles. That pair gets a range CHECK, so the column can't store a value the field can't read, and if one still arrives, because the CHECK was removed outside morm, decoding returns `OutOfRange`, never a wrapped value. `db.check_schema()` runs at startup and refuses a column of a kind the field can't decode, such as `text` for an integer field, which is a question of compatibility, so it doesn't show that a field or the code using it is ready for a wider value. A decision proves nothing. It says what's listed may break and leaves the reading to you, and it can't show you where a limit sits or which queries a built string can become. Read each object and what it calls before you accept it, and after that only production shows whether a value fits. If you accept a decision because `plpgsql_check` isn't installed, your `proof` lines are all that's proven. Neither check shows that a body still means what it did, such as a `s::text = 'old'` comparison that stops matching.

reqs.text: - **A changed column is one decision, in either direction.** `plpgsql_check` can't see a length or precision limit, so morm uses what it already knows: the old and new definition of the column the op changes. Any change to a column's type, length or precision opens one decision for the migration, in that direction, listing everything R-1038's walk finds that R-1102 keeps, of any kind, managed or not. A migration that changes several columns still opens one, listing each object once and naming each table, each column and both definitions. It says anything on the list with a limit of its own, such as a variable, a cast or a column it writes to, can fail or round once a value doesn't fit, that being listed doesn't mean it's broken, and that each one needs reading before this is accepted. A widening such as `numeric(6,2)` to `numeric(20,4)` opens one too, because that's the change that breaks a `numeric(6,2)` variable, and it passes the check and every call until a value needs it. A widening's decision also carries this fixed line, word for word and once, however many columns widen: `Values can now exceed the old limit anywhere that reads them, including code morm can't see.` That's the walk's stated limit, in plain words, and it isn't a gap to close: `pass_f(max(n))` isn't found, because R-1038's walk follows objects and not values. A column is widened unless its new definition can hold nothing the old one couldn't. That's when it keeps its type and no limit grows or goes away, which for `numeric` means no more digits before the point and none after it, when `text` becomes a `varchar` or a `char` with a length, or when R-1080's `pg_cast` test, read from the old type to the new one, calls it a narrowing. Any other change counts as a widening, so a pair morm can't tell gets the line, which costs one line. morm has no SQL parser, so being found is all it knows: a common name gives a false hit, which costs one line. The changed column and its table aren't listed, so a change with nothing on the table that R-1102 keeps, on a table and a column nothing names, opens no decision. A migration that widens a column and opens no decision, because nothing is listed, still shows the fixed line, word for word and once, however many columns widen: `makemigrations` prints it in its output and writes it as a comment in the migration file, and it stops nothing, so `makemigrations` exits as it would without it. This is the only decision the walk opens for such a change, so nothing on the list is asked about twice by it. A managed function on the list is still refreshed by R-1039 and proven by R-1066 and R-1076, what those report stays a decision of its own, because it names a line or a path, and an object another op in the migration hits keeps that op's decision. Its default refuses, so `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` until it's accepted.

reqs.text: - **In-comment options are refused.** `plpgsql_check` can read options from a comment, in a line holding `@plpgsql_check_options`, and a body could carry one that hides an `error`. Step 55's proof 18 tests that, and it stops for the owner on any result but that one can, so this rule stands unless `proofs.md` records an owner-approved change. Before checking, morm searches the `pg_proc.prosrc` of each function R-1076 checks for `@plpgsql_check_options`, in any case, and a hit stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the function, with no file written. It isn't a decision, and a `proof` doesn't get past it. The text in a string stops it too, and taking the text out is the fix. `plpgsql_check` reads a pragma from a string constant after Postgres has decoded it, so an `E'...'` or `U&'...'` literal can spell one with escapes the raw source doesn't show. So before searching, morm decodes every `E'...'` and `U&'...'` literal in `prosrc` by Postgres's rules, `\x`, octal, `\u` and `\U` in an `E` string, and `\XXXX`, `\+XXXXXX` and `UESCAPE` in a `U&` string, through `morm-core`'s scanner, which already finds strings, comments and dollar quotes, and searches the decoded text as well as the raw text, for each word this rule and R-1080 search for. It reads the `E` and `U&` prefixes in either case, as Postgres does. A plain `'...'` literal is decoded as an `E` string too whenever `standard_conforming_strings` is off for the function: which in morm's check session only the function's own `SET` clause can do, in `pg_proc.proconfig`, which `plpgsql_check` applies before it checks, because the session sets `standard_conforming_strings = on` itself, overriding any database or role default. On 18.6 a function declared `SET standard_conforming_strings = off` returning `'PRAGMA:DISABLE:\x43HECK'` returned `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK`, while `prosrc ~* 'disable:check'` was false. Before checking, morm also searches each such `prosrc` for `performance_warnings`, in any case, and a hit stops `makemigrations` the same way, with exit code `2`, naming the function, with no file written; it isn't a decision, and a `proof` doesn't get past it. On Postgres 15 to 18 with `plpgsql_check` 2.10.16, `PERFORM 'PRAGMA:DISABLE:PERFORMANCE_WARNINGS';` in either case, and `plpgsql_check_pragma('disable:performance_warnings')` in a `PERFORM` or a `DECLARE`, each hid R-1080's narrowing, as did `PERFORM E'PRAGMA:DISABLE:PERFORMANCE\x5fWARNINGS';`, `PERFORM U&'PRAGMA:DISABLE:PERFORMANCE\005FWARNINGS';` and `plpgsql_check_pragma(E'disable:performance\x5fwarnings')`, which a search of the raw text misses, while `'disable:performance' || '_warnings'` didn't, because only a constant is read, and nothing morm acts on is a `performance` finding but that one. Owner decisions SH, EF3, EG5 and EH7, with this fix's choices the owner approves through PR #3: plain literals decoded only under the function's own `SET` clause, and the check session setting `standard_conforming_strings = on` itself.

reqs.text: **A decision about a database object keeps its ID across a rerun.** A decision about a database object, of any kind, gets an ID built from the migration's `id`, the decision's kind and the object's signature, plus a hash of its source, in the form `<id>/<kind>/<signature>/<hash>`. So the ID stays the same across a rerun, and changes if the object's source does. `makemigrations` and the preflight of `migrate`, `rollback` and `rehearse` build it with the same code, because an unmanaged function already accepted on scratch must match on the live database and not be asked about again. The hash is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the source. Every read below runs with `search_path` set to `pg_catalog`, because otherwise the text depends on the session: the same function reads `sf(ty,integer)` in one and `app.sf(app.ty,integer)` in another, and a view, a default and a check read the same way. A function's signature is its `regprocedure` text, and its source is `prosrc`, or `pg_get_function_sqlbody(oid)` when `prosqlbody` isn't null, because a `BEGIN ATOMIC` or `RETURN` body leaves `prosrc` empty, and hashing that would miss an edit. A view's signature is its `regclass` text, and its source is `pg_get_viewdef`. A default's signature is its table's `regclass` text and the column's name, and its source is `pg_get_expr`. A check's signature is the `regclass` text of its table, or the `regtype` text of its domain, and the constraint's name, and its source is `pg_get_constraintdef`. Any other kind's signature is the `identity` column of `pg_identify_object`, and its source is what `pg_get_triggerdef`, `pg_get_indexdef`, `pg_get_ruledef`, `pg_get_constraintdef`, `pg_get_statisticsobjdef`, `pg_get_partkeydef` or `pg_get_expr` prints for it, where one of those fits, and otherwise its signature alone. A decision that lists several objects has the signature `list`, and its hash covers the sorted lines `<signature> <hash>`, one per object, so adding or changing any of them gives a new ID. `meta.json` keeps those lines with an accepted list, so a later preflight can leave out what's already accepted. A `BEGIN ATOMIC` body is deparsed, and so are a view, a default and a check, so a rename in an earlier step of the same migration changes the source, and with it the hash and the ID, of the object or the list holding it. `--resume` then asks again, because the recorded answer is for the old ID. That's safe: it costs one extra stop. A migration's `id` doesn't depend on any answer, so the ID a stopped run prints still holds when the same command runs again with the answer. A name can hold a space or an `=`, so morm prints each ID quoted for the shell, and `--decide` splits at the last `=`. `meta.json` records each answer with the direction of the decision it answers, `up` or `down`, and a decision open in both directions is recorded for both.

reqs.text: - **Answering a decision at `migrate`.** Some decisions only appear against the live database, in preflight, because scratch can't see what they're about. `migrate` takes `--decide ID=OPT` for them, in the same form as `makemigrations`, once per answer. It never prompts for a decision, `--yes` answers none, and each open one is printed with its ID, evidence and options, in `--json` too, before the run stops with exit code `3`. An answer stands only for the same migration id, checksum, direction and decision ID, so an `up` answer doesn't cover `rollback`, and editing the migration cancels it. A decision is open unless `meta.json` holds an answer to it for this direction, or `_morm.decisions` holds a row matching all four. An answer is committed to `_morm.decisions`, with its history row, as soon as its decision opens, while the run holds the advisory lock. So it survives a failed or killed run, a rerun or step 34's `migrate --resume` doesn't need it again unless the decision's ID has changed, as step 32 says of a deparsed body, and a run that stops on a second decision keeps the first answer. A new answer to the same decision replaces the row and gets its own history row. An answer that refuses stops the run with exit code `2`, because the decision is answered and the guard holds. Preflight runs before each migration, so an answer to a later migration in the run waits for it. An ID no migration in the run opened is reported and recorded nowhere, and an option the decision doesn't offer stops the run with exit code `1`, with nothing recorded. `--plan` shows what's open and records nothing.

reqs.text: - **What the walk lists.** R-1038's walk can find anything, and it keeps only what carries code or an expression, because nothing else can hold a stale type. That holds for every decision the walk opens, after any op. morm decides it from the catalog, with no SQL parser. An object is kept if it's one of these: a `pg_proc` row of any `prokind`; a view or a materialized view, a `pg_class` row with `relkind` `v` or `m`; a `pg_rewrite` row; a `pg_trigger` row with `tgisinternal` false; a `pg_policy` row; an index whose `pg_index` row has `indexprs` or `indpred`; a `pg_attrdef` row, or a `pg_constraint` row with `conbin`, whose stored expression isn't constant; a `pg_constraint` row whose `conindid` index has `indexprs` or `indpred`, such as an exclusion constraint over an expression; a `pg_statistic_ext` row with `stxexprs`; a partitioned table whose `pg_partitioned_table` row has `partexprs`; a `pg_publication_rel` row with `prqual`; or a row of any catalog this rule doesn't name, so a kind it never names costs one line and is never hidden. An expression is constant when the text of its `adbin` or `conbin` holds no node but `CONST`, `RELABELTYPE` and `FUNCEXPR`, when every `FUNCEXPR` is a cast, with `funcformat` `1` or `2`, and when every `funcid` is below `16384`, so a cast a user wrote counts as code. So `0` on a `numeric(6,2)` column, `'ab'` on a `varchar(3)`, `1.5::numeric(6,2)` and `'{}'` are constant, and `now()`, `nextval(...)`, `1 + 1`, `ARRAY[1, 2]` and a default through a domain aren't. A check that reads a column holds a `VAR` node, so it's never constant, and `CHECK (true)` is. Anything that isn't sure comes out as not constant, which costs one line. On a table with a column whose type, length or precision changes, a default or a check on its other columns that only calls built-ins isn't kept either, because it can't depend on the changed column. That's a `pg_attrdef` row that isn't a generated column's expression, or a `pg_constraint` row with `conbin`, whose `pg_depend` rows against that table all name its other columns, with none against the changed column or the table as a whole, and whose other `pg_depend` rows are each against a sequence or an object with an OID below `16384`, and which calls no built-in that runs query text or reads whole tables. Those built-ins count as code, because what they run can read any column: the `query_to_xml` family, which is `query_to_xml`, `query_to_xmlschema` and `query_to_xml_and_xmlschema`; `schema_to_xml`, `schema_to_xmlschema`, `schema_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, `database_to_xml`, `database_to_xmlschema` and `database_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, which read every table in a schema or the database, so their output holds the changed column's values and the xmlschema forms its type; `table_to_xml`, `table_to_xmlschema` and `table_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, which read the table they're given as a `regclass` that can be built at run time, such as `('t'::text)::regclass`, so no `pg_depend` row names that table; `cursor_to_xml` and `cursor_to_xmlschema`, which read whatever query a cursor opened elsewhere runs, found only by its name; `ts_stat`; and `ts_rewrite(tsquery, text)`. morm finds such a call in the stored expression, as a `FUNCEXPR` in the text of its `adbin` or `conbin` whose `funcid` is one of them, looked up in `pg_catalog` by name and argument types, so it doesn't rest on `pg_depend`. So `DEFAULT now()`, `DEFAULT nextval(...)`, `DEFAULT ARRAY[1, 2]` and `CHECK (a > abs(-1))` on another column aren't kept, while a default or a check there that calls a user's function, or goes through a domain or a user's cast, is, because it holds a `pg_depend` row against that object, and so is one that calls one of those built-ins, such as `CHECK (b > 0 AND query_to_xml('SELECT max(n)::numeric(6,2) FROM t', true, false, '') IS NOT NULL)` on another column `b`. A check holding a whole row, such as `to_jsonb(t)`, has its `pg_depend` row against the table as a whole, and so does a check that reads no column, so both stay on, and so does a generated column. On the changed column itself the rule above stands, so a default there that isn't constant is kept. Not kept, and walked all the same where a row leads to them, because they're how the walk reaches what lies beyond: a table and its columns, a partition, a TOAST table, a type of any kind, such as a row type, an array, a domain or a composite type, a sequence, a plain index, a plain statistics object, a constant default, a `pg_constraint` row with no expression, which is a `NOT NULL`, a primary key, a unique constraint or a foreign key, an operator, a cast and an operator class. A `NOT NULL` has `conbin` null on Postgres 18, where it's a `pg_constraint` row, and it has no row on a table before that, so both come out the same. A function in `pg_catalog` or `information_schema` is never found, by a row, by the source search or through a trigger, because it ships with Postgres, so the `RI_FKey_*` functions behind a foreign key aren't kept, and a word that names one doesn't lead on to everything that calls it. An object Postgres keeps as an internal part of another, with `deptype` `i`, is walked, and it's left off the list only when the object it's part of is on it. So a view's stored query and an exclusion constraint's index are left off, and a generated column's expression stays on, because its column isn't listed. The list test is the one place the walk's code looks at a kind, apart from a trigger's function.

reqs.text: - **Reading a column whose type changed.** A migration can change a column's type under a running binary, so each field also decodes every column type in its family, through the decoder for the column's real type, which step 14 chooses once per statement. These are the families, and there are no others: a field of a Rust integer type reads `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint` and `numeric(p,0)` with any `p`, and never a `numeric` with a scale or with no precision; `Decimal` reads `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, because every one of their values fits in its 28 digits; `morm::Numeric` reads `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, as `Decimal` does; `String` reads `text`, and `varchar` with any length or none; a `String` built against `char(n)` reads `char` with any length, through a decoder that trims trailing spaces back to `n`, because Postgres pads a `char` value with spaces to its length and treats them as insignificant, so on `char(4)` `'ab  '` reads as `'ab '`, as it did on `char(3)`, and a value with no spaces to trim, such as `'abcd'`, reads whole; `DateTime<Utc>` and `Timestamp` read `timestamptz` with any precision, and `NaiveDateTime` reads `timestamp` with any precision; and an array reads an array of its element's family. A field wider than the column reads every value losslessly. A field narrower than the column checks each value's range, and only a value that can't fit errors: an integer field returns `Error::OutOfRange` naming the column, never a wrapped value, and `Decimal` returns `Error::Decimal` for a value it can't hold exactly, past its 28 significant digits, as on unbounded `numeric`, and never on an integer column. `morm::Numeric`, and `String` on `text` and `varchar`, read every value whole. Nothing read is rounded, as R-0423 says. A write goes as the column type the field was built against, and Postgres converts it to the column's real type, so a value the column can't hold, such as a number with more digits before the point than it allows or a text longer than its length, gets the database's error for that write. Where Postgres would round or cut a write silently instead, to a lower scale, a lower timestamp precision or a shorter length that drops trailing spaces, step 41 never runs the change under a binary built for the old shape, and its `db.check_schema()` refuses such a binary that starts after the change.

reqs.text: - **Decoding follows the column's real type.** When a statement is prepared, morm reads each result column's type from the row description Postgres returns, chooses each field's decoder from it once, and keeps that choice with the statement in its cache entry. A `query_typed` call, which has no cache entry, chooses once from its own result's row description. The internal query entry point then reads all of that statement's rows through `from_row` when every column has the type the binary was built against, so that path is unchanged, and through `from_row_as` with the statement's choice otherwise, deciding once before the first row and never per row. A re-prepare after a migration, on `0A000` as R-0718 says, chooses again, so a statement cached before a cutover picks the new column type's decoder. Every statement is prepared with each parameter's built-in carrier, as `query_typed` sends it. reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside the `Decimal` and `Numeric` rows. `Decimal` holds up to 28 significant digits. The limit comes from `rust_decimal`, which keeps every value in a fixed 16 bytes, as a 96-bit whole number and a scale, so it needs no heap and is `Copy`. A `Decimal` on a `numeric(p,s)` with `p` or `s` above 28 is a compile error. A `numeric` with no precision compiles with `Decimal`, because existing tables have it, and a value that doesn't fit fails at read with `Error::Decimal`. So does a value past 28 digits in a column a migration has widened. A `Decimal` field also reads `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, because every one of their values fits in 28 digits, so a column changed from `numeric` to an integer type doesn't stop a running app built for `numeric`. When that change drops a scale, Postgres would round what such an app writes, so `migrate` holds it for `contract`, and an app built for that scale that starts after it fails the schema check morm runs when a pool starts, rather than rounding what it writes. `morm::Numeric` reads `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` the same way. morm never rounds a `Decimal`, on read or on write. Use `morm::Numeric` when values can exceed 28 digits, or be `NaN` or `Infinity`, or when you don't know a column's range.

reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside the rolling deploy rows. A type change never stops a running app. An app built before a migration changes a column's type, length or precision keeps working through it, and still starts after it, apart from the one case below, while the column stays in the same family: integers; `numeric`, where `Decimal` and `Numeric` fields also read `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`; `text` and `varchar`; `char`; or timestamps. `timestamp` and `timestamptz` stay apart, because a change between them shifts every value by the time zone of the session that runs it, with no error. It reads each value through the decoder for the column's real type, chosen once per statement, so it costs nothing when the types match. After a widening, every value the old column could hold reads as before, and a value only the new column can hold fails on its own: an integer field returns `Error::OutOfRange` naming the column, and `Decimal` returns `Error::Decimal` past its 28 digits. `Numeric` and `String` read every value whole, apart from `char`: Postgres pads a `char` value with spaces to its length and treats them as insignificant, so a field built for `char(3)` reads `char(4)`'s `'ab  '` as `'ab '`, as it did before, and `'abcd'` whole. After a narrowing, every value fits the old field, so every read works, and a write the column can no longer hold, such as a number with too many digits before the point or a text too long, gets the database's error for that write. Some narrowings would change a write with no error instead: a lower scale stores `1.0051` as `1.01`, and `numeric(12,2)` to `integer` stores `1.25` as `1`, a lower timestamp precision stores `.123456` as `.123`, and a shorter `varchar` or `char` stores `'abc  '` as `'abc'`. morm never runs one of those while an app built for the old shape may be running, and in an ordinary online `migrate` it always assumes one is, without trying to find out. So `migrate` refuses it, naming the column, what would change, and the two ways to run it: `migrate --phase contract` once the new release is out everywhere, or `makemigrations --fast` for a maintenance window with apps stopped. An old app never sees one: through the rollout its column keeps the old shape, and every value it writes is stored as written. So an old app keeps running through the deploy, because the narrowing waits until it's gone. Only a build brought back after `contract` has run, such as a rollback of the app to an older release, would write to the narrower column, so it's refused at startup: morm runs `check_schema` when each pool starts, and `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch`, naming the column and what would change, so the app fails loudly rather than storing values other than the ones it writes, unless that pool is set to `check_schema = "off"`. A narrowing that raises a real error on a write that doesn't fit still lets such a build start. `rollback` holds the same narrowings when one is the down of a widening, and runs it with `--phase contract` once every app runs the release built for the narrower shape, or `--fast` with apps stopped. Such a narrowing also changes the rows already stored, so a `1.0051` already in the column becomes `1.01`, and `makemigrations` asks you to accept that as a `lossy` decision before it writes the migration. `migrate` and `rollback` count the rows in the live table it would change, and when there are any they stop and ask, showing the count, answered with `--decide`. When there are none they run with no question, so rolling back a widening asks only when rows were written since that need the wider column. Nothing read is ever rounded. A change to an unrelated kind, such as `text` to `integer`, still fails the startup check.

reqs.text: **A narrowing Postgres would change silently waits for `contract`.** Postgres rounds or cuts some writes to a narrower column with no error, so an app built for the old shape would store a value other than the one it wrote, and nothing would tell it. These are the silent narrowings, and there are no others: a lower scale, where a `numeric` with no precision counts as unlimited and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` count as 0, so `1.0051` written to a column changed from `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)` is stored as `1.01`, `1.00005` from `numeric` to `numeric(20,4)` as `1.0001`, and `1.25` from `numeric(12,2)` to `integer` as `1`; a lower precision on `timestamptz` or `timestamp`, where no precision counts as 6, so `.123456` from `timestamptz` to `timestamptz(3)` is stored as `.123`; and a shorter length on `varchar` or `char`, where `text` and a `varchar` with no length count as unlimited, because Postgres cuts trailing spaces to fit, so `'abc  '` from `text` to `varchar(3)` is stored as `'abc'`, and `'abc '` from `char(4)` to `char(3)` as `'abc'`. The same change to an array's element type is one too, because Postgres applies it to each element, so `{1.0051}` from `numeric(20,4)[]` to `numeric(20,2)[]` is stored as `{1.01}`. morm reads which it is from the column's old and new definition, as `format_type` prints them, with no SQL parser. A change that's one of these and widens something else, such as `numeric(8,4)` to `numeric(10,2)`, is one. Every other narrowing raises a real error on a write that doesn't fit, such as fewer digits before the point, `bigint` to `integer`, `numeric(12,0)` to `integer`, or a shorter length for a value whose extra characters aren't all spaces, so it runs online as R-0612 says, with no gate. In online mode, which is a live run of a migration `makemigrations` wrote without `--fast`, morm always assumes an app built for the old shape is still running, and never tries to detect one. So `makemigrations` puts every step of a silent narrowing in `contract`, the online swap's shadow column, sync trigger and copy included, because the sync trigger would already narrow what an old app writes. The same holds for a migration `revert` writes, because a widening's down is a narrowing. It runs only under `migrate --phase contract`, which the operator runs once the new release is out everywhere. `makemigrations --fast` writes it in the one-transaction form, because `--fast` means a maintenance window with apps stopped. That form takes phase `contract` too, and plain `migrate` runs it. Plain `migrate` refuses the online form in preflight with exit code `2`, before that migration's first step, naming the table and column, the old and new definition, the silent change it would cause, such as `1.0051` stored as `1.01`, and the two ways to run it: `migrate --phase contract` once the new release is out everywhere, or `makemigrations --fast` for a maintenance window with apps stopped. `--phase expand` runs the migration's other `expand` steps and leaves the narrowing pending for `contract`.

reqs.text: **A silent narrowing of stored data is `lossy`.** A type change that's one of R-1108's silent narrowings also changes rows already stored, as it does a write, with no error: `1.0051` becomes `1.01` when `numeric(20,4)` becomes `numeric(20,2)`, `1.25` becomes `1` as `integer` from `numeric(12,2)`, `.123456` becomes `.123` as `timestamptz(3)`, `.5` becomes the next second as `timestamp(0)`, `'abc       '` becomes `'abc'` as `varchar(3)` from `varchar(10)`, and `{1.0051}` becomes `{1.01}` as `numeric(20,2)[]`. The online swap's batched copy and sync trigger change them the same way. So the op that runs one in direction `up` has data effect `lossy`, in the online form and in the `--fast` form alike, and `makemigrations` opens a decision for it, as step 32 does for every lossy change, naming the table and column, both definitions and the change, such as `1.0051` stored as `1.01`. An accepting answer writes the migration, and an answer that refuses exits with code `2`, under step 32's exit codes. A `revert` plans its forward migration the same way, so a revert of a widening opens it too. A widening's `down` is one of these narrowings, but `makemigrations` opens no decision for it: scratch holds no live rows, so whether rolling a widening back changes any is asked at `rollback`, as R-1114 says. `makemigrations` sees only scratch, so `migrate` also counts the live rows the change would alter, and asks again showing the count when there are any, as R-1115 says. A narrowing that raises a real error, such as `bigint` to `integer`, changes no stored row, because a row that doesn't fit stops the change, so it isn't `lossy`. That column isn't a preserved column in step 32's with-data proof, because `up` is meant to change its values, and every other column still is.

reqs.text: **Counting the rows a silent narrowing would change.** Before `rollback` undoes, or `migrate` runs, a step that's one of R-1108's silent narrowings, its preflight counts the live rows that step would change, on the live database. morm builds the count from the column's old and new definition as `format_type` prints them, with no SQL parser. A row counts when the change would leave it a value that isn't equal, in the old type, to the one it holds, and the change raises no error on it. For a lower scale `s`, where `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` count as 0, that's `col <> round(col, s)`. For a lower timestamp precision `p`, it's `col <> CAST(col AS timestamptz(p))`, or `timestamp(p)`. For a shorter length `n`, to `varchar(n)`, it's `length(col) > n AND length(rtrim(col, ' ')) <= n`, and to `char(n)` from `text` or `varchar`, it's `col <> rtrim(col, ' ') AND length(rtrim(col, ' ')) <= n`, because a `char` value loses its trailing spaces when read as text. From `char` to a shorter `char`, no row counts, because Postgres treats a `char` value's trailing spaces as insignificant, so `'abc '` in `char(4)` and `'abc'` in `char(3)` are equal. On an array, a row counts when any element does, through `unnest`. A `NULL` never counts, and neither does a row the change refuses with an error, such as `'abcd'` into `varchar(3)` or `NaN` into `integer`, because that row stops the change instead. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, each of these counts matched the rows `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` changed, compared in the old type, including `-1.0050` to `numeric(20,2)`, `1.50` and `-1.50` to `integer`, `9999.9999` from `numeric(8,4)` to `numeric(10,2)`, `'ab '` from `text` to `char(3)`, and `{{1.0051},{2}}`. The count is one `SELECT count(*)` per column, in a read-only transaction of its own, with `statement_timeout` off, so a role's timeout can't leave it unknown. It takes only `ACCESS SHARE`, so reads and writes go on while it runs: on both versions, an `UPDATE`, an `INSERT` and a `DELETE` from another session with a `500ms` `lock_timeout` went through while it was held. No index can answer it, so it reads the whole table, and Postgres can run it as a parallel sequential scan. It always runs to the end, however big the table, because only a full read shows that no row would change. That stays cheap beside the change itself, because every silent narrowing rewrites the whole table and its indexes, under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` in the one-transaction form, or copies every row in the online form: on both versions, the table's file changed for `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)`, `timestamptz` to `timestamptz(3)`, `varchar(10)` and `text` to `varchar(3)`, and `numeric(20,4)[]` to `numeric(20,2)[]`, and stayed the same for a widening. So the count adds one read of what the change reads and rewrites anyway. reqs.text: **`rollback` asks before it changes stored rows.** When R-1113's count for a step `rollback` would undo is above 0, `rollback` opens a decision in its preflight, in direction `down`, under step 34's rules, in every form, `--last`, `--to`, `--orphans` and `--failed`, before the first step of that migration it would undo, changing nothing. It reads the column's definitions from the ledger's copy of `meta.json`, so it works when the migration's files are gone. It names the table and column, both definitions as the down changes them, the silent change, such as `1.0051` stored as `1.01`, and the count, such as `2 rows would change`, and it offers to accept or refuse, refusing by default. The run stops with exit code `3` until `rollback --decide ID=OPT` accepts it, and an answer that refuses exits with code `2`. `--yes` and `--accept-data-loss` don't answer it. With a count of 0 it opens no decision, and the step runs. Its ID is built as step 32 builds one for a database object, with the table's `regclass` text and the column's name as its signature, and its hash covers both definitions and the count. So an answer covers only the count it was shown: if the count changes before the run that answers it, the ID changes, and that run stops again with exit code `3`, showing the new count. This is apart from R-1110's hold, which still needs `--phase contract` or `--fast`.

reqs.text: **`check_schema` runs when a pool starts.** morm runs `check_schema` by itself on every pool, before the pool serves anything, so a build that doesn't match the schema refuses to start. `Db::connect`, `connect_as` and `connect_to` run it on the first connection their pool opens, before they return, and return `Error::SchemaMismatch` when it fails, holding every finding. Each finding names the table and column, the definition the field was built against, the column's, and what's wrong: a missing column, an unrelated kind, one of R-1108's silent changes, such as `1.25` stored as `1.3`, one of R-0612's two insert cases, R-1190's partition column that its model's inserts send, R-1194's `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column that its model's inserts send, or R-1198's `BY DEFAULT` one. So `let db = morm::Db::connect().await?;` stops the app at startup with that error, and none of the app's queries has run. A pool that `db.pool(name)` adds runs it before its first query. While it fails, every call through that pool returns the same error and runs the check again, so a replica that hadn't yet replayed a migration passes once it has. A pool that passed never checks again. Every pool runs it, `read_only` ones included, because a named pool can reach another host or log in as another role, and the pool must be able to serve every model the binary holds. The check covers every model in the binary, through the per-model column list, in one statement over the catalog, run through `query_typed` with no prepare round trip and no session state. So it works unchanged behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, where it checks the database PgBouncer connects that connection to, as the app's queries reach it. It costs one round trip on a pool's first connection and none after: checkouts, later connections and queries send nothing more. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with 2,000 tables in the catalog, reading every column of 200 tables of 20 columns, with type, `NOT NULL`, default and enum labels, took 3.2 to 3.7 ms on a local connection and returned about 95 KB, and 20 tables took 0.6 to 1.2 ms. The connection `morm-mgr` opens to run a data hook doesn't run it, because a hook runs in the middle of a migration, against a schema no build matches, and it uses raw SQL only. `db.check_schema()` runs the same check whenever it's called, whatever R-1117's setting says. In every pool, straight to Postgres as behind a pooler and with the statement caches on or off, the same statement also reads the statement generation from the `_morm` schema's comment in `pg_description`, for step 14's pool's last-read `<n>` and, behind a pooler with the caches on, its marker, with no extra round trip, in place of step 14's own catalog query, and a database with no `_morm` reads as `0`. A pool with `check_schema = "off"` doesn't run that statement, so it reads the generation with step 14's own catalog query on its first connection, and starts under the current `<n>` all the same. Owner decisions SD and EF5.

reqs.text: **Turning the startup check off.** The pool setting `check_schema` is `"on"` by default, and `"off"` turns R-1116's startup check off for that pool and nothing else. It's set like any pool setting: in `[pool]`, in one `[pools.<name>]`, or by `MORM_POOL_CHECK_SCHEMA` for the pool a process opens at startup. Any other value is `Error::Config`. With it off, that pool starts against any schema, so a missing column fails each query that names it, and a build brought back after `contract` stores rounded or cut values with no error. The session's zone isn't checked either at the pool's start, so behind a pooler that drops morm's `TimeZone` parameter a role not set to UTC goes unnoticed and raw SQL converts times in its zone.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the rolling deploy rows:

> **Turning off the startup check lets a build run against a schema it can't use.** morm runs `check_schema` when each pool starts, so a build that doesn't match the database refuses to start. `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch`, naming each table and column, the definition the build expects, the one the database has, and what's wrong, before any of your queries run. A pool added with `db.pool(name)` returns the same error from every call until a check passes.
>
> **What it does.** One query over the catalog, on a pool's first connection, covering every model in the binary, and nothing after: no work on later connections or queries. 200 tables took about 3 ms on a local connection. Every pool runs it, replicas included, so a replica that hasn't replayed a migration yet fails it until it has. It works behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, checking the database PgBouncer connects you to.
>
> ```toml
> [pools.legacy]
> check_schema = "off"     # this database holds none of this binary's models
> ```
>
> **When it's right.** Only for a pool whose database isn't meant to hold the binary's models, such as a pool used only for raw SQL on another database. `MORM_POOL_CHECK_SCHEMA=off` does the same for the pool a process opens at startup. Never turn it off to get a failing build to start: the check failed because that build can't use this schema.
>
> **What you give up.** A build brought back after a migration's `contract`, such as a rollback of the app to an older release, starts anyway, and Postgres changes what it writes with no error: a field built for a wider scale, timestamp precision or length than its column stores `1.0051` as `1.01` or `'abc  '` as `'abc'`. A missing column or an unrelated type fails each query that reaches it, in production, instead of failing at startup. The session's zone isn't checked either: behind a pooler that drops morm's `TimeZone` parameter, a role that isn't set to `timezone = 'UTC'` goes unnoticed, and raw SQL then converts and truncates times in that role's zone. `db.check_schema()` still runs the check whenever you call it, the zone included.

reqs.text: **What changes together.** A type change on a column that a foreign key references, where the table has to be rewritten or the column's collation changes, and the old and new types are in the same one of the type families step 41's `check_schema` accepts, runs online by default in this form, in either direction. That's every such change within one family, not only between `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`: an `integer` primary key becoming `bigint` or going back, an `integer` key becoming `numeric(20,0)`, a `numeric(20,4)` key becoming `numeric(20,2)`, a `varchar(10)` key becoming `varchar(3)`, or a `char(3)` key becoming `char(5)`. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, the table's file changed for a change of `numeric` scale, a lower `numeric` precision, `numeric(10,0)` to `bigint` or `numeric(8,0)`, `integer` to `bigint` or `numeric(12,0)`, a lower timestamp precision, a shorter `varchar`, `text` to `varchar(n)`, every change of a `char` length, longer included, and every array change, such as `int[]` to `bigint[]` or `varchar(5)[]` to `text[]`. It stayed the same for a higher `numeric` precision at the same scale or unbounded `numeric`, a higher timestamp precision, and a longer `varchar` or `text`. So a `char` or array key reaches this form even when it gets longer, and so does every narrowing that rewrites. The group is every column of the changed key, plus every column that references it, followed transitively: a referencing column that is itself referenced brings its own referencing columns in. The group also includes the identity or owned sequence, every index and constraint on those columns, and the views and materialized views over them, carried as step 39 carries them. A composite key changes only the columns whose type changes, and keeps its other columns in each index and foreign key. A self-referencing table gets a shadow column for the key and one for the referencing column, with one sync trigger. A referencing column whose type doesn't change, such as a `bigint` column referencing an `integer` key that becomes `bigint`, stays in the group with no shadow column, and step 5's new foreign key starts from that column itself. Step 06's typed foreign keys make the models change every referencing column with the key, so the diff shows the whole group, and the planner makes it one op. A widening that needs no rewrite, such as a longer `varchar` or a higher precision on `numeric(p,0)`, stays step 39's change in place, and a change across families, such as `integer` to `uuid`, or `timestamp` to `timestamptz`, keeps step 39's refusal on a live table, with `--fast`.

reqs.text:
**The steps,** each with its own boundary, and each brief lock taken under `lock_timeout` with retries, as step 33 says:

1. `tx` per table, the key table first: add a shadow column for each changed column, with its new type and its collation named, as step 39 does, and one sync trigger, `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE`, that copies each old column into its shadow. `ADD COLUMN` takes `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` and `CREATE TRIGGER` takes `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE`, each for under a millisecond.
2. `batch` per table: copy by the table's copy key, as R-1148 says, up to its bound, the highest key read once that table's trigger has committed, as step 52's copy does, with the cursor in `_morm.steps`.
3. `no-tx`: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for each primary key or unique index that holds a changed column, and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for every other index that holds one, each with the shadow column in place of the old one, so a composite key keeps its other columns. Each new index is named `_morm_new_<name>`, from the real index's name through the 63-byte name function, so step 14 maps a unique violation on a shadow index to the key's field.
4. `tx`, then a separate `tx`: add a `CHECK ... NOT VALID` on each shadow column, then `VALIDATE` it. The check is `(new IS NOT DISTINCT FROM CAST(old AS <new type>))`, with `new IS NOT NULL AND` in front for a `NOT NULL` old column, and for a type with a collation the cast side names the new column's collation, as `CAST(old AS <new type>) COLLATE "<collation>"`. That's one rule for every change: `new = old` can never pass where the values change, as `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)` showed when it failed `VALIDATE` on 200,000 rows, and doesn't exist between arrays of different types. reqs.text:
**The cutover** is one short transaction across every table in the group, and it gives way to live transactions under step 39's rule, with the same settings, the same `--terminate-blockers` and the same `--resume`. In order:

1. Take each carried view's lock with its own `DROP VIEW`, from the outside in, as step 39 does. Then lock the tables `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`: the key table first, then the referencing tables in name order. Readers, and writers going from a parent to its children, lock the key table first, and under nonstop traffic a cutover that locked the referencing tables first got in on none of 176 attempts.
2. Walk the group again under the lock, reading `pg_constraint` for every foreign key that references a changed column. Anything new stops the cutover with nothing changed.
3. Take the sequence's lock with a same-value `ALTER SEQUENCE ... INCREMENT BY <current>`, because `LOCK TABLE` refuses a sequence, then read `last_value` and `is_called`.
4. Drop the sync triggers and the old foreign keys.
5. On each table: drop the identity, which drops its sequence, the old primary key or unique constraints and the other old indexes on the changed columns. Retire each old column as step 38 does, dropping its `NOT NULL` and default and renaming it to its retired name. Rename each shadow column to the real name, then `SET NOT NULL` where the old column had it, which the validated check proves with no scan, and set the old column's default. Re-attach the primary key with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` and each unique constraint with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> UNIQUE USING INDEX`, then carry the sequence as R-1124 says.
6. Drop the checks, and rename the new foreign keys and indexes to the real names. Move a `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on a replaced index to its new index, because dropping the old one leaves the table with no replica identity index.
7. Recreate the carried views and swap the materialized views, as step 39 does, refresh functions, as step 37 does, copy column comments and grants, and write the step as `done` in `_morm.steps`, all in this same transaction.

It holds `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` on every table in the group, `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` and then `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` on the sequence, and each carried view's lock. Everything inside it is a catalog change, with no scan and no rewrite.

reqs.text: **The sequence.** An identity key keeps its sequence's name and position. Once the shadow column has the real name, the cutover runs `ADD GENERATED ALWAYS` or `BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (SEQUENCE NAME <old name>, <old options>)`, the same kind as before, with the old start, increment, cache and cycle, and with a minimum or maximum the old sequence set past its type's default. A minimum or maximum that was the old type's default becomes the new type's, so an `integer` identity widened to `bigint` can reach `bigint`'s maximum. Then `setval` sets the `last_value` and `is_called` read under the lock. The new sequence doesn't keep the old one's owner, grants or comment, so the cutover copies them. A session open across the cutover gets `55000` from `currval` and `lastval` on that sequence until its next `nextval`, because the sequence is new under the same name, and the README says so. A `serial` key, with an owned sequence and no identity, keeps the same sequence, with its OID and position: `ALTER SEQUENCE ... AS <new type>` changes its type, moving a maximum that was the old type's default to the new type's and keeping one set explicitly, and `OWNED BY` and `SET DEFAULT` move it to the new column. Postgres allows identity, and sequences, only on `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, so all of this holds within those three types, and R-1125 refuses an op that takes a generated key out of them while dropping its generation. A `serial` key's `ALTER SEQUENCE ... AS` runs only when its new type is one of the three. A `serial` key moved to `numeric(p,0)` with its `nextval` default kept keeps its sequence as it was, with `OWNED BY` and `SET DEFAULT` moved to the new column, and on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11 one did keep working, with its sequence still `integer`. Its position is checked as R-1127 says, because a `numeric(5,0)` key with a `nextval` default got `numeric field overflow` on the insert after its sequence passed 99,999.

**Refused online, with the evidence.** Each of these is refused with exit code `2` before the op's first step, changing nothing. `makemigrations` checks what scratch shows, `migrate` and `rollback` preflight check the live database, and the cutover's second walk checks again under its lock, where anything new stops it with nothing changed.

1. A foreign key on a changed column from a table no model declares, or one the models don't declare. The evidence is the referencing table, the constraint's name and `pg_get_constraintdef`, its deferrability and the table's estimated rows. morm can't change a column it doesn't manage, and if that column stayed narrow, its foreign key would fail once a value passed the old limit. It's a refusal, not a decision, because no answer would make the change safe. The fix is to declare the table in the models, or to drop that foreign key first. `--fast` refuses it too, as R-1126 says. The cutover's `DROP CONSTRAINT`, which never uses `CASCADE`, is the last check, because Postgres refuses to drop a key a foreign key needs, with `2BP01`.
2. A partitioned table or a partition in the group, because `ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX` isn't supported on a partitioned table, Postgres 15 to 17 can't add a `NOT VALID` foreign key from one, and Postgres can't add a column to a partition. `--fast` handles it when every partition the change reaches is declared by a model with the same change, as R-1126 says.
3. A table in the group that's in any publication, or is a subscription's target, naming the publication or subscription, because the shadow columns and the cutover each stop replication with `missing replicated column`. `--fast` handles it, and the subscriber keeps working.
4. What step 52 refuses for an enum swap, on a column in the group: exclusion constraints and extended statistics, stored generated columns that read one, a domain or composite type, and a view or materialized view that would still read the retired column once recreated, such as `SELECT *`. Each of these needs a rewrite, or a definition morm can't move with no lock. `--fast` handles them.
5. Anything step 39 refuses above a swapped column, such as a view no model declares.
6. A table in the group that's in old-style inheritance, as a parent or as a child, naming the table and its parent or children, because `ADD COLUMN` on a parent adds the column to every child, `ALTER TABLE ONLY` can't stop that, and an inherited column's type can't change on the child alone. `--fast` handles it when every child the change reaches is declared by a model with the same change, as R-1126 says.
7. A table in the group with no primary key and no unique `NOT NULL` key, naming the table, because its copy has no key to bound it or resume it by, as R-1148 says. `--fast` handles it.
8. A referencing column whose new type is in a different btree operator family from the key's new type, naming both columns, such as a `bigint` column referencing a key that becomes `numeric(20,0)`. Postgres allows that foreign key, but compares through a cast, so it can't use the referencing column's index: deleting 10 keys took 683 ms on 18.6 and 668 ms on 17.11, with a parallel sequential scan of the referencing table filtered on `(pid)::numeric`, against 2 ms with matching types. `--fast` refuses it too.
9. When the change alters stored values, as R-1149 says, a referencing column that doesn't take exactly the key's new type, naming it, because a reference left at the old scale would no longer match its key. `--fast` refuses it too.
10. One op that takes a generated key, an identity column or a `serial` key with its owned sequence, out of `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` while dropping its generation, naming the column. Postgres allows identity and sequences only on those types: on 18.6 and 17.11, `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE numeric(20,0)` on an identity column, the `ADD GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY` this op's cutover would run on a `numeric` column, and `CREATE TABLE` with a `numeric` identity column each failed with `identity column type must be smallint, integer, or bigint`, and `CREATE SEQUENCE ... AS numeric` failed with `sequence type must be smallint, integer, or bigint`. So no sequence can count past `bigint`'s maximum, and a generated key gains no room as `numeric`. `--fast` refuses it too, because Postgres can't do it either. The way through is two migrations: the first drops the identity or the default, which changes no rows, and the second changes the type, with no sequence involved. `DROP IDENTITY` keeps the data and drops the sequence, and step 41 refuses at pool start a build that still leaves that column out of its inserts.
11. A collation change on a key with a nondeterministic collation on either side, naming both collations, because it can merge keys, as `'abc'` and `'ABC'` did when a key went from `"C"` to a case-insensitive collation, and Postgres refuses a foreign key between two different collations when either is nondeterministic. Between two deterministic collations, equality is byte equality, so nothing merges, and the change runs online. `--fast` handles it, as R-1126 says, and a merge there fails on the unique index and changes nothing.

An enum key keeps step 52's refusal, because an enum swap isn't a change within one family.

TYPE` in one transaction, as step 39 does, naming each column's collation. A column in the group that's inherited, or on a table with children or partitions, changes only through its top parent, in one `ALTER`, under step 39's rule, so a partitioned or inherited table in the group runs only when every child and partition the change reaches is declared by a model with the same change, and `migrate` and `rollback` preflight otherwise refuse with exit code `2` before the first step, naming the column, its top parent and those tables. Every other statement this form runs on such a table follows step 39's rule for statements Postgres carries to children and partitions in the same way, once, on the top parent: dropping and adding back the group's foreign keys, and the index check's rebuilds, each of which on a partitioned table reaches every partition. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, changing an inherited column on a child or a partition alone failed with `cannot alter inherited column`. It refuses a foreign key from a table no model declares, or one the models don't declare, with exit code `2` and R-1125's evidence, because Postgres would change the key and leave that column as it was, so its foreign key would fail once a value passed the old limit. It refuses R-1125's referencing column of another operator family, a referencing column that doesn't take the key's new type when values change, and a generated key leaving the integer types the same way. Postgres can't change the columns with the foreign keys in place when the change alters stored values, when the key's old and new types are in different btree operator families, as `integer` and `numeric(20,0)` are, or when the key's collation changes with a nondeterministic collation on either side. The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **Changing a key other tables reference can be refused.** A type change on a key that foreign keys reference, such as an `integer` primary key becoming `bigint`, or any other change within one kind of type that rewrites the table, such as `numeric(20,4)` becoming `numeric(20,2)`, runs online with apps up. morm changes every column that references the key, and the identity sequence, with it. It adds a new column beside each one, copies the rows in batches, builds the indexes and foreign keys with no long lock, and swaps them all in one cutover of milliseconds. `rollback` and `revert` go back the same way.
>
> **What it refuses, and how to go on.** In these cases morm stops the migration with exit code `2`, naming the cause, before it changes anything:
>
> - **A foreign key your models don't declare,** on a table they don't declare or on one they do. morm can't change a column it doesn't manage, and if that column stayed narrow, its foreign key would fail once an id passed the old limit. `--fast` refuses it too. Declare the table in your models, or drop that foreign key first.
> - **A partitioned table, a partition, a table in old-style inheritance, or a table in a publication or a subscription.** Postgres can't swap a partitioned table's key without a scan, a new column on an inheritance parent lands on every child, and the new columns would stop replication. Run `makemigrations --fast` instead. On a partitioned or inherited table, `--fast` needs every partition and child declared in your models with the same change, as the notice on inherited columns says.
> - **A table with no primary key and no unique key on `NOT NULL` columns.** The copy has no key to walk by. Add one first, or run `makemigrations --fast` instead.
> - **An exclusion constraint, extended statistics, a stored generated column, a domain or composite type, or a view such as `SELECT *`, on a column in the change, or a view your models don't declare.** morm can't move these with no lock. Run `makemigrations --fast` instead.
> - **A change to another kind of type,** such as `integer` to `uuid`, or `timestamp` to `timestamptz`. Run `makemigrations --fast` instead.
> - **A generated key leaving the integer types, a reference of another kind of number, keys that would merge, and some collation changes.** The notices below say why, and how to go on.
> - **Going back down,** such as a `rollback` from `bigint` to `integer`, **once a value or the sequence has passed the old type's limit.** Nothing makes that safe, so nothing forces it. Leave the column wide, or remove the values that don't fit first.
>
> **When `--fast` is right.** Only with apps stopped, in a maintenance window, or on tables small enough that a full lock for their rewrite doesn't matter.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` rewrites each table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on any of them waits until it's done, and `max_rewrite_mb` refuses a table bigger than its limit. Going back down online, an app write the old type can't hold, such as a new id past `2^31 - 1`, fails with `22003` from the migration's first step, not only after the cutover.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the cutover settings:

> **A cutover that takes many locks can be refused before it starts.** A cutover gives way to your app: each lock waits at most `cutover_lock_timeout`, and then the attempt changes nothing and tries again, so Postgres never has to kill one of your transactions to break a deadlock. Postgres starts looking for a deadlock once a lock has waited `deadlock_timeout`, and an attempt holds every lock it has while it waits for the next, so morm shrinks each lock's wait to `deadlock_timeout / (2 × locks)` when that's shorter, and says so. Postgres counts `lock_timeout` in whole milliseconds and reads 0 as no limit, so when that wait comes to under 1 ms, `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before the change's first step, naming `cutover_lock_timeout`, `deadlock_timeout` and the number of locks, and change nothing.
>
> **How to go on.** Raise `deadlock_timeout` on the server, so each lock gets at least a millisecond: its default of `1s` covers a cutover of up to 500 locks. If `cutover_lock_timeout` is the one set under 1 ms, raise that instead. Or write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it in a maintenance window.
>
> **What you give up.** With a higher `deadlock_timeout`, a real deadlock between your own transactions takes that long to be broken. `--fast` changes the tables in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on them waits until it's done.

> **An online change needs a key to walk the table.** When morm changes a column's type online, swaps an enum online, or changes a key other tables reference, it copies the rows in batches, walking the table by its primary key, so the copy stops at a fixed point and carries on after a crash. A table with neither is refused before anything changes, with exit code `2`, naming the table.
