>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` rewrites the table in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on it waits until it's done.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A generated key stays an integer.** Postgres allows identity columns, and sequences, only on `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, and no sequence can count past `bigint`'s maximum, so a generated key gains nothing as `numeric`. So `identity` on any other type is a compile error, and a migration that takes a key out of the integer types while dropping its identity, or a `serial` key's sequence, is refused with exit code `2` when it's made.
>
> **When it's right to go there anyway.** When your app supplies its own ids, such as `u64` ids from another system, stored as `numeric(20,0)`.
>
> **How to go on.** Use two migrations. The first drops the identity, or the default, which changes no rows. The second changes the type, with no sequence involved.
>
> **What you give up.** The database no longer makes the ids, so every insert must supply one, and a build that still leaves the id out of its inserts is refused when its pool starts. If you add identity back later, morm sets its sequence past the highest key, so the next insert doesn't collide.

**R-1139** The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A generated key stays an integer.** Postgres allows identity columns, and sequences, only on `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, and no sequence can count past `bigint`'s maximum, so a generated key gains nothing as `numeric`. So `identity` on any other type is a compile error, and a migration that takes a key out of the integer types while dropping its identity, or a `serial` key's sequence, is refused with exit code `2` when it's made.
>
> **When it's right to go there anyway.** When your app supplies its own ids, such as `u64` ids from another system, stored as `numeric(20,0)`.
>
> **How to go on.** Use two migrations. The first drops the identity, or the default, which changes no rows. The second changes the type, with no sequence involved.
>
> **What you give up.** The database no longer makes the ids, so every insert must supply one, and a build that still leaves the id out of its inserts is refused when its pool starts. If you add identity back later, morm sets its sequence past the highest key, so the next insert doesn't collide.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **Changing a key's values changes them everywhere.** A key change that lowers a scale, a timestamp precision or a length, such as `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)`, changes the stored keys: `1.0051` becomes `1.01`. morm runs it online and changes every column that references the key the same way, so no reference is lost. Like every change Postgres would round or cut silently, it waits for `migrate --phase contract`, or for `--fast` with apps stopped. `makemigrations` asks you to accept it as a `lossy` decision, naming every referencing column, and `migrate` asks again with the number of rows that would change.
>
> **What it refuses.** Two keys that would become one, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149`, both `1.01`, stop `migrate` or `rollback` with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming them, because no answer can make two keys one. A referencing column that doesn't change to exactly the key's new type is refused when the migration is made, because it would no longer match its key.
>
> **How to go on.** Change or remove the keys that would merge, then run it again.
>
> **What you give up.** Copies of the key held outside the database, such as in caches, URLs, other services, logs and exports, keep the old values and won't match any more. While it runs, a write whose key matches another only once rounded fails with `Error::Unique` on the key's field.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A narrower key is refused while a value doesn't fit.** Going down to a narrower key, by `rollback`, `revert` or a narrowing migration, such as `bigint` to `integer` or `varchar(10)` to `varchar(3)`, stops with exit code `2` before anything changes when a live value doesn't fit the narrower type, naming the table, the column, one such value and how many there are. A sequence past the narrower limit is refused the same way. Nothing makes that safe, so nothing forces it.
>
> From the migration's first step until it's done, a write the narrower type can't hold fails with the database's error for that write, such as `22003` for an id past `2^31 - 1` or `22001` for a text too long. A row that doesn't fit and arrives before the migration's trigger is in place stops the copy with the same message, and `rollback --failed` cleans up.
>
> **How to go on.** Leave the key wide, or change or remove the values that don't fit first.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A reference must stay the key's kind of number.** When a key changes, every column that references it must end up the same kind of type as the key. Postgres accepts a `bigint` column referencing a `numeric(20,0)` key, but compares the two through a cast, so the foreign key can't use the referencing column's index, and every delete of a key reads the whole referencing table: deleting 10 keys took 683 ms, against 2 ms with matching types. So `makemigrations` refuses it with exit code `2`, naming both columns, with `--fast` too.
>
> **How to go on.** Give the referencing column the key's new type.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **Some collation changes on a key are refused online.** morm names a column's collation in every type change it writes, because Postgres would otherwise reset it to the default, and a collation change on its own runs through the online swap, because it rebuilds the column's indexes. A key whose collation changes between two deterministic collations, where equal means the same bytes, changes online like any other key change. A change to or from a nondeterministic collation, such as a case-insensitive one, is refused online with exit code `2`, naming both collations, because it can turn two keys into one, such as `'abc'` and `'ABC'`, and Postgres won't keep a foreign key between the two collations while the change runs.
>
> **How to go on.** Write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it with apps stopped. If two keys would become one, it fails on the unique index and changes nothing.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` rewrites every table in the change in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on them waits until it's done.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the rolling deploy rows:

> **A change between `timestamp` and `timestamptz` asks which zone your values are in.** Postgres converts each value through the time zone of the session that runs the change, with no error, so the same stored `12:00` becomes `12:00` UTC on one host and `17:00` UTC on another. So `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` and asks which zone the stored values are in, then writes that zone into the migration, so it gives the same data wherever it runs, and its down converts back through the same zone.
>
> **How to answer.** `makemigrations --decide ID=<zone>`, such as `ID=UTC`, with the zone your app wrote the values in.
>
> **What you give up.** One zone covers every row of the column, so rows written in different zones need fixing first. On a key other tables reference, the change can't run online, so it needs `makemigrations --fast`.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **`--fast` on a key rebuilds its foreign keys and indexes.** With `--fast`, a key change that changes stored values, moves to another kind of number, such as `integer` to `numeric(20,0)`, or changes to or from a nondeterministic collation can't run with the foreign keys in place. So morm drops the foreign keys on the key, changes every column, and adds them back with the same names and rules, checking every row, all in the one transaction. Then it rebuilds any index on those columns that Postgres changed on its own, such as one whose operator class it replaced, so every index ends as your models declare it.
>
> **What you give up.** All of this runs under the one full lock, so checking the foreign keys and rebuilding the indexes adds to the time every read and write on those tables waits.

reqs.text:
**Key values that change.** A key change that's one of step 41's silent narrowings, a lower scale, a lower timestamp precision or a shorter length that drops trailing spaces, changes stored keys, such as `1.0051` to `1.01`, and runs in this form, held for `contract` as step 41 holds every silent narrowing, or under `--fast` as R-1126 says. A `char` key that gets shorter changes no value, because Postgres compares `char` without its padding. Step 4's cast check passes where `new = old` can't, and a key and its references round alike. Before the op's first step, `migrate` and `rollback` preflight refuse with exit code `2` any key values that would merge, naming them, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149`, which both become `1.01`, with one `GROUP BY` per key, built from the new type, in a read-only transaction with `statement_timeout` off. The same check runs for every other unique index that holds a changed column, such as one on a single column of a composite key, where two keys can stay distinct while that column's values merge, built as step 39 builds it for its swap, naming the table, the index, the values and how many rows hold each. No answer can make two keys one, so it's a refusal, not a decision. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a merge made `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` fail with `Key (id_new)=(1.01) is duplicated` and left the index invalid, `timestamp` to `timestamp(3)` merged `.123456` with `.123`, `varchar(10)` to `varchar(3)` merged `'abc  '` with `'abc'`, and `--fast` failed the same way. A merge written after preflight fails step 3's unique index build, and the step stops as `failed`. Every referencing column must take exactly the key's new type, as R-1125 says, and step 41 words the `lossy` decision and its live counts for a key. During the window, a write whose key collides with another only once rounded fails on the shadow unique index, and step 14 maps that index's name to the key's field, so the error reads as one on the key. In `contract`, apps are built for the narrower shape, and step 13 stops them writing extra decimals, so this is rare.

Measured on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11: a key table of 300,000 `numeric(20,4)` primary keys, each ending `.0051`, referenced by 400,000 `NOT NULL` rows with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, went to `numeric(20,2)` through steps 1 to 6 and the cutover, run by hand with the cast check and the key table locked first. 8 `pgbench` clients ran nonstop, writing two-decimal keys: inserting a parent and a child, deleting by key range with its cascade, updating a parent and then reading its children, moving a child to another parent, and a join. On 18.6, 89,098 transactions ran and none failed, the copies took 61 and 81 bounded batches, and the cutover got in on attempt 3, holding its locks for 8.3 ms. On 17.11, 74,116 ran and none failed, with the same batches, and the cutover got in on attempt 2 at 7.0 ms. On both, no row was orphaned, every parent's new key was its old key rounded, every child whose key differed from its retired one had moved to another parent after the cutover, and the tables ended `numeric(20,2)`, with `parent_pkey` and `child_pid_fkey` on the new columns and no trigger left. Each was a single short run with no fault injection, which T-0230 and T-0231 add.

reqs.text:
**Checking that a value fits a narrower type.** R-1127's check covers every narrowing in this form that raises a real error on a value that doesn't fit, in any family, because the silent ones change values instead, as R-1149 says. A write's assignment cast is the authority, and `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE`, `UPDATE ... SET` and a plpgsql trigger's `NEW.x := NEW.y` all use it. An explicit `CAST` isn't, because `CAST('abcd' AS varchar(3))` gives `'abc'` with no error, while assigning `'abcd'` to a `varchar(3)` fails with `22001`. So preflight builds a predicate from the old and new definitions as `format_type` prints them, as step 41's row count is built, with no SQL parser, and runs one `SELECT count(*), min(v)` per column where it holds, in a read-only transaction with `statement_timeout` off. A value `v` doesn't fit when:

| New type | Doesn't fit when |
|---|---|
| `numeric(p,s)`, from `numeric` | `v <> 'NaN' AND (abs(round(v, s)) >= 10::numeric ^ (p - s) OR v IN ('Infinity', '-Infinity'))` |
| `numeric(p,s)`, from an integer type | `abs(round(v::numeric, s)) >= 10::numeric ^ (p - s)` |
| `smallint`, `integer` or `bigint`, from `numeric` | `v IN ('NaN', 'Infinity', '-Infinity') OR round(v) < <min>::numeric OR round(v) > <max>::numeric` |
| `smallint` or `integer`, from a wider integer type | `v::numeric < <min>::numeric OR v::numeric > <max>::numeric` |
| `varchar(n)` or `char(n)` | `length(rtrim(v, ' ')) > n` |
| a lower timestamp precision | never, because it rounds and never raises an error |
| an array of any of these | any element doesn't, through `unnest` |

`p`, `s` and the type's range, `<min>` and `<max>`, are written in as constants from `format_type`, so `10::numeric ^ (20 - 0)` for `numeric(20,0)`. Every bound and comparison stays in `numeric`. Written as `10^(p-s)`, the bound is `double precision`, because `^` with integer operands resolves to `float8`, and `numeric >= float8` compares as `float8`, so a value of 16 digits or more just under the bound, such as 20 nines into `numeric(20,0)`, rounds up to it and is refused though it fits, and a bound past `10^308`, which `numeric(400,0)` needs, fails with `value out of range: overflow`. `abs(v)` on an integer type fails on its minimum, such as `integer out of range` for `-2147483648`, which `numeric(10,0)` holds, so the integer value is cast to `numeric` first. `round` applies to an integer source too, because a negative scale rounds it: `9999960` into `numeric(5,-2)` rounds to `10000000` and fails the cast. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, these agreed with the assignment cast on all 40 value and type pairs first tried: numeric overflow after rounding, such as `99.995` into `numeric(4,2)`, a negative scale from `numeric`, `NaN` and `Infinity`, `numeric` into `integer` and `bigint` at the edges, such as `2147483647.50`, `bigint` into `numeric(5,0)`, trailing spaces, tabs, newlines, non-breaking spaces and multibyte text into `varchar(3)` and `char(3)`, timestamps at the top of the range, and one- and two-dimensional arrays. With the bounds in `numeric`, they also agreed on 49 pairs on both: 20 nines into `numeric(20,0)` and `10^20` past it, 18 nines and `10^18` from `bigint` into `numeric(18,0)`, the minimum of `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` into the `numeric(p,0)` that just holds it and one digit short, `9999960`, `-9999950` and `9999949` from `integer` into `numeric(5,-2)`, a scale above the precision, such as `numeric(2,5)`, 400 and 1,000 nines into `numeric(400,0)` and `numeric(1000,0)` and one past each, and `numeric` into `integer` and `bigint` half a unit inside and past each end of their range. The `double precision` forms refused the first two that fit, failed on the integer minimums and on `numeric(400,0)`, and passed `9999960`. Without its `NaN` guard the `numeric` predicate disagreed on `NaN` on 18.6, because Postgres sorts `NaN` above every number, while `NaN` fits `numeric(4,2)`, so a CI test pins every row against the assignment cast. Timestamp precision rounds even at the top of the range: `294276-12-31 23:59:59.999999` became `294277-01-01 00:00:00` with no error. The sync trigger's assignment and the copy are exact backstops, so a wrong predicate can only cause a stop that `rollback --failed` cleans up, never wrong data. `pg_input_is_valid` would be exact, but Postgres 15 doesn't have it, and a `pg_temp` function assigning each value reads row by row in one backend with no parallel scan, and needs the `TEMP` privilege.

Written as `10^(p-s)`, the bound is `double precision`, because `^` with integer operands resolves to `float8`, and `numeric >= float8` compares as `float8`, so a value of 16 digits or more just under the bound, such as 20 nines into `numeric(20,0)`, rounds up to it and is refused though it fits, and a bound past `10^308`, which `numeric(400,0)` needs, fails with `value out of range: overflow`. `abs(v)` on an integer type fails on its minimum, such as `integer out of range` for `-2147483648`, which `numeric(10,0)` holds, so the integer value is cast to `numeric` first. `round` applies to an integer source too, because a negative scale rounds it: `9999960` into `numeric(5,-2)` rounds to `10000000` and fails the cast. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, these agreed with the assignment cast on all 40 value and type pairs first tried: numeric overflow after rounding, such as `99.995` into `numeric(4,2)`, a negative scale from `numeric`, `NaN` and `Infinity`, `numeric` into `integer` and `bigint` at the edges, such as `2147483647.50`, `bigint` into `numeric(5,0)`, trailing spaces, tabs, newlines, non-breaking spaces and multibyte text into `varchar(3)` and `char(3)`, timestamps at the top of the range, and one- and two-dimensional arrays. With the bounds in `numeric`, they also agreed on 49 pairs on both: 20 nines into `numeric(20,0)` and `10^20` past it, 18 nines and `10^18` from `bigint` into `numeric(18,0)`, the minimum of `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` into the `numeric(p,0)` that just holds it and one digit short, `9999960`, `-9999950` and `9999949` from `integer` into `numeric(5,-2)`, a scale above the precision, such as `numeric(2,5)`, 400 and 1,000 nines into `numeric(400,0)` and `numeric(1000,0)` and one past each, and `numeric` into `integer` and `bigint` half a unit inside and past each end of their range. reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **An online change refuses partitioned and inherited tables.** When morm changes a column's type or collation online, swaps an enum online, or changes a key other tables reference, it adds a new column beside the old one, copies the rows, builds the indexes with no long lock, and renames them at cutover. Postgres can't do that on a partitioned table or a partition: it can't build an index concurrently on a partitioned table, or add a column to a partition. On a table in old-style inheritance, a new column on a parent lands on every child, and an inherited column's type can't change on a child alone. So `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the table and its partitions, parent or children.
>
> **How to go on.** Write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it in a maintenance window. On a partitioned table or an inheritance parent, Postgres changes the column on every partition and child with it, so morm runs it only when your models declare every one of them with the same change, as the notice on inherited columns says.
>
> **When `--fast` is right.** Only with apps stopped, or on tables small enough that a full lock for their rewrite doesn't matter.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` changes the column in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, on every partition and child too, so every read and write on them waits until it's done.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **A type change rebuilds an index Postgres changed on its own, and stops on one that can't fit.** `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` rebuilds a column's indexes from their old definitions without checking them against your models: it silently replaced an explicit `int4_ops` with `bigint`'s default class, and kept `varchar_pattern_ops` on a column changed to `text`. So after every type change, in place, under `--fast` or in an enum swap, morm compares each index on the column with what your models build on scratch and rebuilds any that differs: in place on a live table with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, and under `--fast` in the same transaction. An online swap builds its new indexes from your models in the first place. An index whose `ops` doesn't accept the new type stops `makemigrations`, naming the index and its `ops`, such as `operator class "int4_ops" does not accept data type bigint`.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: an index whose class doesn't accept the new type can't exist on it, so there's no override.
>
> **How to go on.** Change that index's `ops` in your model to one for the new type, or remove it to use the type's default class, then run `makemigrations` again.
>
> **What you give up.** Under `--fast`, a rebuild adds to the time every read and write on that table waits. In place, the new index is built beside the old one, so it takes the time and space of a fresh index. While it builds, and while an online swap runs, a write whose value matches another row's only once converted, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149` both becoming `1.01`, fails with `Error::Unique` on the column's field.

reqs.text: **Inherited columns.** Postgres changes an inherited column only through the table it comes from. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` on a child's or a partition's inherited column alone failed with `cannot alter inherited column`, and so did a collation change, while the same change on the top parent changed it on every child, grandchild and partition. `ALTER TABLE ONLY` on the parent was refused with `type of inherited column ... must be changed in child tables too`, and a column a child inherits from two parents couldn't be changed from either, each failing with `cannot alter inherited column ... of relation`. So every `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` morm runs, in place, under `--fast`, in a `down.sql` or in a later step's one-transaction form, changes an inherited column only through its top parent, in one `ALTER`. Scratch is built from the models, so it has no inheritance, and `migrate` and `rollback` preflight read `pg_inherits` and `pg_attribute` on the live database for every column the migration changes. A column on a table with children or partitions, or one a table inherits, changes only when the migration makes the same change, to the same type and collation, on its top parent and on every child and partition the change reaches, each declared by a model. Then preflight runs the top parent's step where the first step in that tree sits. That step takes the top parent's lock, reads `pg_inherits` again and stops with nothing changed if the tree has changed since preflight, then runs the one `ALTER`. Each other step in the tree finds by its precondition that its column already has the new type and collation, so it changes nothing apart from R-1152's check on its own table. Otherwise preflight refuses with exit code `2` before the first step, changing nothing, naming the column, its top parent and every child and partition the change reaches: a change to a child's or a partition's inherited column without the same change on its top parent, a change that would reach a child or a partition no model declares or whose model doesn't make the same change, and a change to a column inherited from more than one parent, which no one `ALTER` can make. morm never changes a table it doesn't manage, and Postgres would change such a child with no model asking for it. The message says to declare every child and partition in the models with the same change. A column a child adds of its own isn't inherited, so it changes on that child like a column of any other table.

**Foreign keys on a rebuilt index.** A foreign key depends on the unique index it references, so Postgres won't drop that index, or the primary key or unique constraint that owns it, while the foreign key is there. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a `varchar(10)` key with a unique index on `varchar_pattern_ops`, referenced by a foreign key, kept that class when changed in place to `text`, and `DROP INDEX` failed with `cannot drop index ... because other objects depend on it`, and `DROP CONSTRAINT` on a referenced primary key with `2BP01`. A foreign key added beside the old one, `NOT VALID`, with a column list or without, was tied to the old index, not to a new one built beside it, so Postgres gives no way to move a foreign key to a new index while the old one is there. So when R-1152's check must rebuild an index that a foreign key references, morm drops and adds back each such foreign key around the rebuild, in every form, never with `CASCADE`. Under `--fast` and in a one-transaction form, in the same transaction: it drops them, drops and creates the index again, attaching its primary key or unique constraint to it, and adds them back, validated, under the lock it already holds. In place on a live table, with no long lock and no moment when a row that breaks a foreign key could be written:

1. `no-tx`: build the new index as R-1152 says, under `_morm_new_<name>`.
2. `tx`: one short transaction that gives way to live transactions under R-1072's rule, with its settings, its scaled wait and `--terminate-blockers`. Lock the referenced table `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, then each referencing table in name order, drop the foreign keys, drop the old index or its constraint, rename the new index to `<name>`, attaching a primary key or unique constraint to it with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` or `UNIQUE USING INDEX`, and add each foreign key back with its name, columns, actions, `MATCH` type and deferrability, `NOT VALID`. Every statement is a catalog change, with no scan.
3. `tx` per foreign key: `VALIDATE`, which takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` on the referencing table and `ROW SHARE` on the referenced one, so writes carry on.

The new foreign keys hold from the moment step 2 commits, so every write after it is checked, and every row before it was checked by the old ones, with no write in between while step 2 held its locks. `NOT VALID` only skips the scan of rows already there, which `VALIDATE` then proves. A foreign key from a table no model declares, or one the models don't declare, is refused with exit code `2` before the first step, naming it with `pg_get_constraintdef`, because morm would drop and recreate a constraint it doesn't manage: `makemigrations` checks scratch, and `migrate` and `rollback` preflight check the live database. On `--resume`, a rerun of step 2 reads the catalog first and does only what's missing, and a foreign key left `NOT VALID` is validated again. Measured on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with a key table of 200,000 rows referenced by two tables of 200,000 rows with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, under 8 `pgbench` clients nonstop inserting a parent and its children, moving a child to another parent, joining, and deleting the parent: step 2 got in on its first attempt, each of its statements took under 1 ms, the two `VALIDATE`s took 200 to 240 ms together, no app transaction failed, no row was orphaned, an orphan inserted between steps 2 and 3 was refused, and both foreign keys ended validated on the new primary key under their own names. A `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` foreign key came through the same way. On 18.6 the key's `NOT NULL` constraint stayed when the primary key was dropped, and on 17.11 `attnotnull` did, so attaching the primary key again took no scan.

Lock the referenced table `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, then each referencing table in name order, drop the foreign keys, drop the old index or its constraint, rename the new index to `<name>`, attaching a primary key or unique constraint to it with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` or `UNIQUE USING INDEX`, and add each foreign key back with its name, columns, actions, `MATCH` type and deferrability, `NOT VALID`. Every statement is a catalog change, with no scan.
3. `tx` per foreign key: `VALIDATE`, which takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` on the referencing table and `ROW SHARE` on the referenced one, so writes carry on.

The new foreign keys hold from the moment step 2 commits, so every write after it is checked, and every row before it was checked by the old ones, with no write in between while step 2 held its locks. `NOT VALID` only skips the scan of rows already there, which `VALIDATE` then proves. A foreign key from a table no model declares, or one the models don't declare, is refused with exit code `2` before the first step, naming it with `pg_get_constraintdef`, because morm would drop and recreate a constraint it doesn't manage: `makemigrations` checks scratch, and `migrate` and `rollback` preflight check the live database. On `--resume`, a rerun of step 2 reads the catalog first and does only what's missing, and a foreign key left `NOT VALID` is validated again. Measured on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with a key table of 200,000 rows referenced by two tables of 200,000 rows with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, under 8 `pgbench` clients nonstop inserting a parent and its children, moving a child to another parent, joining, and deleting the parent: step 2 got in on its first attempt, each of its statements took under 1 ms, the two `VALIDATE`s took 200 to 240 ms together, no app transaction failed, no row was orphaned, an orphan inserted between steps 2 and 3 was refused, and both foreign keys ended validated on the new primary key under their own names. A `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` foreign key came through the same way. On 18.6 the key's `NOT NULL` constraint stayed when the primary key was dropped, and on 17.11 `attnotnull` did, so attaching the primary key again took no scan.

reqs.text: **Values that would merge on a unique index.** A swap's conversion can make two values equal, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149` both becoming `1.01` in `numeric(10,2)`, `'01'` and `'1'` both becoming `1` from `text` to `integer`, `'abc'` and `'ABC'` under a case-insensitive collation, or `02:30` and `03:30` on the day clocks go forward, both becoming the same `timestamptz`. On a unique index that holds the column, R-1153's concurrent build would then fail mid-run and leave the index invalid. So before R-0566's swap changes anything, it runs one `GROUP BY` for each unique index that holds a swapped column, in a read-only transaction with `statement_timeout` off, and refuses with exit code `2` any values that would merge, naming the table, the index, the values and how many rows hold each. No answer can make two rows one, so it's a refusal, not a decision. The query is built with no SQL parser. Its keys and predicate are the shadow index's, read on scratch with `pg_get_indexdef` and `pg_get_expr` as R-1153 reads them, and it reads from a subquery that adds the shadow column under its own name, with the value the copy gives it: the cast with its collation, the migration's `USING`, or R-1135's zone. A row with a null in any key is left out, unless the index is `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. `migrate` and `rollback` preflight run it. When the new type doesn't exist yet, because the migration creates it, as every enum swap's does, preflight runs it in a transaction of its own, with `statement_timeout` off, that first runs the migration's statements creating that type, then the `GROUP BY`, and always rolls back. So a merge is a preflight refusal with exit code `2`, with nothing recorded and no migration left `failed`, as for any other type. `CREATE TYPE` is transactional, so the rollback leaves no type behind, and the transaction takes only `ACCESS SHARE` on the table and its indexes, and on the schema and the old type: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with it held open after the `GROUP BY` had found a merge, an `UPDATE`, an `INSERT`, a `DELETE`, and `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` on the old type, from another session with a `500ms` `lock_timeout`, each went through, and after the rollback `pg_type` held no new type. It's skipped only for a change between `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, where each value keeps its number or fails with an error. A merge written after the check fails the concurrent unique build, which stops that step as `failed`, and `rollback --failed` drops the shadow objects. Until cutover, a write that would merge gets `Error::Unique` on the shadow index, as R-1153 says. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, this query found `1.01` twice for `numeric(10,4)` to `numeric(10,2)`, the same `(1, 1)` twice on a partial two-column unique index for `text` to `integer`, rows outside its predicate left out, and `abc` twice for a change to a case-insensitive ICU collation, with the nulls left out, while building the same unique index concurrently on the copied values failed with `could not create unique index` and left it invalid. Both `America/New_York` times above gave the same `timestamptz`, and so did `01:30` before and after clocks went back, going the other way.

reqs.text: **Partitioned tables in the other safe forms.** Postgres can't build an index concurrently on a partitioned table, or attach an index to a constraint there. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on one failed with `cannot create index on partitioned table ... concurrently`, and `ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX` failed with `ALTER TABLE / ADD CONSTRAINT USING INDEX is not supported on partitioned tables`, even on an index built without `CONCURRENTLY`. So R-0319's concurrent indexes, R-0560's unique key, R-0561's primary key, R-0562's index, and R-1152's and R-1158's rebuilds in place each refuse a partitioned table with exit code `2` before the migration's first step, naming the table and saying `--fast` handles it. The models can't declare a partitioned table, so scratch never has one, and `migrate` and `rollback` preflight check the live database. Under `--fast` each runs as one plain `CREATE INDEX`, `ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE (...)` or `ADD PRIMARY KEY (...)` on the partitioned table, which builds the index on every partition under the lock it takes. It reaches every partition, so it runs only when each is declared by a model, under R-1168's rule, and is refused otherwise, under `--fast` too. Postgres refuses a unique key or a primary key on a partitioned table that leaves out a column of the partition key, with `unique constraint on partitioned table must include all partitioning columns`, so preflight refuses that too, under `--fast` as well, naming the partition key's columns. A partition on its own is a plain table to these forms: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX` on one worked on both versions, so they run there with no long lock.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **An inherited column changes only through its top parent.** On a partitioned table, or a table in old-style inheritance, a column the children inherit can only be changed on the table at the top. Postgres refuses to change it on a child or a partition alone, with `cannot alter inherited column`, and a change on the top parent changes it on every child and partition with it. So when a migration changes such a column's type or collation, `migrate` and `rollback` run one `ALTER` on the top parent, and only when your models declare every child and partition it reaches, each with the same change. Otherwise they stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the column, its top parent and every child and partition: a change to a child's or a partition's column without its top parent, a change that would reach a child or a partition your models don't declare, or declare with the old type, and a change to a column a child inherits from two parents, which no one `ALTER` can make.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: morm never changes a table your models don't declare, and Postgres can't change a child's inherited column on its own.
>
> **How to go on.** Declare every child and partition in your models with the same change, make it on the top parent too, and run `makemigrations` again. A column a child inherits from two parents can't be changed by morm, so change it by hand outside morm, then let your models follow.
>
> **What you give up.** A child or a partition you'd rather leave out of your models has to be declared before its inherited column can change.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **A type change drops and adds back the foreign keys on an index it rebuilds.** When morm rebuilds an index after a type change, as the notice above says, and a foreign key references that index, Postgres won't drop the index while the foreign key is there, and has no way to move the foreign key to a new index. So morm drops the foreign key and adds it back with the same name and rules. In place on a live table, it builds the new index first with no long lock, swaps the index and the foreign keys in one short transaction that gives way to your app, as a cutover does, and then checks the existing rows with `VALIDATE`, which doesn't block writes. Every write is checked by the old foreign key or the new one, so no row that breaks it can get in. Under `--fast`, all of it runs in the one transaction. A foreign key your models don't declare on that index stops the migration with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming it.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: the index can't be rebuilt any other way.
>
> **How to go on.** For a foreign key your models don't declare, declare its table in your models, or drop that foreign key first.
>
> **What you give up.** The short transaction takes a full lock on the key table and every table that references it, for a few milliseconds. Until `VALIDATE` finishes, Postgres marks the foreign key `NOT VALID`, although it checks every write, so the planner can't use it to leave out a join.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **An online change refuses values that would become one on a unique index.** A type change, a collation change or an enum's map can make two different values equal: `1.0051` and `1.0149` both become `1.01` in `numeric(10,2)`, `'01'` and `'1'` both become `1` as an `integer`, `'abc'` and `'ABC'` become equal under a case-insensitive collation, and mapping `pending` to `active` puts two rows on `UNIQUE (uid) WHERE status = 'active'`. Before an online change touches a table, morm looks for such values on every unique index that holds the column, and stops `migrate` or `rollback` with exit code `2`, naming the table, the index, the values and how many rows hold each. When the new type comes from the same migration, as an enum swap's does, it creates that type in a transaction of its own, looks, and rolls the transaction back, so nothing is left behind and the migration isn't marked `failed`. The check only reads, so your app's reads and writes go on while it runs.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: no answer can make two rows one on a unique index.
>
> **How to go on.** Change or remove the rows that would merge, or drop the unique index first if equal values are what you want, then run it again.
>
> **What you give up.** The check reads the whole table once. A row that would merge, written after the check, stops the migration as `failed` when the new unique index is built, and `rollback --failed` cleans up. While the change runs, such a write fails with `Error::Unique` on the column's field.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **Adding an index or a unique key to a partitioned table needs `--fast`.** On an existing table, morm builds an index with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and turns a unique index into a unique key or a primary key with `USING INDEX`, so writes never wait. Postgres can do neither on a partitioned table. So adding an index, a unique key or a primary key to one, or rebuilding an index on one after a type change, stops `migrate` and `rollback` with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the table. Your models can't declare a partitioned table, so this only happens on one made outside morm. A single partition is a plain table, so these run there with no long lock.
>
> **How to go on.** Write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it in a maintenance window. A unique key or a primary key on a partitioned table must include every column of its partition key, so morm refuses one that doesn't, under `--fast` too, naming those columns. Under `--fast` the index reaches every partition, so each must be declared in your models, as the notice on changes that reach a child or a partition says.
>
> **When `--fast` is right.** Only with apps stopped, or on tables small enough that building the index under a lock doesn't matter.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` builds the index on every partition under a lock that blocks writes to the table until it's done.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **A foreign key from a partitioned table needs `--fast` on Postgres 15 to 17.** On an existing table, morm adds a foreign key `NOT VALID`, which checks no rows, then checks the rows already there with `VALIDATE` in a separate step, which doesn't block writes. Postgres 15 to 17 can't add a foreign key `NOT VALID` on a partitioned table, and Postgres 18 can. So on 15 to 17, adding a foreign key from a partitioned table, adding one back after an index rebuild, or restoring one in a `rollback` stops `migrate` or `rollback` with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the table, the foreign key and the server's version. A foreign key from a single partition, or from a plain table to a partitioned one, runs as usual.
>

>
> **How to go on.** Write the migration with `makemigrations --fast`, or roll back with `rollback --fast`, and run it in a maintenance window, or upgrade the server to Postgres 18, where the usual form runs.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` adds the foreign key in one statement that checks every row of every partition while writes to those tables, and to the table it references, wait. A row that breaks it stops the statement, naming the partition, with nothing changed. In a `rollback` of a retire, keeping the foreign key `NOT VALID` isn't offered for such rows.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **A change that reaches a child or a partition needs every one declared.** On a partitioned table, or a table in old-style inheritance, Postgres carries most changes from the table to every child and partition: adding, dropping or renaming a column, `NOT NULL`, a default, a CHECK, and on a partitioned table also an index, a unique key, a foreign key, a trigger and identity. Dropping a partitioned table drops every partition. And Postgres refuses most of these on a child or a partition alone when it holds the column or the constraint from its parent. So `migrate`, `rollback` and `purge` run such a change once, on the top parent, and only when your models declare every child and partition it reaches, each making the same change to its columns. Otherwise they stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the change, the table, its top parent and every child and partition it reaches: a change that would reach a child or a partition your models don't declare, or declare without that change, and a change to what a child or a partition holds from its parent, made without its top parent. `--fast` doesn't change this. Retiring a table with children or partitions retires every one of them in the same migration, or none.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: morm never changes a table your models don't declare, and Postgres would change such a child with no model asking for it.
>
> **How to go on.** Declare every child and partition in your models with the same change, make the change on the top parent too, and run `makemigrations` again.
>
> **What you give up.** A child or a partition you'd rather leave out of your models has to be declared before its parent can change. A child created by hand after a column is retired stops that column's `purge` until it's declared.

SET SCHEMA _morm_retired` stayed attached to its partitioned table, which kept routing new rows to it and returning its rows, and an inheritance child moved the same way stayed in `pg_inherits` under its parent, whose reads still returned its rows. reqs.text: **What a child or a partition holds from its parent.** Postgres puts some of a parent's objects on each child and partition, and they belong to the parent. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a CHECK on an inheritance parent or a partitioned table sat on every child, grandchild and partition under the parent's name, with `conislocal = false` and `coninhcount` counting the parents it came from, and a child of two parents held each one's. A foreign key, a primary key and a unique key on a partitioned table sat on every partition with `conparentid` pointing at the parent's constraint, `conislocal = false` and `coninhcount = 1`: the foreign key under the parent's name, the primary key as `<partition>_pkey`, the unique key under a name Postgres made, such as `q1_v_id_key`, and each under the partition's own name when `ATTACH PARTITION` took over a matching one the partition already had. An index on a partitioned table sat on every partition under a name Postgres made, such as `p1_a_idx`, or under the name of a matching index the partition had before `ATTACH PARTITION`, linked to the parent's index by a `pg_inherits` row whose `inhrelid` is the partition's index. A foreign key that references a partitioned table added a row on the referencing table for each partition, with `conparentid` set, named `r_x_fkey1` on 17.11 and `r_x_fkey_1` on 18.6. On 18.6 a `NOT NULL` is a `pg_constraint` row, and a child held its parent's under the parent's name, such as `parent_id_not_null`. An inheritance parent's foreign keys, primary key, unique keys and indexes weren't copied, and a CHECK marked `NO INHERIT` stayed on the parent. A child or a partition couldn't drop what it held, failing with `cannot drop inherited constraint` and `cannot drop index ... because index ... requires it`. `indisclustered` follows no tree: `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER ON` a partitioned table's index failed with `cannot mark index clustered in partitioned table`, and on a partition's index or an inheritance parent's index it marked that index alone. After `DETACH PARTITION`, everything the partition held became its own, with `conislocal = true`, `coninhcount = 0` and no `pg_inherits` row for its indexes, and after `NO INHERIT` a child's CHECKs became its own the same way. So the catalog reader reads each constraint with `coninhcount > 0` or `conparentid <> 0`, and each index with a parent index in `pg_inherits`, as part of the object it was copied from, which it reads once, on the table it was created on, and leaves it out of the child's, the partition's and the referencing table's own objects. A child's or a partition's model declares only its own constraints and indexes, the ones with `coninhcount = 0`, no `conparentid` and no parent index, and the parent's model declares the rest, once, apart from a partition's primary key, which R-1183 covers. Nullability stays a column's, read from `attnotnull` on every version, so Postgres 18's `NOT NULL` rows are never objects of their own. Postgres prints every index on a partitioned table with `ON ONLY`, as `CREATE INDEX p_a_ix ON ONLY x.p USING btree (a)` for one created without it, so the reader reads that definition as the same index on a plain table, which is how scratch builds it. A CHECK an inheritance child declares itself and also inherits, with `conislocal = true` and `coninhcount > 0`, is the parent's while it's inherited. When the parent's is dropped, Postgres keeps it on the child, with `coninhcount = 0`, as an object of the child's own that no model declares. > **A partition's `pk` must stay on its parent's key.** A partition's model may mark `pk` on the key the partition holds from its partitioned table, on the parent's key columns, in their order. The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **A partition's model can't have identity, and the column its parent's identity fills is `db_set`.** A partition takes its values from its parent's identity, with no sequence of its own, and Postgres refuses identity of its own on a partition. `base = "common"` and `base = "pk_only"` add `id` as identity, and so does a field marked `identity`. So `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before anything changes when a partition's model has identity, naming the partition, the column and the parent's identity column. A partition's model whose inserts send the column its parent's identity fills is refused too, when a pool starts: under `GENERATED ALWAYS`, Postgres refuses every such insert with `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column`, and under `BY DEFAULT`, the keys you send can collide with the ones the parent's sequence gives later. So `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch`, naming the partition, the column and the parent's identity column, and saying to mark the field `db_set`. The compiler and `makemigrations` can't see either, because your models don't say a table is a partition, so they show up when a command or a pool reaches the database.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: Postgres would refuse the identity partway through the migration, and would refuse every insert that sends a `GENERATED ALWAYS` column.
>
> **How to go on.** Declare the partition's model with `base = "bare"`, mark `pk` on the parent's key columns, with no identity, and mark the column the parent's identity fills `db_set`, so inserts leave it out and Postgres gives each row the parent's next value, which the insert fills in on the row. When a migration adds identity to the parent's column, the partitions' models leave identity out and mark that column `db_set`, in the same release that marks the parent's column `identity`, deployed with the builds that insert into the table stopped, as the next notice says.
>
> **What you give up.** Inserts through a partition's model can't choose the key: each row gets the parent's next value. To write keys you choose, insert through the parent's model with `.explicit_ids()`, and Postgres puts each row in its partition.

Postgres refuses each such insert into a column with `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity, while `COPY` doesn't. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, after a plain `integer` key holding 1 and 2 got `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` with its sequence set to 2, `INSERT INTO t (id, v) VALUES (3, 'x')` failed with `428C9` `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"`, and so did one sending `NULL`, while one leaving `id` out took `3` and one with `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` stored its key. `COPY t (id, v)` stored a sent `3` with no error, and the next insert leaving `id` out was given `3` and failed with `23505`, on a plain table and on a partition. So `check_schema`, at pool start as R-1116 says and in `db.check_schema()`, fails a model of any table whose inserts send a column whose `attidentity` there is `a`, as one more insert case. The finding names the table and the column, says the column is `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity, which a build made before the migration that gave it identity doesn't know, and says to mark the field `db_set`, so inserts leave the column out and the row Postgres returns fills it, or `identity`, which leaves it out the same way and is what a model of a table morm migrates declares, so that the next `makemigrations` keeps the identity. A field marked `identity` or `db_set` passes, and `.explicit_ids()` never meets this, because it sends `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, and its `COPY` takes the key under either kind. On a partition, that column gets R-1190's finding, naming the parent's identity column, and no second one. reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the rolling deploy rows:

> **A build whose inserts send an identity column won't start.** Postgres refuses every insert that sends a value into a `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column, even `NULL`, with `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column`. Into a `GENERATED BY DEFAULT` one it takes the key you send, but the sequence doesn't move past it, so it hands that key out again later, and that insert fails with `duplicate key`. A field your model marks `identity` or `db_set` is left out of every insert, and `.explicit_ids()`, on `insert`, `insert_many`, `insert_stream`, `upsert` and `upsert_many`, lets your keys in under either kind and moves the sequence past them. Any other field is sent, an `Option` one whenever it holds a value. So when a pool starts, `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch` for a model whose inserts send a column with identity of either kind, naming the table, the column and the kind, and saying to mark the field `identity`, or `db_set`, and to write keys you choose with `.explicit_ids()`, before any of your queries run. On a partition, the notice above says what to do.
>
> **When it's right.** Always, for a build you mean to run. This is how a build made before a migration gave that column identity shows up, such as an older release brought back: it's refused at startup instead of failing each insert in production, or storing keys that collide later. It's worse with `insert_stream`: `COPY` stores the keys it sends with no error under either kind, and the sequence hands the same keys out again later, so a later insert fails with `duplicate key`. It also catches a newer build that took `identity` off a field before the migration that drops the identity has run, and a model that writes its own keys into a `BY DEFAULT` column with plain inserts, which works only until the sequence reaches them.
>
> **How to go on.** Mark the field `identity`, as the build made with the migration does, or `db_set` in a partition's model. In a model of a table morm migrates, mark it `identity` rather than only `db_set`, so `makemigrations` keeps the identity. To write keys you choose, under either kind, use `.explicit_ids()`, which keeps the sequence ahead of them. Plan the deploy that adds identity as the next paragraph says.
>
> **What you give up.** Keys you choose go in only through `.explicit_ids()`, never through a plain insert. The role that writes them needs `UPDATE` on the table as well as `SELECT` and `UPDATE` on its sequence, and moving the sequence holds the table's other writes back for a moment, as the notice on `.explicit_ids()` says. A build made before such a migration can't start again after it, so rolling the app back past it needs the migration rolled back too. A running one isn't stopped: morm checks once, when a pool starts, so its inserts into that table keep failing, or keep sending keys that collide later, until you stop it. `check_schema = "off"` lets such a build start, with those inserts.

So adding identity to a column that has a default is one op, in one transaction, under the table's `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, taken first. It takes the lock of each sequence the default calls, found through `pg_depend` from the default's `pg_attrdef` row, with a same-value `ALTER SEQUENCE ... INCREMENT BY`, because `LOCK TABLE` refuses a sequence, and reads each one's next value from `last_value`, `is_called` and its increment. It drops the default. The inverse is one op in one transaction too. It reads the next value, owner, privileges and comment of the identity's sequence the same way, drops the identity, which drops its sequence, rebuilds the old sequence under its name from the definition the schema before holds, with its type, start, increment, minimum, maximum, cache and cycle, `OWNED BY` the column, with that owner, those privileges and that comment, sets it so that its next value is the greater of the identity's next value and the value after the column's highest, and sets the old default back as `pg_get_expr` printed it. It takes the lock of each sequence the default calls, found through `pg_depend` from the default's `pg_attrdef` row, with a same-value `ALTER SEQUENCE ... INCREMENT BY`, because `LOCK TABLE` refuses a sequence, and reads each one's next value from `last_value`, `is_called` and its increment. It drops the default. It drops the sequence the column owns, found through `pg_depend` with `deptype = 'a'`, as `serial` makes one, after reading its privileges and comment. A sequence the column didn't own, whose last value 51 the table held, gave the identity 52, and after it was set back to 10 the inverse moved it to 53. On a partitioned table, a partition made by `PARTITION OF` and one attached with its own default on the parent's sequence both lost their default and read the parent's identity, inserts through a partition and through the parent got the carried values, and the inverse put the default back on all three.

**R-1201** The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **A sequence something else uses can't become a column's identity.** When a migration gives identity to a column whose default calls a sequence the column owns, such as `serial`'s, morm drops that sequence and gives the identity's sequence its name and position, in one transaction. Postgres won't drop a sequence anything else depends on, such as another table's default, a view or a function. An inheritance child's default on it would be dropped with the parent's, and Postgres gives the parent's identity to partitions but not to inheritance children. So `migrate`, and `makemigrations` when it can see it, stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the sequence, the column and each thing that uses it. `rollback` stops the same way when something has come to depend on the identity's sequence since.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: Postgres would refuse the drop partway through the migration, and an inheritance child would be left with no default and no identity, so each of its inserts would fail with `null value in column`.
>
> **How to go on.** Keep the default on that column, or in an earlier migration give each other user a sequence or default of its own, then add the identity.
>
> **What you give up.** A sequence that several columns or objects share stays a plain sequence and default, for as long as it's shared.

reqs.text: - **Chosen keys through `upsert`.** `db.upsert(&mut p, target).explicit_ids()` and `db.upsert_many(&mut rows, target).explicit_ids()` write the keys you give into an identity column, under either kind: every `INSERT` they send, on every path, including the chunked one and `DO NOTHING`, carries `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, which Postgres takes with `ON CONFLICT`. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, `INSERT ... OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE` stored a new row under its given key and updated the existing one, through `VALUES` and through `UNNEST`, `DO NOTHING` took the clause the same way, and without it a sent key failed with `428C9` before any conflict was checked. The identity column is never in the `DO UPDATE SET` list, though the row supplies it: under `GENERATED ALWAYS` Postgres refused `SET id = EXCLUDED.id` with `column "id" can only be updated to DEFAULT`, and under `BY DEFAULT` it changed the existing row's key. So a row that conflicts on another target keeps the key it has, and the row Postgres returns fills the field with it. An upsert with a chosen key takes no value from the sequence and doesn't move it: after one stored 10, the next insert leaving the key out was given 3, so the sequence would give 10 again. So it moves the sequence past the highest key it sends, before sending any row, in the same transaction, the way inserts' `.explicit_ids()` does, and a single `upsert` with `.explicit_ids()` runs in the internal transaction with confirmed commit. A key left unused, because its row conflicted on another target, leaves a gap in the sequence, which is harmless.

**R-1204** The README shows this notice loudly, beside the `.explicit_ids()` row:

> **`.explicit_ids()` moves the identity's sequence, and the move has costs.** On `insert`, `insert_many`, `insert_stream`, `upsert` and `upsert_many`, `.explicit_ids()` writes the keys you give into an identity column and moves its sequence past the highest one, in the call's transaction, so later inserts aren't given those keys again. To read the sequence and move it safely, it takes an advisory lock on the sequence, so two imports into one table run one after the other, and then, briefly, `LOCK TABLE ... IN SHARE MODE` on the table. That costs four things. **A grant:** the role that writes chosen keys needs `UPDATE` on the table, or `MAINTAIN` on Postgres 17 and later, beside `SELECT` and `UPDATE` on the sequence, which normal identity inserts don't need. Without it the call fails with `permission denied`. On a partitioned table, grants on the parent are enough. **A brief hold on the table's other writes:** the lock waits for transactions already writing to the table to finish, and holds back every new insert, update and delete on it while it waits, inserts straight into a partition too, for up to `lock_timeout`, past which the call returns `LockTimeout`. Reads go on. `insert`, `insert_many`, `upsert` and `upsert_many` take it before sending any row, so a timeout leaves nothing written. **A deadlock with a stream:** `insert_stream` moves the sequence only after its `COPY`, so while it runs a normal insert can be given a key the stream writes, and a normal insert that waits on a streamed row, over that key or any other unique column, deadlocks with the stream's lock. Postgres breaks it by failing the stream with `deadlock detected`, so the stream returns `Deadlock`, rolled back with nothing written. **Collisions the move can't stop:** on a sequence with `CACHE` above 1, a chosen key at or below where the sequence stood may sit unused in another connection's cache, and that connection's later insert fails with `Unique`. A `nextval` called directly, other than by an insert into the table, isn't held back by the lock, so a value it draws can still collide with a chosen key.
>
> **When it's right.** When rows already have their keys and must keep them: an import, a copy from another database, rows restored from an export. Leave keys to Postgres everywhere else.
>
> **How to go on.** Give those grants only to the role that imports. Run imports while the table is quiet, and keep the app's write transactions on it short. `lock_timeout`, or `.lock_timeout()` on the import's transaction, is the longest the move holds the table's writes back, and after a `LockTimeout` from `insert`, `insert_many`, `upsert` or `upsert_many` nothing was written, so run the call again. While `insert_stream` writes chosen keys, stop normal inserts into the table, or load the rows in chunks with `insert_many`, which moves the sequence before sending any row and holds no table lock while the rows go in, so it can't deadlock this way. After a `Deadlock` nothing was written: once normal inserts have stopped, run the stream again from the start of its source. Keep the sequence at `CACHE 1`, Postgres's default, with `ALTER SEQUENCE ... CACHE 1`, or don't import chosen keys into a sequence with a larger cache, and don't call `nextval` on it directly while an import runs.
>
> **What you give up.** Chosen keys need a wider grant on the table, a brief pause in its writes each time a call moves the sequence, and a quiet table while a stream with chosen keys runs. The sequence must stay at `CACHE 1`, with no direct `nextval` while imports run, or a later insert can fail with `Unique`.

> **morm's sessions always run in UTC.** Every connection starts with `TimeZone = 'UTC'`, whatever the server's or the role's zone, through PgBouncer in transaction mode too, and no setting changes it. Postgres converts between `timestamp` and `timestamptz`, formats a time and truncates one to a day in the session's zone, so if the zone varied by host or by role, the same query would give different rows on different machines, and raw SQL would disagree with what morm writes for a field. When code needs a user's local day or wall time, pass the zone in the SQL, as in `date_trunc('day', {Order::F.at}, ${zone: String})` or `{Order::F.at} AT TIME ZONE ${zone: String}`. PgBouncer 1.20 and later keeps each client's `TimeZone`, so the role's zone doesn't matter there. A pooler that drops the parameter, such as PgBouncer with `TimeZone` in `ignore_startup_parameters`, leaves the session in the role's zone: let it pass `TimeZone`, or set the role, `ALTER ROLE app SET timezone = 'UTC'`. If the session's zone is anything but `UTC` or one of its fixed aliases, such as `Etc/UTC`, `GMT` or `UTC0`, the pool refuses to start, with an error naming the zone the session reported, and a `timezone` key in `morm.toml` is refused too, because nothing can change the zone.
>
> **What you give up.** There's no session-local zone. In morm's sessions `current_date`, `now()::date`, `localtimestamp` and `date_trunc('day', now())` give the UTC day and time, and a `timestamptz` turned into text, as `fetch_raw` or a `::text` cast returns it, reads with `+00`. A column default or view that leans on the session's zone, such as `DEFAULT current_date`, works in UTC for rows morm writes and in the role's zone for other clients, such as `psql`, so write the zone into it, as in `DEFAULT (now() AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Berlin')::date`.

**R-1215** The README shows this notice loudly, beside `sql_unchecked`:

> **`sql_unchecked` skips every check morm has for SQL.** It takes a `String` built at runtime, so `sql!`'s compile-time refusals can't see it, `check-sql` never sees it, and nothing stops a value from a request being pasted into the text, which is SQL injection. morm still writes each parameter's type, so a wrong shape is a Postgres error, but a free value compared with a column of another type, such as a `String` against a `citext` column, is silently case-sensitive, and only a `#[morm::test]` that runs that exact text reports it. **R-1216** The README shows this notice loudly, beside transactions:

> **Inside a transaction, a setting lasts until the transaction ends.** On `db`, `.lock_timeout(d)`, `.statement_timeout(d)` and `.transaction_timeout(d)` go before `.transaction(..)` and cover that transaction. On `tx`, `tx.lock_timeout(d).await?` takes effect at once and holds for the rest of the transaction, inside and after `tx.transaction(..)`, which is a savepoint, so set it back yourself if only one statement needs it. A setting changed inside a savepoint that then fails is undone with it. `tx` has no `.isolation(..)` or `.retry(n)`: the isolation level is fixed before a transaction's first query, and a savepoint can't retry a deadlock or a serialization failure, so set both on `db`, before `.transaction(..)`.

- **R-1223** **`sql!`'s syntax.** `sql!` takes one string literal. Outside strings, quoted identifiers, comments and dollar quotes, which the `morm-core` scanner skips, it reads three forms, and neither `{` nor `${` is valid SQL there:

  | Form | Writes | Checked at compile time |
  |---|---|---|
  | `{Order::F.vendor_id}` | The quoted column name, `"vendor_id"`, from the `F` constant | — |
  | `${vendor_id: Order::F.vendor_id}` | `($n::int8)`, the column's cast | The value fits the field's Rust type without loss |
  | `${ids: Order::F.id[]}` | `($n::int8[])`, the column's list cast | A `Vec`, slice or array whose elements fit |
  | `${since: NaiveDate}` | `($n::date)`, the type's `SqlType` cast | The value is that type, or a reference to it |

  Each value sits where it's used, so values can't be misnumbered. `[]` binds a list for `= ANY(..)`, `<> ALL(..)` and `unnest(..)`; an array column binds a whole array without `[]`, and `[]` on one is a compile error. An `Option` value fits only a nullable field, and a free `Option<T>` is cast as `T`. A cast of your own after a value is kept, so `${s: String}::citext` is written as `($1::text)::citext`. A free value's type must be concrete, because the query is registered in a static, so `${v: T}` inside a generic `fn` fails with `E0401`. The text is a compile-time constant, built by `const` concatenation of the literal's pieces, the `F` names and the casts. `sql!` returns a `morm::Sql<'a, P>`: the text, its registration, and `P`, the query's own set of values, which the compiler fills in at each `sql!`: a flat tuple of borrows, each tagged with its carrier, with nothing boxed or allocated, of at most 64 values, the sizes `Params` is implemented for. `Params` is `Send` and `Sync`, so a query taken by value or by reference through `&impl Conn` keeps the future `Send`. `sql!` writes it as struct literals, so `let q = sql!(..)` keeps any temporary a value makes alive as long as `q`. A query can be stored in a variable, run several times, passed to a function and run there, and a function returning one writes `-> Sql<'a, impl Params>`. `db.sql()` and `db.raw()` are generic over `P`, so its values are encoded straight from the tuple. Owner decisions DH2, choice A, and DJ3; DK3 and DK6.

reqs.block: **R-1234** **The startup check also checks the session's zone.** morm's sessions always run in UTC, because every connection sends `TimeZone = 'UTC'` as a startup parameter, through PgBouncer 1.20 or later in transaction mode too, which tracks it per client. A pooler that drops it, such as PgBouncer 1.26.1 or later with `TimeZone` in `ignore_startup_parameters`, or one that doesn't track it, leaves the session in the role's zone, and this check is the backstop for that. So `check_schema`'s one catalog statement also reads `current_setting('TimeZone')`, with no extra round trip. It passes `UTC` and these aliases, each a tzdata zone that's a permanent zero offset with no daylight saving and no other history: `Etc/UTC`, `Etc/UCT`, `UCT`, `Etc/Universal`, `Universal`, `Etc/Zulu` and `Zulu`, which tzdata links to `Etc/UTC`, and `Etc/GMT`, `GMT`, `Etc/GMT0`, `GMT0`, `Etc/GMT+0`, `GMT+0`, `Etc/GMT-0`, `GMT-0`, `Etc/Greenwich` and `Greenwich`, which it links to `Etc/GMT`. It also passes one POSIX TZ string, `UTC0`, which Postgres parses itself rather than reading from tzdata, and which reads back as `UTC0` with offset 0 and abbreviation `UTC` at all times; no other POSIX form passes, such as `UTC+0`, `+00` or `<+00>-00`. The comparison is exact and case-sensitive, because Postgres reports a zone name in tzdata's own spelling however it was set: `utc` reads back `UTC`, `etc/utc` `Etc/UTC`, `ZULU` `Zulu`. Anything else, such as `Europe/London`, `Africa/Abidjan`, `WET`, `Etc/GMT+1` or a POSIX spec like `+00`, stops the pool: `Db::connect`, `connect_as`, `connect_to` and a pool `db.pool(name)` adds return `Error::Config`, naming the zone the session reported and saying to let the pooler pass `TimeZone` or to run `ALTER ROLE <role> SET timezone = 'UTC'`, before any of the app's queries has run. A wrong zone is reported as `Error::Config` ahead of any schema finding from the same statement. While it fails, every call through that pool returns the same error and runs the check again, as for a schema finding. A session given `UTC` by the startup parameter or by the role reports `UTC`, so a direct connection, or one through a PgBouncer that passes the parameter, always passes, whatever the role's zone. With `check_schema = "off"` the statement isn't run at the pool's start, so the zone isn't checked there either. `db.check_schema()` checks the zone too, whatever R-1117's setting says, and returns the same `Error::Config` for it, ahead of any finding. Owner decisions DI1, DI3, DI4 and DJ2; `proofs.md`, proof 9.

**R-1236** The README says this plainly, beside `sql!` and the field types, each with how to go on:

- **A free value's type must be concrete.** `sql!` registers each query in a static, which can't use a type parameter, so `${v: T}` inside a generic `fn` fails with rustc's `can't use generic parameters from outer item` (`E0401`), which doesn't say what to do. Name a concrete type, as in `${v: i64}`, or bind the value through its field, as in `${v: Order::F.id}`.
- **An `Option` value binds only through a nullable field.** Comparing an `Option<i64>` with a `NOT NULL` column, as in `.by(F.id, &maybe_id)`, fails to compile with ``the trait bound `Option<i64>: Fits<i64>` is not satisfied``, because a `NULL` there would match no row. Handle `None` in your code and bind the value inside it: a `NOT NULL` column has no `NULL` to match.
- **A non-text Rust type can't sit on a domain made by hand.** `#[col(sql = "posint")] pub n: i32`, on a domain over `integer` that morm doesn't know, is a compile error naming the field, because only text fields may sit on a SQL type morm doesn't know. Derive `PgDomain` on a one-field struct, `pub struct PosInt(pub i32);`, and use it as the field's type.
- **One `sql!` query holds at most 64 values.** Its values are a tuple, and stable Rust can't implement a trait for tuples of every length, so morm implements it for up to 64 values, and `sql!` refuses a 65th at compile time with an error naming the limit. Split the query, bind a list through a field with `[]` in place of many single values, or, for SQL built at runtime, use `sql_unchecked`.

The README ends with a "Contributing" section, which step 12 starts and this step keeps, showing this notice loudly:

> **A green `pooler` job can have skipped a PgBouncer version.** When a version can't be installed in a run, after one retry, or its download doesn't match its pinned SHA-256, its cases are skipped, not failed, and the job writes a `::warning::` naming the PgBouncer and Postgres versions, such as `PgBouncer 1.22 skipped on Postgres 17: install failed`. - **Enum and composite result columns are read as text.** `tokio-postgres` looks up any result column type that isn't built in, with named statements of its own, once per connection per type. Behind PgBouncer with no prepared statements, 1.20.1, or a later version with `max_prepared_statements = 0`, those statements reach other server connections and fail with `26000` `prepared statement "sN" does not exist`: 83 of 120 enum decodes failed on 1.20.1 with a pool of 4, and 86 of 120 on 1.22.0 with `max_prepared_statements = 0`. So morm never lets the driver see such a column. Every result column morm writes, in a model's or a view's column list, `filter_cols`, `RETURNING`, related rows and keyset pages, whose type is an enum, a composite, a domain over either, or a type morm doesn't know that a field with a text form sits on, such as `citext` or `ltree`, is read as `"col"::text`, or `"col"::text[]` for an array, which keeps the column's name. `SqlType` says how through `READ_AS`, the cast written after a result column, or nothing: `text` for `PgEnum` and `PgComposite` and for a `PgDomain` over one of them, `text[]` for a list of any of these, and for a list of a `PgDomain` over a built-in type its base type's array, such as `int4[]` for a list of a domain over `integer`, because Postgres sends an array of a domain as the domain's own array type, with an OID of 16384 or more, where it sends a scalar domain as its base type; every other type writes nothing. Stable Rust can't build a generic `Vec<T>`'s string from `T`'s, so each type also gives `READ_AS_LIST`, the cast for a list of it, beside `CAST_LIST`: `text[]` for `PgEnum`, `PgComposite` and a `PgDomain` over either, `T::CAST_LIST`, such as `int4[]`, for a `PgDomain` over a built-in `T`, and nothing for every other type; `Vec<T>` and `&[T]` take `T::READ_AS_LIST` as their `READ_AS`. `#[model]` and `#[view]` also read as text a field with a text form whose `sql` names a type morm doesn't know. The cast is written into the compile-time column list, so it costs nothing at run time. `PgEnum`'s and `PgComposite`'s `FromSql` accept only `text`, so an uncast column can't decode by luck on one connection and fail on another. `PgComposite` decodes Postgres's text form, `(a,b)`, with no lookup: a field with nothing between its delimiters is NULL, `""` is an empty string, a backslash escapes the next character, inside quotes `""` is one `"`, and a nested composite or array field is passed to its own type's decoder. It checks every position and length against the input, and returns an error, never a panic, on a field count that doesn't match, a NULL in a field that isn't an `Option`, a missing delimiter, an unclosed quote or anything after the closing parenthesis. A scalar domain over a built-in type needs no cast, because Postgres sends a domain's base type in the row description: on 18.6 a column of a domain over `text` came back as `text`, and one of a domain over an enum as that enum, while on 18.6 and 17.7 `posint[]`, `dtext[]` and `denum[]` came back as their own array types, and `SELECT d::int4[]` read `{1,2}`. Owner decisions EA and EF2.
