**The stale-session signals, recognised in any language.** `lc_messages` translates every message but an `elog`'s, and a server set to another language sends that language to every client, so morm reads no translated text. It knows each signal by something that doesn't change with the language: the SQLSTATE, the routine field, which Postgres never translates, an identifier in the message, which is never translated either, or the message of an `elog`, which is always English. R-1270's machine sorts the signals into two classes by what cures them, which is all it needs to know. On Postgres 15 to 18:

| Signal | Recognised by | Class | Cured by | Can client input cause it? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0A000` from a cached statement | routine `RevalidateCachedQuery` | statement | a fresh statement | Yes: a `search_path` set per transaction over tables of different shapes, with no schema change |
| `22P02` from a cached statement that casts a parameter to a non-built-in type, not holding that cast's type name as a whole identifier, with or without its schema, which Postgres prints only when the type isn't on the `search_path` | routine `enum_in` and that name test | statement | a fresh statement, when it's stale | Yes: a client's label converted to another enum, or a row it changed between two runs |
| Any other error from a cached statement that casts a parameter to a non-built-in type, outside a transaction (choice I) | none | statement | a fresh statement, when it's stale | Yes: every ordinary error, such as `23505` |
| `XX000` from a cached statement | message starting `cache lookup failed for type` | statement first: a fresh run tells it from compiled code | a fresh statement, or a new session when plpgsql raised it | No: it needs DDL |
| `XX000` from a fresh run, or from a statement that isn't cached | message starting `cache lookup failed for type` | session | a new session | No |
| `42804` from any statement | routine `plpgsql_param_eval_recfield`, `plpgsql_param_eval_generic` or `plpgsql_param_eval_generic_ro` | session | a new session, when stale | Yes: a record variable fed rows of the caller's choice, with no schema change |
| `22P02` from any statement, holding `_morm_retired_`, with no bound parameter's text holding it | routine `enum_in` and the identifier | session | a new session, when stale | Yes: stored or transformed text |
| `22P02` holding `_morm_retired_` that a bound parameter's text holds | R-0981's parameter test | none: returned as it is | | It's the client's own label |
| `XX000` from any statement | message starting `could not open relation with OID` | transient, R-0981 | | No |
| A lost connection, SQLSTATE class `08`, `40`, `53` or `57`, `55P03`, or `25P02` | the connection, or the SQLSTATE | not a signal; as a fresh run's outcome it neither confirms nor fails | | A timeout can be; `25P02` comes from the app's own transaction on a `db.hold()` connection |

**A confirmation** is a fresh run of the same statement text with the same parameter bytes, where the cached statement or the old connection failed, that succeeds, with or without rows, as an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `CALL` that returns only its command tag does, or that ends in a server error other than the first one and off the no-confirm list. reqs.text:
**Behind PgBouncer, a statement generation every process shares.** PgBouncer keeps one server statement per text and hands it to every client that prepares that text, so a stale one survives a re-prepare and a new client connection, and a counter inside each process starts at the same value in every process. So with `pooler = "transaction"` and the statement caches on, the text morm prepares for a cached statement starts with `/* morm g<n> */`, before any `.tag()`, where `<n>` is the database's statement generation, read from the `_morm` schema's comment, `morm statement generation <n>`, which every migration `tx` step raises in its own transaction, as `contracts.md` says. Any role reads it from `pg_description` with no grant, and a database with no `_morm`, or no such comment, reads as `0`. It's one fixed comment per generation, not per request, so R-0755 holds, and `pg_stat_statements` ignores it, as R-0714 says. Straight to Postgres, or with the caches off, there's no marker. A pool reads `<n>` when it starts, with one catalog query on its first connection, until step 41 folds that read into its startup statement; a pool whose startup check is off keeps that catalog query, so it reads `<n>` at start too. If that read fails, the pool's start fails with its error, as a failed first connection does, so no call runs before the pool holds `<n>` and its marker, R-1270's.

- **The marker moves two ways.** A read that counts as moved, after a migration, by R-1270's read order, is adopted in the step that applies it, as R-0982's event E1 says: the marker becomes `g<n>`, dropping any salt, the statement generation rises, and every pending and cool-down entry is removed, with no gate, because migrations pace it. An adopted `<n>` that isn't above every `<n>` the pool has adopted, its start read's included, as after a lowered `<n>` or a migration raising it back to a value the pool has held, makes the marker `g<n>.<salt>` with a fresh salt instead, so a pool never returns to a text it has used, whose server statements PgBouncer may still hold from before a later change; that takes one word, the highest adopted `<n>`. A read that doesn't count never moves the marker, so a read that arrives late never sets it back to a `g<n>` the database no longer holds. A process started after a lowering reads the lowered `<n>` at its start and uses `g<n>` unsalted, which other processes may have used before the change that lowered it, so step 50's README says to send `RECONNECT` after anything that lowers `<n>` while PgBouncer's server sessions stay up. In a pool that reaches several servers the marker never goes back: after a restore or a failover lowers `<n>` it keeps the old `g<n>` until `<n>` passes it, R-1270's. A *salt* action, taken through R-0982's gate when a stale statement is confirmed, or on `0A000`, with `<n>` unmoved, as after DDL made outside morm, makes it `g<n>.<salt>`, a new random 64-bit salt replacing any earlier one, and then, in the same step, raises the statement generation, R-1270's, even when a checkout's compare-and-swap started the take, so every connection clears its caches at checkout or its next cached run and prepares the new text, never the old one under the new generation, and the process's texts meet no stale server statement. Behind PgBouncer `<n>` is read in R-0718's row C1, on a confirmation or `0A000`, and in row D1, after the whole transaction's rollback, and a request never reads it.
- **Fresh runs are unnamed,** R-0718's, and while a statement has a pending entry every run of it is unnamed.
- **A stale session is never acted on pool-wide.** morm reaches a server session only through a client connection, so R-1245's session class behind PgBouncer moves no marker, adds no salt, raises nothing, and opens or discards no client connection. The statement's pending entry is removed, and after its first failure its session-class errors return at once for `stale_cooldown`, through the cool-down, R-1270's. It heals when PgBouncer replaces the server connection, through `RECONNECT` or its `server_lifetime`, as step 59 says.

| # | Signal | morm does | Caller gets | May request | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C2 | Session class, outside a transaction | Remove the statement's pending entry. If the statement is in the cool-down, nothing more; otherwise retry once on another client connection, and if that fails the same way, the statement enters the cool-down | The retry's result, or as it is | Nothing, ever | One run; under light load it usually reaches the same server session, under load another |
| D2 | Session class, inside a transaction | Remove the statement's pending entry. If the statement is in the cool-down, nothing more; otherwise the statement enters the cool-down and the whole transaction is rolled back | As it is in the cool-down; otherwise `Error::SchemaChanged`, failing the whole transaction | Nothing, ever | None |

Row D2 is built in step 20. With the caches off, as on PgBouncer 1.20.1, no statement is cached, so only C2 and D2 occur; `db.hold()` isn't available behind PgBouncer.

- `pool_stats()` shows the marker, `g<n>` or `g<n>.<salt>`, and counts the stale statements run unnamed, the salts added, the markers adopted and the cool-down's size.
- **What it costs.** One catalog read when a pool starts. Per call, outside a transaction at most one unnamed run, one catalog read and, for a stale session, one retry on another client connection; inside one at most one catalog read after the whole transaction's rollback. Stale handling never opens or discards a client connection. At most one salt per `stale_cooldown`, plus one adoption per migration. While old and new processes run side by side, or after salts, each server connection holds one set of statements for each marker in use, which PgBouncer's `max_prepared_statements` bounds per server connection.

Owner decisions SD, SE, SF, EJ5, EK1, EL2, EM1, EM2, MB, overlapping reads of `<n>` ordered by ticket, an overlapping read never counting, `<n>` only rising in a pool that reaches several servers, the machine's steps running under a short pool lock, the three stale-copy cases closed, a failed start read failing the pool, and `SchemaChanged` failing the whole transaction.

reqs.text: - **A hot standby ends a connection inside a transaction.** Replaying DDL on a hot standby, such as a migration's `ALTER TABLE`, ends a standby session that sits in a transaction that read the table, after `max_standby_streaming_delay`, with `FATAL` `40001` `terminating connection due to conflict with recovery`, and its next statement finds the connection closed. That transaction never committed and, on a standby, wrote nothing, and Postgres's own SQLSTATE says it may run again. So when a statement in a transaction finds its connection closed, the error morm's connection task kept, as step 12 says, was a `FATAL` with `40001`, and the statement wasn't the `COMMIT`, morm returns `Error::Serialization` and discards the connection, so `.retry(n)` runs the transaction again on a fresh one. A connection found closed by the `COMMIT` stays `Error::CommitUnknown`, as for any connection lost then. The routine Postgres names for the conflict differs by version, `ProcessInterrupts` on 15 and 16 and `ProcessRecoveryConflictInterrupt` on 17 and 18, so morm reads only the severity and the SQLSTATE. Owner decision SG.

reqs.text: - **Every `tx` step ends with a reset.** Postgres marks a cached plan invalid when an object it depends on changes, but a plain enum type gives it no such dependency, so after a swap a cached statement can keep the old type, and while the old type is kept under a retired name, a label both types share runs on the old order with no error. Creating and dropping an operator marks every cached plan in every session of the database invalid at commit, protocol-level statements and plpgsql's expressions included, as if each had run `DISCARD PLANS`, behind PgBouncer too, and it replays on a standby. So every `tx` step morm runs, in any command, `migrate`, `rollback`, `revert`, `rehearse`, `--resume` and `purge` among them, ends in its own transaction with `CREATE OPERATOR _morm.### (LEFTARG = int4, RIGHTARG = int4, FUNCTION = int4eq)`, `DROP OPERATOR _morm.### (int4, int4)` and `COMMENT ON SCHEMA _morm IS 'morm statement generation <n>'`, with `<n>` one more than the comment held, read in the same transaction, or `1` when it held none. It's one rule, with no list of kinds. `no-tx` and `batch` steps change no type and don't send it, and a step that rolls back sends nothing. It waits on no lock: on Postgres 15 to 18 it committed while another session sat in a `REPEATABLE READ` transaction that had read the table, and on 18.7, `pgbench -S` with 8 clients showed no change outside noise with one sent every 0.2 seconds. `COMMENT ON SCHEMA` needs the schema's owner, so the preflight of `migrate`, `rollback`, `rehearse` and `purge` checks that the migrating role owns `_morm`, or is a member of its owner, and has `CREATE` on it, and otherwise refuses with exit code `2`, naming `ALTER SCHEMA _morm OWNER TO <role>`, before anything changes. `status` shows the generation. reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the enum rows:

> **After an online enum swap, the old values read as `_morm_retired_<label>` until `purge`.** The cutover keeps the old type under a retired name, so the retired column holds every old value, and it renames each of that type's labels to `_morm_retired_<label>`. A query on the retired column shows `_morm_retired_pending` where it held `pending`. morm's ledger records every label, so down and rollback map each back and restore the real labels, and `purge` drops the column and the type. The rename is there for code still compiled against the old type, such as a cached statement or a plpgsql variable in an open session: it fails with `22P02` naming the retired type instead of answering by the old type's order, which after a reorder would be wrong with no error. morm apps recover from it by themselves.
>
> **How morm recovers, and what it costs.**
>
> - Outside a transaction, the call is retried once on a newly opened connection, which compiles the function fresh and takes the old connection's place.
> - Inside one, the app gets `Error::SchemaChanged`, and `.retry(n)` runs the transaction again on a newly opened connection; with no `.retry(n)`, each connection that had the function compiled fails one transaction and is replaced.
> - A label you send that holds `_morm_retired_` gets its `22P02` at once, with no retry.
> - Text holding `_morm_retired_` that your function reads or builds, such as a value read from a table or `lower(p)` of a client's text, costs each connection that was open at its first failure one replacement, then nothing: again at most once per `stale_cooldown`, 60 seconds by default, per pool, and again after each migration, never more than the pool's `max` replacements per `stale_cooldown`.
> - If Postgres refuses the new connection for too many connections, morm closes the stale one and opens the new one in its place, and does the same for the other replacements of that `stale_cooldown`, without first trying a connection beside each; if even that can't open, as during a failover, replacements pause for `stale_cooldown`, and the call gets its `22P02`.
> - Behind PgBouncer morm can't reach the server session: outside a transaction such a call is retried once on another connection, inside one it returns `Error::SchemaChanged` once, and then that statement's `22P02` returns at once for `stale_cooldown`, until PgBouncer replaces the server connection, as the PgBouncer notice says.
>
> **Rolling back the swap.** A materialized view above the column is built again on the restored type, in the rollback's transaction, so its contents come from today's table: `rollback` opens a decision saying so, whose default refuses, so the rollback stops with exit code `3`, having changed nothing, until you answer it on the same command, as `rollback --decide ID=OPT`; plan for that before you need an urgent rollback. The retired copy keeps the old rows until `purge`. The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **A transaction open across a cutover can see the old answers until it takes its next lock.** Postgres applies a committed schema change to a transaction that's already open only when that transaction next takes a lock. In a `READ COMMITTED` transaction begun before an enum swap's cutover, a statement that touches no table the cutover changed, such as a comparison of two labels, returns the answer it would have given a moment before the cutover, until the transaction reads another table. This happens with any DDL in Postgres, morm's or not, ends with the transaction, and isn't repeated by the next one, and a transaction that touches a swapped table can't straddle the cutover at all, because the cutover takes that table's lock.
>
> **What to do.** Keep transactions short around a migration.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside transactions:

> **On a hot standby, a migration can end a transaction.** Replaying a migration's DDL on a standby, such as an `ALTER TABLE`, waits up to the standby's `max_standby_streaming_delay` behind a session sitting in a transaction that read an affected table, and then Postgres ends that session with `40001`, so the standby lags meanwhile. morm returns `Error::Serialization` inside the transaction, which `.retry(n)` runs again on a fresh connection, and `Error::CommitUnknown` if the connection was found closed at `COMMIT`. A `db.hold()` connection gets `ConnectionLost`, naming the recovery conflict, and loses its session state.
>
> **What to do.** Don't sit in a transaction on a `read_only` pool, and give `.retry(n)` to transactions that run there.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside `pooler = "transaction"`, and it covers both modes:

> **A schema change made outside morm can fail calls inside transactions until morm repairs it, straight to Postgres and behind PgBouncer.** A change morm didn't make, such as an `ALTER` run by hand, can leave a cached statement stale: it fails every time until it's prepared again. Behind PgBouncer it's worse, because PgBouncer shares a prepared statement between clients by its text.
>
> - Outside a transaction a stale statement never reaches you: morm runs the call once more on a fresh statement, unnamed behind PgBouncer, and returns that answer.
> - Inside one you get `Error::SchemaChanged`, once per connection straight to Postgres, or once per `stale_pending_expiry`, 60 seconds by default, per process behind PgBouncer. `.retry(n)` hides it: once an attempt gets `Error::SchemaChanged`, every later attempt of that transaction runs all its statements unnamed, so it meets no stale statement, however many it runs and whatever changes while it retries. What that costs: Postgres parses and plans each statement of those attempts, as it does a statement morm doesn't cache, and only on retries after a `SchemaChanged`; a transaction's first attempt, and every call outside one, runs on cached statements as before.
> - **Inside `tx.transaction(..)`, a savepoint, `Error::SchemaChanged` fails the whole transaction,** as the notice on savepoints says, so `.retry(n)` runs the whole closure again. On a `db.hold()` connection inside a transaction you opened yourself, a stale statement's own error reaches you instead, as the notice beside `db.hold()` says.
> - **Each stale thing a transaction meets costs it one attempt.** Its stale statements cost one between them; straight to Postgres a stale session, such as a plpgsql function compiled before the change, costs one, because the next attempt runs on a newly opened connection; and a deadlock or a serialization failure costs its own, as always. So straight to Postgres `.retry(1)` hides a stale statement or a stale session, and **`.retry(2)` hides a stale statement and a stale session together**. Behind PgBouncer `.retry(1)` hides a stale statement, and a stale session heals only when PgBouncer replaces the server connection, as the notice on stale functions behind PgBouncer says.
> - morm clears every connection's statement caches, or behind PgBouncer moves every process's statements to fresh text, at most once per `stale_cooldown`, 60 seconds by default, per pool, plus once per migration.
> - Behind PgBouncer, a statement run only inside transactions, with no `.retry(n)` and different values each time, fails once per `stale_pending_expiry` until it runs outside a transaction, PgBouncer gets `RECONNECT`, or its `server_lifetime` passes.
>
> **Two cases give a wrong answer with no error,** because Postgres itself raises none:
>
> - **A transaction open across a schema change,** morm's or anyone's: its statements that take no new lock see the catalog as it was before the change.
> - **A type swap made outside morm that keeps the old type without renaming its labels:** a cached statement, or a plpgsql function compiled before the swap, that compares or converts a label both types share answers by the old type's order. For a statement that ends when it's prepared again, which morm does on every connection within `stale_cooldown` of the first stale error it confirms after the swap, or when its own stale error is repaired, or when its connection is replaced; for a function, when its session ends, which straight to Postgres is when morm replaces the connection and behind PgBouncer is `RECONNECT` or `server_lifetime`. If nothing in the pool ever errors, it lasts until the connection, or the server session, is replaced. While morm keeps such a statement pending, straight to Postgres and behind PgBouncer alike, its runs are unnamed and right, but between those times, and always with pending checks off, the old order can come back until one of those ends it.
>
> morm's own migrations leave only the first: they re-plan every cached statement and rename a kept type's labels, so stale code fails loudly instead. Run schema changes through morm, and use `.retry(n)`.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside raw SQL with `db.sql()`:

> **In raw SQL, read enum and composite columns as `::text`.** morm reads an enum, a composite or a type it doesn't know, such as `citext`, as text in every query it writes, because otherwise the driver looks the type up with statements of its own, which fail behind PgBouncer with no prepared statements. It can't add the cast to SQL you write, so write it yourself: `SELECT id, state::text FROM orders`, and `::text[]` for an array. A column holding an array of a domain over a built-in type needs its base array's cast, such as `::int4[]`, because Postgres sends it as the domain's own array type. An enum or composite column left uncast returns `Error::SchemaMismatch` naming the column and the cast, on every connection, and `check-sql` and `#[morm::test]` report every such column, a `citext` one included.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the migration commands:

> **The migrating role must own `_morm`, and each migration step makes every session re-plan once.** After each step that runs in a transaction, morm writes its statement generation into the comment of its `_morm` schema, which only the schema's owner can do. So `migrate`, `rollback`, `rehearse` and `purge` refuse with exit code `2`, before changing anything, unless the migrating role owns `_morm`, or is a member of its owner, and has `CREATE` on it. If another role created `_morm`, such as an admin role that set up the database, run `ALTER SCHEMA _morm OWNER TO <migrating role>` once as that role or a superuser. The same step also creates and drops a placeholder operator in `_morm`, which makes every session on the database, other applications' included, plan each cached statement again the next time it runs, once per step. That's how stale statements are cleared after a type swap; it costs one planning per cached statement, which a migration's other work usually dwarfs.

When it's set, `migrate`, at the end of every migration it applies, after that migration's last step has committed and the ledger records it as applied, connects to each listed admin console in turn and sends `RECONNECT` as a simple query with no parameters, because the console refuses the extended query protocol, as with `extended query protocol not supported by admin console` on 1.20.1 and 1.26.1, which closes each server connection of every database on that PgBouncer once it's released and opens new ones as clients need them, so a server connection in a transaction is never interrupted and the next one compiles every function fresh and prepares every statement fresh, which also clears a server statement a schema change made by hand left stale: on 1.26.1 in front of 17.12 and 18.6, after `RECONNECT`, new and old clients preparing a text whose server statement had gone stale got the right answer. `rollback` and `purge` do the same, because their steps change types too. A run that stops with an error after committing any `tx` step of a migration, such as an online swap whose cutover has committed and whose next step fails, also sends `RECONNECT` to each listed PgBouncer before it exits with that step's error, reporting failed sends as below, because the swapped type is live. Several PgBouncer processes can share one address with `so_reuseport = 1`, and a connection to it reaches only one of them, so a `RECONNECT` through it would leave the others stale with no error: after each `RECONNECT` over TCP, morm reads `SHOW CONFIG`, also as a simple query, and when `so_reuseport` is `1` it reports that PgBouncer as a failed send, naming the setting and saying to list each process's own Unix socket instead, its own `unix_socket_dir`, which reaches that process alone and works only from the PgBouncer's own host, or, from another host, to leave it out and let `server_lifetime` heal it; it treats every TCP URL to such a PgBouncer so, because `SHOW CONFIG` can't say whether the address is shared. Over a Unix socket morm sends `RECONNECT` with no `SHOW CONFIG`. `--plan`, `rehearse`, a run that applies nothing, and a schema change made by hand send nothing. If sending fails for any PgBouncer, because its console can't be reached, refuses the login or rejects the command, or it shares its address through `so_reuseport`, the migration stays applied, and `migrate` goes on to the next migration and to the other PgBouncers. When it ends it prints, for each PgBouncer that failed, its host and port, never its password, the error, and that its server sessions heal within its `server_lifetime` or after `RECONNECT` run by hand on that PgBouncer's console, because running `migrate` again applies nothing and sends nothing; it records each failure in `_morm.history`, and exits with code `1`, so a deploy step sees it. With no URL set, nothing is sent, and a stale server session heals when PgBouncer closes it after `server_lifetime`, 3600 seconds by default, which R-1040's decision text and the README say. morm never ends a server session itself, with `pg_terminate_backend` or otherwise, because that could end another client's transaction. On PgBouncer 1.20.1 and 1.26.1 in front of 18.6, with one server connection: after a relabel swap, a `DECLARE v st` function called through PgBouncer before the swap failed with `22P02` naming the retired type for a new client on the same server session; a transaction begun before `RECONNECT` ran on, on the same server session, and committed; and the next client after it was released reached a new server session and got the right answer. Owner decisions EJ5 and EK2, with this fix's choices the owner approves through PR #3: the key's name, its environment variable, `rollback` and `purge` sending it too, exit code `1` on a failed send, plain `RECONNECT`, for every database on that PgBouncer, this rule and its test living in step 59, which has the `pooler` job, and the `so_reuseport` check run only after a `RECONNECT` over TCP.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside `pooler = "transaction"`:

> **Behind PgBouncer, a stale function heals at the next server reconnect.** A plpgsql function compiled before a migration that morm couldn't refresh, one your migrating role doesn't own, stays stale in each PgBouncer server session that called it, because PgBouncer hands a new client the same server session. It heals when PgBouncer replaces that server connection. Without anything set, that's within PgBouncer's `server_lifetime`, an hour by default: lower it, such as `server_lifetime = 300`, if an hour of failures is too long.
>
> **To heal it at once,** list every PgBouncer process's admin console in `[migrations] pgbouncer_admin_urls`, or `MORM_PGBOUNCER_ADMIN_URLS`, and `migrate`, `rollback` and `purge` send each one `RECONNECT` after every migration, and when a run stops partway after one of its steps has committed. Each URL must name the `pgbouncer` database, or morm stops with `Error::Config`. Each URL gets `sslmode`'s default, `require`, as every connection morm opens does, and PgBouncer offers its clients TLS only when its `client_tls_sslmode` is set, so a TCP URL to a PgBouncer without it fails its send, with an error naming the notice on `sslmode`: give PgBouncer client TLS, or add `?sslmode=disable` to that URL if you reach it over a network you trust; a Unix-socket URL needs neither. Nothing in flight is interrupted: each server connection closes once its transaction ends. `RECONNECT` also clears the prepared statements a schema change left stale in PgBouncer's server sessions, because every server connection is replaced.
>
> **What it costs.** The URLs carry an admin login, so give PgBouncer a user that's in `admin_users` and nothing else, and pass its password through `${MORM_PGBOUNCER_ADMIN_PASSWORD}` or a secret, never in `morm.toml` itself. List every PgBouncer process: one left out keeps its stale sessions until `server_lifetime`. With `so_reuseport`, several processes share one address and a connection reaches only one of them, so morm must reach each process through its own Unix socket, which works only from the PgBouncer's own host: run `migrate` there, with each process's socket listed. Any TCP URL to such a PgBouncer is reported as a failed send on every migration, because morm can't tell which process it reached. From another host, such as a deploy runner, leave such a PgBouncer out and let `server_lifetime` heal it, or run `RECONNECT` on each process yourself. A hosted pooler with no admin console, such as a cloud provider's proxy, can't be told to reconnect, so it heals only by its own connection lifetime. After each migration every server connection on each listed PgBouncer is replaced as it's released, so expect a burst of new server connections to Postgres, as many as the PgBouncers' pools hold. If a `RECONNECT` fails, `migrate` reports which PgBouncer and exits with code `1`, with the migration still applied: run `RECONNECT` on that PgBouncer's console yourself, because running `migrate` again applies nothing and sends nothing.
>
> **After lowering morm's statement generation while PgBouncer's server connections stay up, send `RECONNECT`.** The generation, `<n>`, is the number in the `_morm` schema's comment, and morm's statement text behind PgBouncer starts with `/* morm g<n> */`. Restoring a dump into the live database, which puts back an older comment, or setting the comment lower by hand, lowers it without ending PgBouncer's server connections, so they can still hold statements prepared under an older `g<n>` text before a later schema change. A running pool that sees the lower `<n>` adds a fresh salt to its text, so it never meets them, but a process started after the lowering reads the lower `<n>` and uses that `g<n>` text unsalted, and can meet those statements: one more `Error::SchemaChanged` inside a transaction, or, after a type swap made outside morm that kept the old type, a wrong answer with no error until its first salt. `RECONNECT` on each PgBouncer's admin console replaces every server connection as it's released, so no such statement survives. It's right after any lowering that leaves the server connections up; a restore that recreates the database, a point-in-time restore and a failover end them anyway. What you give up: a burst of new server connections, as after a migration with `pgbouncer_admin_urls` listed. How to proceed: run `RECONNECT` on every PgBouncer process yourself, or run any migration with `pgbouncer_admin_urls` listed, before starting new processes; until then start no new app processes, or accept the cases above.
>
> **Meanwhile, behind PgBouncer,** a call whose function hits a retired enum label, or another error from code compiled in the server session before a migration, `type of parameter ... does not match` or `cache lookup failed for type`, is retried once on another connection outside a transaction, and inside one returns `Error::SchemaChanged`; after that its error returns at once for `stale_cooldown`, 60 seconds by default, because morm can't reach the stale server session. For a stale function morm never clears its statement caches or adds a salt, because new statement text runs in the same server session and calls the same compiled function; it heals when PgBouncer replaces that connection.

reqs.text:
**The stale-session settings.** Every tunable of the stale-session machine, these four, is a pool setting, set like any other: in `[pool]`, in one `[pools.<name>]`, or by its `MORM_POOL_*` variable for the pool a process opens at startup. Each holds per pool. The retry count and the hash and salt widths are part of the design, not settings. R-1289's `servers` is a pool setting the machine reads too, but it declares what the pool reaches rather than tuning the machine. Each default is the value the machine was designed and simulated with. A duration is written as a string with a unit, as every pool duration is.

| Setting | Default | Governs | Allowed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stale_cooldown` | `"60s"` | R-0982's window for pool-wide actions; straight to Postgres, the length of R-0981's epoch; behind PgBouncer, how long R-1246's cool-down returns a statement's session-class error at once | `"1s"` to `"10m"`; shorter, `"0s"`, `0` or `"off"` is `Error::Config`, because with no window every request would clear or replace the whole pool, as `wait_timeout` can't be off |
| `stale_cooldown_max` | `64` | how many statements the cool-down holds per pool, behind PgBouncer, the oldest dropped; straight to Postgres it holds nothing | `1` to `4096`; `0` is `Error::Config`, because a cool-down that holds nothing would give a statement hitting a stale server session a retry or a `SchemaChanged` on every call |
| `stale_pending_expiry` | `"60s"` | how long a pending entry, R-0718's, lasts from its creation | `"off"` or `"0s"`, which turn pending entries off, or up to `"10m"`; `0` and `"0"` are bare numbers, refused like every other bare duration |
| `stale_pending_max` | `64` | how many pending entries a pool holds, the oldest dropped | `0` to `4096`; `0` turns pending entries off |

A value outside these bounds, or a duration written as a bare number, stops the pool at start with `Error::Config`, naming the key and the bound it broke, the floor or the ceiling, before any of the app's queries has run. The ceilings keep memory bounded, at most about 200 KB per pool, and keep a misset value from delaying a real stale session's healing for hours. There's no `stale_first_failure_max`: with one epoch per pool there are no first-failure records to bound, and a `stale_first_failure_max` key stops loading with `Error::Config`, naming the key and saying it was removed, in whichever table it's in, `[pool]`, any `[pools.<name>]` or any other, as step 10's config loading says, so a setting copied from an earlier draft of these rules can't seem to work while it does nothing. The values aren't changed at run time. Owner decisions on the tenth review, EO3, EO4, MA and MC.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the pool settings:

> **The stale-session settings change how fast stale state heals and what it costs, and two of them can turn a check off.** `stale_cooldown`, `stale_cooldown_max`, `stale_pending_expiry` and `stale_pending_max` default to 60 seconds and 64 entries, the values morm's rules were designed and tested with. Each holds per pool. What a longer and a shorter value cost:
>
> - **`stale_cooldown`,** `1s` to `10m`, the one window for pool-wide repairs: morm clears every connection's statement caches, moves its statements to fresh text behind PgBouncer, or replaces every connection, at most once per window, plus once per migration. Longer: fewer clears and replacements when clients cause stale errors on purpose; but straight to Postgres a connection opened just before a change can return its stale error that long, a refused connection pauses replacements that long, and behind PgBouncer a statement hitting a stale server session returns its error at once that long. Shorter: up to the pool's `max` replacements and one cache clear per window.
> - **`stale_pending_expiry`,** up to `10m`, how long morm keeps a statement pending after a stale error inside a transaction. Longer: a client's bad label makes that statement run unnamed, straight to Postgres and behind PgBouncer alike, for every caller that long. Shorter: a statement run only in transactions with no `.retry(n)` fails with `Error::SchemaChanged` more often after a change made by hand, more so below `stale_cooldown`, where a pending check can end before the repair it asked for; `.retry(n)` hides it either way, because its later attempts run every statement unnamed.
> - **`stale_cooldown_max` and `stale_pending_max`,** at most `4096`. Each entry is a few bytes, keyed by statement text, so client values add none, and the ceilings hold morm to about 200 KB per pool. A value smaller than the number of statements pending, or hitting a stale server session, at once makes them push each other out: a statement pushed out costs a transaction with no `.retry(n)` one more `Error::SchemaChanged`, or behind PgBouncer one more retry on another connection, never a connection. `stale_cooldown_max` matters only behind PgBouncer.
>
> **What's refused.** `stale_cooldown` under one second, `"0s"`, `0` or `"off"`; `stale_cooldown_max` at `0`; any duration above `10m`; any count above `4096`; and a duration written as a bare number, `stale_pending_expiry = 0` and `"0"` among them, stop the pool at start with `Error::Config`, naming the key and the limit. So does `stale_first_failure_max`, a setting morm no longer has.
>
> **What `"off"` turns off.** `stale_pending_expiry = "off"` or `"0s"`, and `stale_pending_max = 0`, turn pending checks off. Straight to Postgres a statement a change made by hand left stale still heals, as each connection's copy fails once. Behind PgBouncer such a statement, run inside transactions, returns `Error::SchemaChanged` on every transaction's first attempt, until a call outside a transaction repairs it, PgBouncer gets `RECONNECT`, or its `server_lifetime` passes, though `.retry(n)` still hides it, because its later attempts run the statement unnamed, and while an old type is kept, a value both types share can run on the old type's order meanwhile, with no error. Leave them on unless you've read that and accept it.

> - **`stale_pending_expiry`,** up to `10m`, how long morm keeps a statement pending after a stale error inside a transaction. Longer: a client's bad label makes that statement run unnamed, straight to Postgres and behind PgBouncer alike, for every caller that long. Shorter: a statement run only in transactions with no `.retry(n)` fails with `Error::SchemaChanged` more often after a change made by hand, more so below `stale_cooldown`, where a pending check can end before the repair it asked for; `.retry(n)` hides it either way, because its later attempts run every statement unnamed.
> - **`stale_cooldown_max` and `stale_pending_max`,** at most `4096`. Each entry is a few bytes, keyed by statement text, so client values add none, and the ceilings hold morm to about 200 KB per pool. A value smaller than the number of statements pending, or hitting a stale server session, at once makes them push each other out: a statement pushed out costs a transaction with no `.retry(n)` one more `Error::SchemaChanged`, or behind PgBouncer one more retry on another connection, never a connection. `stale_cooldown_max` matters only behind PgBouncer.
>
> **What's refused.** `stale_cooldown` under one second, `"0s"`, `0` or `"off"`; `stale_cooldown_max` at `0`; any duration above `10m`; any count above `4096`; and a duration written as a bare number, `stale_pending_expiry = 0` and `"0"` among them, stop the pool at start with `Error::Config`, naming the key and the limit. So does `stale_first_failure_max`, a setting morm no longer has.
>
> **What `"off"` turns off.** `stale_pending_expiry = "off"` or `"0s"`, and `stale_pending_max = 0`, turn pending checks off. Straight to Postgres a statement a change made by hand left stale still heals, as each connection's copy fails once. Behind PgBouncer such a statement, run inside transactions, returns `Error::SchemaChanged` on every transaction's first attempt, until a call outside a transaction repairs it, PgBouncer gets `RECONNECT`, or its `server_lifetime` passes, though `.retry(n)` still hides it, because its later attempts run the statement unnamed, and while an old type is kept, a value both types share can run on the old type's order meanwhile, with no error. Leave them on unless you've read that and accept it.

reqs.text: - **The stale-session checks on the cached-statement path.** A cached statement's run with no pending entry in the pool, against the same run with no check at all, over a single-row read and a 1,000-row read: the pending check is one acquire atomic read of the pool's generation word per run, the same instruction as a plain load on x86-64, which holds the entry count beside the generations a connection compares itself with, and a checkout's check for a due pool-wide action rides on the one atomic read of the generation word that checkout already does, so the two stay within noise. A run with one unrelated entry pending, whose text doesn't match, and a run of a statement with its own entry, which runs unnamed straight to Postgres and behind PgBouncer alike, are measured too, so the cost of the text comparison, and of an unnamed run against the cached one it replaces while the entry lasts, is known. So is a `.retry(1)` transaction's second attempt after an `Error::SchemaChanged`, its statements run unnamed, against the same attempt run cached, over a one-statement and a five-statement transaction, so what a retry costs is known.

reqs.text:
**The stale-session machine is one pure module.** Every stale-statement and stale-session rule of this step and of step 20 is one state machine, built as one module of `morm`, such as `stale.rs`, with no I/O. It holds the pool's stale-session state, below, and its functions take a signal, the call's context (straight to Postgres or behind PgBouncer, inside a transaction or not, inside a `tx.transaction(..)` savepoint or not, on a held connection or not, from a cached statement or a fresh run) and the clock, and return a decision: answer with a fresh run, replace the connection, discard it, retry on the same connection, retry on another connection, return `Error::SchemaChanged`, or return the error as it is, with any pool-wide action to request. The pool and connection code carries the decisions out, and step 20's simulation drives this same module, so it tests the code that ships. The machine keeps two things apart:

- **Every call is repaired locally, always.** A stale statement gets one fresh run of the same call. A stale session straight to Postgres gets the call retried on a newly opened connection that takes the old one's slot. Inside a transaction the call returns `Error::SchemaChanged`, which fails the whole transaction, inside `tx.transaction(..)`'s savepoint too, and `.retry(n)`'s later attempts run every statement unnamed, on a newly opened connection when the old one was discarded; a stale session's error it returns as it is inside a savepoint, row B4's, is a Postgres error the savepoint clears. Nothing about the window, the epoch or a table changes what one call returns, beyond what its row says.
- **Every pool-wide action passes one gate,** R-0982's: clearing every connection's statement caches, adding a salt behind PgBouncer, and replacing every connection, each at most once per pool per `stale_cooldown`, plus once per migration.

The rows are R-0718's (the statement class, both modes), R-0981's (the session class straight to Postgres, the parameter test and the transient `XX000`), R-1246's (the session class behind PgBouncer) and R-0982's (the gate and the events). This step builds the state, the rows outside a transaction, A and C, and the events, E; step 20 adds the rows inside one, B and D, which this step's requirements state so the machine is written once.

**The state, per pool.** Each item is stated here once, with its bound and what clears it.

| State | What it is | Bound | Set or cleared by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marker `g<n>` or `g<n>.<salt>` | behind PgBouncer with the caches on, the comment starting each cached text, R-1246 | one value: its `<n>` and salt words and a sequence word, so a prepare's read with no lock gets a whole marker | set to `g<n>` by the start read; by `on_moved` to `g<n>` with no salt when its `<n>` is above the highest adopted `<n>`, and otherwise to `g<n>.<salt>` with a fresh salt, so a pool's marker never returns to a text it has used; given a new salt by the gate's *salt* action, replacing any earlier salt, in the step that takes it, `take` or `finish_take`; every change is made in a step, before that step raises the statement generation for it |
| Highest adopted `<n>`, behind PgBouncer | the greatest `<n>` the start read or `on_moved` has set the marker from | one word | set by the start read; raised by `on_moved`; never lowered |
| The generation word | one atomic word: the statement generation, whose rise makes each connection clear both statement caches at its next checkout or its next cached run, whichever comes first; step 11's connection generation, whose rise makes each connection be replaced at its next checkout, straight to Postgres only; the due action, two bits, a due *replace* outranking a due *clear* or *salt*; the starting bit, set from a checkout's compare-and-swap until `finish_take` finishes its take of the due action; and the pending entry count | one word | changed by steps only by compare-and-swap: `take` and `finish_take` raise an action's generation and clear the due bits, `finish_take` the starting bit too, `set_due` sets them, `on_moved` behind PgBouncer raises the statement generation and clears them and the starting bit, and a step that creates or removes a pending entry changes the count; outside steps only a checkout's compare-and-swap, which, once a due action's window has ended and with the starting bit clear, sets the starting bit and changes nothing else, so an action's generation is raised only in a step, after the marker it's raised for is set; every read of it with no lock is an acquire read, and every compare-and-swap on it, in a step or a checkout, is acquire-release |
| Last-read `<n>` | the `<n>` of the pool's latest applied read of the `_morm` schema's comment, in both modes, by the read order; behind PgBouncer with the caches on, the marker's `<n>`; the gate and the epoch judge by it | one word | set by the start read, which every pool makes when it starts, straight to Postgres as behind PgBouncer, with the statement caches on or off, with one catalog query on its first connection, which step 41 folds into its startup statement; a start read that fails fails the pool's start with its error, as a failed first connection or startup statement does, so it's set before any call reaches the gate; after that set only by `on_moved` |
| Read order | the ticket counter, from which every read of `<n>` takes a ticket when it's sent, and the horizon, the counter's value when the last applied read was applied | two words | the counter rises by one atomic add per read, the start read's included, with no lock; the horizon is set by each applied read, in its step, as `arrive` says |
| Servers | whether the pool can reach more than one server, by its `servers` setting, R-1289's: `"several"` or `"one"` as declared, and with `"auto"`, the default, when it's `read_only`, or its host list names more than one host and its `target_session_attrs` isn't `"read-write"` | one bit | set when the pool starts, from its settings, its URL and fields merged as step 10 says; never changed at run time |
| The window | the start of the last pool-wide action or adoption, the `<n>` it was taken under, and its end, `stale_cooldown` after its start; the window is closed from its start to its end and open after | O(1); its end is an atomic word, which checkouts read, an acquire read, while an action is due | started by `take` and `finish_take` under the pool's last-read `<n>`, and behind PgBouncer by `on_moved` under the `<n>` it adopts |
| The epoch, straight to Postgres | its start `T`, the `<n>` it was started under, its end `T + stale_cooldown`, whether it's suspended, and whether its extras have ended | O(1) | started by `old`, in the step that applies a session-class failure's read, when there's none, it has ended, or the pool's last-read `<n>` differs from its own; suspended for the rest of its life by `suspend`, when a replacement its own test decided can't be opened; its extras ended for the rest of its life by `no_extra`, when Postgres refuses a replacement's open beside the old connection with `53300`, so its later replacements open in their slots |
| The momentary extra, straight to Postgres | whether a replacement connection is open beside the one it replaces, at most one per pool | one bit | taken in the step that decides a replacement, when no other replacement holds it, the process's budget has room and the epoch's extras haven't ended; given back when that replacement takes the old connection's slot or its open fails, in the step that ends the epoch's extras when that failure is `53300` |
| The stale lock | a short synchronous mutex under which every step runs | one per pool | held for one step, never across I/O or an `.await` |
| Pending entries | held in a fixed array of `stale_pending_max` slots, each four words, the text's hash, the confirming bytes' hash, the expiry with the marked and *replace* bits, and a sequence word, which steps write as a sequence lock, as the marker's; per statement text, keyed by a 64-bit hash of the text: the hash of the confirming parameter bytes, or none once its confirming role has ended, one bit marking that a `0A000` set them, which requested its action at the failure, one *replace* bit, which row B2's `expect_confirm` sets when it discards the connection, so the confirming run requests *replace* in place of *clear*, and an expiry; while it exists every run of its statement is unnamed, in both modes | at most `stale_pending_max`, the oldest dropped | created by a statement-class signal inside a transaction, after any request that signal makes, unless a read of `<n>` that signal made found it moved; a later signal of the same statement sets its confirming bytes, sets the mark by its own signal, a `0A000`'s marked and any other's unmarked, and clears the *replace* bit, which row B2 sets again when that signal discards its connection, never its expiry; its confirming role ends, its bytes cleared so no run confirms it, when its confirming run fails the same way or ends on R-1245's no-confirm list, and the entry stays; removed when it expires, `stale_pending_expiry` after its creation, when its statement hits a session-class signal behind PgBouncer, and all at once when a pool-wide action is taken or `<n>` moves |
| Cool-down, behind PgBouncer | per statement text, keyed by a 64-bit hash of the text: an expiry | at most `stale_cooldown_max`, the oldest dropped | added by a session-class failure that got `Error::SchemaChanged` or a failed retry on another connection; removed `stale_cooldown` later, and all at once when a pool-wide action is taken or `<n>` moves |

Per connection: the time it was opened, the two generations it last saw, and, on a `db.hold()` connection, whether it's marked for replacement on release. A cached statement carries nothing extra: while a pending entry exists its statement runs unnamed on every connection, so no connection's copy needs comparing with the entry, and a connection behind the statement or connection generation clears both caches before its next cached run, so a run that follows a pool-wide action never uses a copy that action was taken to clear, even when its connection was checked out before it. There are no per-statement records straight to Postgres: one epoch decides which connections may be stale, and no table a client can fill decides whether a connection is replaced.

Each call's context carries the savepoint bit: whether the call runs inside a `tx.transaction(..)` savepoint, at any depth, set by the transaction as it makes the call, read with no lock and never pool state. Per transaction, the call carries two things of its own, not pool state, read and set with no lock: whether an earlier attempt of its `.retry(n)` returned `Error::SchemaChanged`, after which every later attempt, whatever ended the one before it, runs each of its statements unnamed, through `query_typed`, in both modes, cached statements included, and prepares none of them; and row B2's or B3's mark on its next attempt, from `expect_confirm`.

**Steps and the stale lock.** The procedure below, with the five things listed after this paragraph that run with no lock, is the only code that reads or changes the pool's stale-session state, and it changes it only in steps, apart from the starting bit a checkout's compare-and-swap sets. A **step** is a stretch of one call's machine work with no I/O in it; the I/O points are the lines marked `# I/O`: a read of `<n>`, a run of the call, a rollback of the call's whole transaction, and a connection's open or close. Every step runs under the pool's stale lock, held for that step alone and never across I/O or an `.await`, so steps of different calls never interleave, and while one call waits on I/O, other calls' steps run. Each `# I/O` line ends a step and what follows it starts the next, so `arrive` and everything after it up to the call's next I/O is one step: `on_moved`, `old`, `entry`, `request` with its `take` or `set_due`, and `expect_confirm`. So is a confirming run's outcome, and so is `finish_take` after a checkout's take: a checkout's compare-and-swap only starts the take, and `finish_take` does all of it in one step, a *salt*'s fresh salt, then the raised generation, then the window. A statement generation is raised only after the marker it's raised for is set, in the same step, so no connection clears its caches for an action or an adoption before the text it moves to exists. Every take a step finishes, a checkout's begun take included, is taken under the last-read `<n>` that step started with, so a take a checkout begins while a step that moves `<n>` runs counts as begun before the move, and the move's own request is judged against the window that take started. The lock is taken only on the stale-session paths: a signal's handling, a read of `<n>` and what follows it, a confirming run's outcome, and the one checkout that takes a due action; a call that meets no stale signal and isn't a confirming run never takes it. A step tests the state as it finds it: the gate by the pool's last-read `<n>` and the window, `old` by the last-read `<n>` and the epoch, and the entries and the cool-down by their tables. Across its I/O a call carries only its own: its signal, whether its read counted as moved, the pending entry its run found, the epoch its test used, and in a transaction whether its attempt is retried.

Five things run with no lock, outside steps:

- **A read's ticket,** one atomic add when the read is sent.
- **The pending check** before a cached run: one acquire read of the generation word, which holds the entry count beside the two generations, so the same read tells whether the connection is behind either generation, which clears both its caches before the run, as a checkout would, and whether any entry exists; while one does, the lookup below.
- **A prepare's read of the marker,** behind PgBouncer with the caches on, when a cached run prepares its statement, after the pending check's read of the generation word: a step writes the marker as a sequence lock, making the sequence word odd, then a release fence, then storing the `<n>` and salt words, atomics stored relaxed, then making the sequence word even with a release store, and the prepare reads the sequence, an acquire read, then the two words, relaxed, then the sequence again after an acquire fence, and reads again if it was odd or changed, so it gets a whole marker some step wrote, whatever generation it read.
- **A pending entry's lookup,** while the pending check's read found the entry count above zero: a scan of the pending array's slots for the text's hash, each slot read as the marker is, its sequence word with acquire, its three words relaxed, an acquire fence and its sequence word again, reading that slot again if the sequence was odd or changed, so it gets each slot whole as a step left it, never one slot's key with another state's bytes or bits. Steps write a slot as they write the marker: sequence odd, a release fence, the three words, sequence even with release.
- **A checkout,** R-0982's: one acquire read of the generation word; while an action is due and the starting bit is clear, one acquire read of the window's end too; and once that window has ended, one acquire-release compare-and-swap that sets the starting bit and changes nothing else, so two checkouts can't both take the due action. The checkout whose compare-and-swap succeeds then runs `finish_take` as one step, which takes the action.

**Why no other interleaving matters.**

- **Steps don't interleave,** so each finds and leaves the state whole. Requests made at once are judged one after another, and each finds the window the one before it started. An epoch is tested and started in the step that applies its read, by the last-read `<n>`, so no call starts an epoch under an `<n>` older than one another call's read has applied.
- **A ticket's add needs no lock.** The counter only rises, and `arrive` compares a read's ticket with the horizon in the step that applies it, so a read whose ticket is at or above the horizon was sent after the last applied read was applied, and its snapshot is newer than that read's, because every read that can apply runs on a snapshot of its own: outside a transaction, or after the call's whole transaction has rolled back, never in an open transaction or after a rollback to a savepoint, where a REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE snapshot is still the transaction's own, older than the read; and on a `db.hold()` connection only R-0981's read after a session-class failure, which, when the app opened a transaction there, Postgres has failed, so the read gets `25P02` and applies nothing.
- **The pending check only chooses** between a cached and an unnamed run, and whether to clear the connection's caches first. A run that misses an entry a step has just made, or a generation a step has just raised, counts as one already running when that step ran, and a confirming run's outcome is judged in a step, against the entry as its run found it.
- **A connection that sees a raised generation sees the marker it was raised for.** Every step sets the marker before the acquire-release compare-and-swap that raises the statement generation for it, and the pending check reads the word with acquire before a prepare reads the marker, so the marker that prepare reads is at least as new. A checkout that sees due bits sees the window they wait for, because each window is set in a step before any later step's compare-and-swap sets due bits, and the checkout reads the window's end, acquire, after the word.
- **A checkout changes the state only by its compare-and-swap,** which sets the starting bit only when the generation word is as the checkout read it, with an action due and the starting bit clear, and raises nothing. So until `finish_take` runs, every connection sees the generations as they were and runs or clears as before the action, and no connection prepares under the old marker for a generation raised for a new one. Steps change the word only by compare-and-swap too, and every step that judges the gate or changes the word first runs `finish_take` if it finds the starting bit set, the step that applies a read before `arrive`, and every take a step finishes is taken under the last-read `<n>` the step started with, so a begun take is finished under the last-read `<n>` it began under, even when the checkout's compare-and-swap lands after that step's own move of `<n>`. So no step judges the gate against a take that's begun and isn't finished, and a step whose compare-and-swap fails because a checkout's came first runs `finish_take` and judges again, except `on_moved` behind PgBouncer: its adoption takes the place of the due action, so its compare-and-swap clears the starting bit with the due bits, and a checkout whose compare-and-swap landed inside `on_moved` takes nothing, so no salt is taken under the adopted `<n>` beside the adoption.
- **So every pool-wide action,** taken in a step or by a checkout, is taken after the window before it ended or after the last-read `<n>` changed from that window's, as R-0982's bound needs, and every epoch starts after the last one ended or after the last-read `<n>` changed from its own, as R-0981's needs.

**The decision procedure.** `pooled` means behind PgBouncer, `ctx.out` and `call.out` outside a transaction, `ctx.held` a `db.hold()` connection, `ctx.sp` the savepoint bit, `read(conn)` a read of `<n>` on that connection, which returns whether it counted as moved, by the read order below, having called `on_moved` if so, and `several` the state table's servers bit, and `call.retried` that the call runs in an attempt after one of its transaction's that returned `Error::SchemaChanged`. `call.tx` is the call's transaction, and `rollback(call.tx)` rolls the whole of it back, savepoints included, never to a savepoint; after it the transaction is failed, and nothing more is sent on it, as step 20 says for savepoints. A request carries no `<n>`: `unread` says only that its call hasn't read `<n>`, isn't in an open transaction and isn't on a `db.hold()` connection, because a request made while its call's transaction is open, or on a held connection, whose session can be inside a transaction the app opened itself, never reads `<n>`.

```text
before_run(call, conn):                             # every run of a cached statement
    w = the generation word                         # one acquire read, no lock
    if conn is behind w's statement or connection generation:
        clear conn's caches                         # as a checkout would; a replacement
                                                    # still waits for the next checkout
    e = w's entry count == 0 ? none : pending(call.stmt)   # no lock: the entry as the last
                                                    # step left it
    if !e and !call.retried: run call cached; return    # a cache miss prepares it, behind
                                                    # PgBouncer under the marker, read after w
    r = run call unnamed                            # I/O; in both modes; every statement
                                                    # of a retried attempt runs unnamed
    # an error from an unnamed run goes to on_error as one from a statement that isn't cached
    if !e or e.bytes is none or call.bytes != e.bytes: return r   # other values confirm nothing
    # the confirming run; its outcome is one step, judged against e
    if r confirms: one request, never two: request(Replace) if e.replace, set by
        expect_confirm, else request(pooled ? Salt : Clear, unread = call.out and
        !ctx.held); none if e.marked: its 0A000 requested at the failure; inside a
        transaction, which is open, or on a held connection, which can be inside one the
        app opened, the request never reads <n>: a REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE
        snapshot is the transaction's, older than the read
    if r ends in the same error: end_confirm(e); go on to on_error as a fresh run's
    if r is on the no-confirm list: end_confirm(e); return r as it is
    # end_confirm(e) clears the statement's entry's bytes only if it still holds e's
    # bytes; the entry stays, so every run of its statement stays unnamed until it
    # expires or a pool-wide action or a moved <n> removes it

on_error(call, conn, err, ctx):
    if param_holds_retired(call): return AsIs
    if err is transient XX000:
        if ctx.out: return RetrySameConn            # a retry that gets 25P02, on a held connection
                                                    # in a transaction the app opened, returns err
        rollback(call.tx); return SchemaChanged     # I/O: the whole transaction
    cls = class(err, cached = !call.fresh)          # R-1245
    if cls == Session: return session(call, conn, err, ctx)
    if cls != Statement: return AsIs
    if ctx.out:                                     # A1, C1
        r = fresh_run(call)                         # I/O
        if confirms(r, err) or err == 0A000:        # a 25P02 never confirms: R-1245
            if pooled:
                mv = read(conn)                     # I/O; C1's read
                if !mv: request(Salt)               # a moved <n> was adopted, never salted: E1
            else: request(Clear, unread = !ctx.held)    # A1: the gate reads if the window is
                                                    # closed, never on a held connection
        if r is 25P02: return err                   # a held connection in a transaction the app
                                                    # opened, failed by err: the fresh run never
                                                    # ran, so the caller gets the original error
        if err is XX000 and r is XX000: return session(call, conn, r, ctx)
        return r
    rollback(call.tx)                               # I/O: rows B1, B2 and D1, the whole
                                                    # transaction, so every read below runs
                                                    # outside it, on a snapshot of its own
    if !pooled: evict(conn, call.stmt)              # B1, B2
    mv = false
    if pooled or err is XX000: mv = read(conn)      # I/O; D1's read, B2's for old
    if !mv and err == 0A000: mv = request(pooled ? Salt : Clear, unread = !pooled)
    if !mv: entry(call.stmt, call.bytes, marked = err == 0A000)   # only a call whose own
                                                    # read counted as moved skips it
    if !pooled and err is XX000 and old(conn):
        discard(conn); expect_confirm(call, Replace)    # the close is I/O after the step
    return SchemaChanged

session(call, conn, err, ctx):
    if pooled:                                      # C2, D2
        remove_entry(call.stmt)
        if in_cooldown(call.stmt): return AsIs
        if ctx.out:
            r = run_on_other_conn(call)             # I/O
            if r fails the same way: cooldown(call.stmt)
            return r
        cooldown(call.stmt)
        rollback(call.tx); return SchemaChanged     # I/O: the whole transaction
    if !ctx.out and !ctx.sp: rollback(call.tx)      # I/O: B3 and B4 outside a savepoint, the
                                                    # whole transaction, before R-0981's read
    if !ctx.sp: read(conn)                          # I/O; R-0981's read: outside a transaction,
                                                    # after the whole rollback, or on a held
                                                    # connection, where a transaction the app opened
                                                    # is failed, so the read gets 25P02, applies
                                                    # nothing, and old() judges by the last-read <n>;
                                                    # inside a savepoint no read: old() judges by
                                                    # the last-read <n>, as after a read that
                                                    # applies nothing
    if !old(conn): return AsIs                      # A3, B4: opened since T, or suspended; inside a
                                                    # savepoint nothing is rolled back but the
                                                    # savepoint, so the app can catch it there
    sure = err in {42804, XX000}                    # confirmed on its own, R-1245
    if sure: request(Replace)                       # once per failure
    if ctx.held: replace_on_release(conn); return SchemaChanged                   # A4
    if ctx.out:                                     # A2
        r = replace(conn, call)                     # I/O: opens, as R-0981 says, and runs the
                                                    # call; a 53300 on the extra: no_extra(call);
                                                    # a failed open: suspend(call)
        if !sure and confirms(r, err): request(Replace)
        return r
    discard(conn); if !sure: expect_confirm(call, Replace)    # B3
    if ctx.sp: rollback(call.tx)                    # I/O: B3 inside a savepoint, the whole
                                                    # transaction, after the step that decided it
```

**R-1270** **The stale-session machine is one pure module.** Every stale-statement and stale-session rule of this step and of step 20 is one state machine, built as one module of `morm`, such as `stale.rs`, with no I/O. It holds the pool's stale-session state, below, and its functions take a signal, the call's context (straight to Postgres or behind PgBouncer, inside a transaction or not, inside a `tx.transaction(..)` savepoint or not, on a held connection or not, from a cached statement or a fresh run) and the clock, and return a decision: answer with a fresh run, replace the connection, discard it, retry on the same connection, retry on another connection, return `Error::SchemaChanged`, or return the error as it is, with any pool-wide action to request. The pool and connection code carries the decisions out, and step 20's simulation drives this same module, so it tests the code that ships. The machine keeps two things apart:

- **Every call is repaired locally, always.** A stale statement gets one fresh run of the same call. A stale session straight to Postgres gets the call retried on a newly opened connection that takes the old one's slot. Inside a transaction the call returns `Error::SchemaChanged`, which fails the whole transaction, inside `tx.transaction(..)`'s savepoint too, and `.retry(n)`'s later attempts run every statement unnamed, on a newly opened connection when the old one was discarded; a stale session's error it returns as it is inside a savepoint, row B4's, is a Postgres error the savepoint clears. Nothing about the window, the epoch or a table changes what one call returns, beyond what its row says.
- **Every pool-wide action passes one gate,** R-0982's: clearing every connection's statement caches, adding a salt behind PgBouncer, and replacing every connection, each at most once per pool per `stale_cooldown`, plus once per migration.

Per connection: the time it was opened, the two generations it last saw, and, on a `db.hold()` connection, whether it's marked for replacement on release. A cached statement carries nothing extra: while a pending entry exists its statement runs unnamed on every connection, so no connection's copy needs comparing with the entry, and a connection behind the statement or connection generation clears both caches before its next cached run, so a run that follows a pool-wide action never uses a copy that action was taken to clear, even when its connection was checked out before it. There are no per-statement records straight to Postgres: one epoch decides which connections may be stale, and no table a client can fill decides whether a connection is replaced.

Each call's context carries the savepoint bit: whether the call runs inside a `tx.transaction(..)` savepoint, at any depth, set by the transaction as it makes the call, read with no lock and never pool state. Per transaction, the call carries two things of its own, not pool state, read and set with no lock: whether an earlier attempt of its `.retry(n)` returned `Error::SchemaChanged`, after which every later attempt, whatever ended the one before it, runs each of its statements unnamed, through `query_typed`, in both modes, cached statements included, and prepares none of them; and row B2's or B3's mark on its next attempt, from `expect_confirm`.

**Steps and the stale lock.** The procedure below, with the five things listed after this paragraph that run with no lock, is the only code that reads or changes the pool's stale-session state, and it changes it only in steps, apart from the starting bit a checkout's compare-and-swap sets. A **step** is a stretch of one call's machine work with no I/O in it; the I/O points are the lines marked `# I/O`: a read of `<n>`, a run of the call, a rollback of the call's whole transaction, and a connection's open or close. Every step runs under the pool's stale lock, held for that step alone and never across I/O or an `.await`, so steps of different calls never interleave, and while one call waits on I/O, other calls' steps run. Each `# I/O` line ends a step and what follows it starts the next, so `arrive` and everything after it up to the call's next I/O is one step: `on_moved`, `old`, `entry`, `request` with its `take` or `set_due`, and `expect_confirm`. So is a confirming run's outcome, and so is `finish_take` after a checkout's take: a checkout's compare-and-swap only starts the take, and `finish_take` does all of it in one step, a *salt*'s fresh salt, then the raised generation, then the window. A statement generation is raised only after the marker it's raised for is set, in the same step, so no connection clears its caches for an action or an adoption before the text it moves to exists. Every take a step finishes, a checkout's begun take included, is taken under the last-read `<n>` that step started with, so a take a checkout begins while a step that moves `<n>` runs counts as begun before the move, and the move's own request is judged against the window that take started. The lock is taken only on the stale-session paths: a signal's handling, a read of `<n>` and what follows it, a confirming run's outcome, and the one checkout that takes a due action; a call that meets no stale signal and isn't a confirming run never takes it. A step tests the state as it finds it: the gate by the pool's last-read `<n>` and the window, `old` by the last-read `<n>` and the epoch, and the entries and the cool-down by their tables. Across its I/O a call carries only its own: its signal, whether its read counted as moved, the pending entry its run found, the epoch its test used, and in a transaction whether its attempt is retried.

Five things run with no lock, outside steps:

- **A read's ticket,** one atomic add when the read is sent.
- **The pending check** before a cached run: one acquire read of the generation word, which holds the entry count beside the two generations, so the same read tells whether the connection is behind either generation, which clears both its caches before the run, as a checkout would, and whether any entry exists; while one does, the lookup below.
- **A prepare's read of the marker,** behind PgBouncer with the caches on, when a cached run prepares its statement, after the pending check's read of the generation word: a step writes the marker as a sequence lock, making the sequence word odd, then a release fence, then storing the `<n>` and salt words, atomics stored relaxed, then making the sequence word even with a release store, and the prepare reads the sequence, an acquire read, then the two words, relaxed, then the sequence again after an acquire fence, and reads again if it was odd or changed, so it gets a whole marker some step wrote, whatever generation it read.
- **A pending entry's lookup,** while the pending check's read found the entry count above zero: a scan of the pending array's slots for the text's hash, each slot read as the marker is, its sequence word with acquire, its three words relaxed, an acquire fence and its sequence word again, reading that slot again if the sequence was odd or changed, so it gets each slot whole as a step left it, never one slot's key with another state's bytes or bits. Steps write a slot as they write the marker: sequence odd, a release fence, the three words, sequence even with release.
- **A checkout,** R-0982's: one acquire read of the generation word; while an action is due and the starting bit is clear, one acquire read of the window's end too; and once that window has ended, one acquire-release compare-and-swap that sets the starting bit and changes nothing else, so two checkouts can't both take the due action. The checkout whose compare-and-swap succeeds then runs `finish_take` as one step, which takes the action.

**Why no other interleaving matters.**
