The README shows this notice loudly, beside `tx.set_local`:

> **A `search_path` set per transaction over tables of different shapes makes cached statements fail when it switches.** A statement prepared under one `search_path` and run under another, where the same table name has another shape, such as a schema per tenant with a column added in one, fails with `0A000` `cached plan must not change result type`, with no schema change at all. A fresh statement can't stop it: one prepared under the new path fails the same way when the path switches back. morm handles it the same way straight to Postgres and behind PgBouncer:
>
> - Outside a transaction morm runs the call on a fresh statement and returns that answer.
> - Inside one you get `Error::SchemaChanged` at most once per `stale_pending_expiry`, 60 seconds by default, per statement and pool, and then morm keeps the statement pending and runs it unnamed, parsed and planned on every run, until the entry expires. Any pool-wide repair morm makes meanwhile, for this statement or another, ends every pending entry, so the next switch can fail once more: those repairs come at most once per `stale_cooldown`, 60 seconds by default, plus once per migration.
> - morm clears its statement caches for it, or behind PgBouncer moves its statements to fresh text, at most once per `stale_cooldown` per pool.
> - **Each failure asks for one repair, once.** A statement failing on a switch asks for a repair at that failure, and a later run of it with the same values, such as the same `id`, asks for nothing more. So one such statement fails about once per `stale_pending_expiry`, whether its values recur or not, and once more per `stale_cooldown` when `stale_pending_expiry` is the shorter. When more than one statement switches, each one's failure asks for a repair, and each repair ends every pending entry, so a repair comes about once per `stale_cooldown` and each such statement fails about once per `stale_cooldown`, or once per `stale_pending_expiry` when that's the shorter, because then its pending entry expires before the next repair ends it.
> - Behind PgBouncer the error comes at prepare too, and for other clients, because PgBouncer hands every client that prepares the same text the server statement another transaction planned.
>
> **What you give up.** Without `.retry(n)`, about one failed transaction per statement per `stale_pending_expiry` inside transactions, plus one after each pool-wide repair, which with several such statements means about one per `stale_cooldown`, or per `stale_pending_expiry` when that's the shorter; and while a statement is pending, an unnamed run instead of a cached one.
>
> **What to do,** any one of these:
>
> - **Name the schema in the SQL,** as `tenant_a.items`, or build it with a fragment, so each tenant's text is its own cached statement and no plan meets another path.
> - **Keep every tenant's tables the same shape,** so a switch changes no result type and nothing fails.
> - **Set `search_path` per pool rather than per transaction,** one `[pools.<name>]` per tenant schema with its own `search_path`, so a pool's statements are only ever planned under one path.
> - **Use `.retry(n)`,** which hides the `SchemaChanged`, because its later attempts run every statement unnamed.
> - **Raise `stale_pending_expiry`, keeping it at least `stale_cooldown`,** for fewer failures and more unnamed runs, when one statement switches, whether its values recur or not. **When several statements switch, raise `stale_pending_expiry` and `stale_cooldown` together:** raising `stale_pending_expiry` alone helps only until it reaches `stale_cooldown`, and past it changes nothing, because each statement's failure asks for a repair that ends every pending entry, and those repairs come once per `stale_cooldown`. A longer `stale_cooldown` holds back every stale repair in the pool too: straight to Postgres a connection opened just before a change can return its stale error that long, a refused connection pauses replacements that long, and behind PgBouncer a statement hitting a stale server session returns its error at once that long, as the notice beside the pool settings says. Or **turn the statement cache off for that pool,** `statement_cache = 0` and `shape_cache = 0` in its `[pools.<name>]`, so every statement is planned per run and none fails.

**morm ships a real `morm.toml`, with every setting at its default.** `crates/morm-core/morm.toml` is part of `morm-core`'s published package, because `morm-core` reads the config and cargo packages only the files inside a crate's folder. It's a working config file, not a template: copied next to an app unchanged, as `morm.toml`, it loads with no error and gives exactly the config no file gives, whatever environment variables are set. A user gets it from the README, which links to it and says to copy it next to the app and change only what they need, or from `morm-core`'s package source; `morm-admin init` writes it as a new project's `morm.toml`, as step 42 says, changing only the `host` and `port` lines a found socket needs, loudly. It lists every setting morm reads, grouped by table in R-0060's order: `[database]`, `[database.migration]`, `[server]`, `[pool]`, the `[pools.<name>]` profiles, `[outbox]`, `[telemetry]` and `[migrations]`. Its header comment says that every value in it is the default, so a line can be changed or deleted with nothing else lost; that morm refuses any key it doesn't read, in any table, so a misspelt or misplaced key stops the app at startup with `Error::Config`; and that this file is where to check a key's spelling and table. Each setting is one line, `key = value`, active apart from the commented-out examples below, with comments above it giving:

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the TLS settings and `sslmode`:

> **Over TCP morm requires TLS by default, so a server without it needs `sslmode = "disable"`.** `sslmode` defaults to `require`: a TCP connection is encrypted, and a Postgres or PgBouncer that doesn't offer TLS is refused, with an error naming this notice. Without the `tls` feature, your app stops at startup when a TCP host would need TLS. `morm-admin` always carries TLS, in every build and in the release binaries, and so does `morm-migrate`, used on its own as a library too, and the `morm-mgr` package `morm-admin init` creates turns `tls` on for its `morm`, so a migration's data hooks have it too: none of them stops for that. Your app is different: `morm-mgr` is a member of your app's Cargo workspace, and Cargo unifies features across the packages one build selects, so a build that includes `morm-mgr`, `cargo build --workspace` or a plain `cargo build` at a virtual workspace's root, gives your app's own `morm` `tls` too, while a build of the app alone, `cargo build -p <app>`, `cargo install` or a plain `cargo build` in your app's own directory, gives it only the features its own `Cargo.toml` turns on. So an app without `tls` that reaches its database over TCP can start in CI or dev and stop at startup in a deploy build, with an `Error::Config` naming `sslmode` and the `tls` feature. A Unix socket never uses TLS, whatever `sslmode` says, so a socket connection, morm's default `host`, works unchanged, with no `tls` feature and nothing set.
>
> **When `disable` or `prefer` is right.** A Postgres or PgBouncer on the same machine reached over TCP, such as `127.0.0.1` or a container's published port, or one on a private network you trust end to end. PgBouncer offers its clients TLS only when its `client_tls_sslmode` is set, so a PgBouncer reached over TCP without it needs `disable` too. Set it in `morm.toml`, as `MORM_DB_SSLMODE=disable`, or as `?sslmode=disable` in the URL, for that pool only.
>
> **What you give up.** With `disable`, and with `prefer` against a server without TLS or with the `tls` feature left out, queries, results and the parameters you bind cross the network unencrypted, and so does the password when the server asks for it in clear text; anyone on the path can read or change them. `prefer` falls back to no TLS whenever the server, or anyone on the path pretending to be it, says it has none. `require` encrypts but doesn't check who answered; `verify-full` does, with `sslrootcert`.
>
> **How to proceed.** On the same machine, connect through the Unix socket instead. Otherwise turn TLS on in Postgres, `ssl = on` with a certificate, and keep the default, or use `verify-full`, and enable morm's `tls` feature, which is off unless you turn it on, in your `Cargo.toml`: `morm = { version = "0.1", features = ["tls"] }`; without it morm stops at startup with an error naming `sslmode` and the feature. `morm-admin` and `morm-migrate` need nothing: every build of them carries TLS. Nor does `morm-mgr`: the `morm` dependency `init` writes for it has `features = ["tls"]`, so keep that line, even when your app leaves `tls` off. Don't count on a workspace build for your app's TLS: if it reaches Postgres over TCP, turn `tls` on in its own `morm` dependency, as above, and check what a deploy build gets with `cargo tree -p <app> -e features`, which shows `morm`'s `tls` only when your app turns it on, or test the binary `cargo build -p <app>` makes, the one you deploy. Set `sslmode = "disable"` only for a server you reach over a network you trust. Every connection morm opens gets the default: your pools, `[database.migration]`, `scratch_url`, each `pgbouncer_admin_urls` entry and `morm-admin`'s own. A connection given a URL of its own, such as `scratch_url` or an admin URL, takes `sslmode` from that URL, as `?sslmode=disable`.

> **A `[database]` value written in `morm.toml` overrides `DATABASE_URL`.** The fields of `[database]`, `host`, `port`, `name`, `user`, `password`, `sslmode` and every other part a URL can carry, override the matching parts of its URL, so a value written in the file wins over that part of the `DATABASE_URL` a deployment sets. The common case is `host` and `port`: the `host = "/run/postgresql"` that `morm-admin init` writes when it finds Postgres's socket somewhere other than `/var/run/postgresql`, or the `port` it writes for a socket on another port, wins over the URL's host and port, so an app deployed with `DATABASE_URL` naming a managed database connects to the local socket instead: silently, if that server runs a Postgres there, or with an error naming a socket path you never set. A `name`, `user` or `password` written for local work is used in every deployment too, and a written `sslmode` replaces the URL's. morm warns at startup whenever a value written in `[database]`, or in `[database.migration]`, overrides a different one in its URL, naming the field and both values, never a password, and `init` puts a `# WARNING:` line above each such line it writes. >
> **When it's right.** Every deployment of the app uses this same value, such as this same socket or host for an app that only ever runs on the database's own machine, and none sets `DATABASE_URL` to another value for that part.

> **What you give up.** `DATABASE_URL` alone no longer moves the app: a deployment that sets only the URL keeps each value the file writes, its host and port, database, user or `sslmode`, with the startup warning as the only sign. A written `sslmode` weaker than the URL's, such as `sslmode = "disable"` against a URL with `?sslmode=require` or `verify-full`, drops the TLS the URL asked for, so queries, results, the parameters you bind and the password can cross the network unencrypted, as the notice on `sslmode`, "Over TCP morm requires TLS by default", says.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside `read_only`, host lists and `servers`:

> **A pool that can reach more than one server never moves morm's statement generation back.** Every migration step raises the database's statement generation, `<n>`, kept in the comment of its `_morm` schema, and each pool reads it to learn that a migration ran, so it can clear its statement caches, replace connections holding stale compiled code and, behind PgBouncer, move its statements to fresh text, at once and once per migration. A `read_only` pool, or one whose host list names more than one host without `target_session_attrs = "read-write"`, can reach several servers whose `<n>` differ, such as standbys replaying a migration at different times, so in such a pool morm lets `<n>` only rise: standbys at different replay positions count a migration once, instead of moving `<n>` back and forth. That's `servers = "auto"`, the default.
>
> **What morm can't see.** One host can stand for several servers: a PgBouncer database entry listing several hosts, which PgBouncer takes in turn by default, a load balancer, or a DNS name with several addresses. Set `servers = "several"` on a pool behind such a host, `read_only` or not, in its `[pools.<name>]` or in `[pool]`, or with `MORM_POOL_SERVERS`. Without it morm counts the pool as reaching one server, so while those servers' `<n>` differ, as when standbys replay a migration at different times, each read that reaches another of them moves `<n>`, up or back, and each move is handled as a migration: behind PgBouncer the pool moves its statements to new text, so every connection clears its statement caches; straight to Postgres the next repair any call asks for passes at once, clearing every connection's caches or replacing every connection, and the next stale-session error starts a new epoch. reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside transactions and `tx.transaction(..)`:

> **`Error::SchemaChanged` inside a savepoint fails the whole transaction.** `tx.transaction(..)` is a savepoint: an error inside it rolls back to the savepoint, and your outer closure can catch it and go on. Not `Error::SchemaChanged`, which a schema change made outside morm gives inside a transaction: like a deadlock or a serialization failure, it fails the whole transaction. morm rolls the whole transaction back at once, before it checks what changed, because after a rollback to a savepoint a `REPEATABLE READ` or `SERIALIZABLE` transaction still sees the database as it was at its first statement, and morm would read an old schema state there. From then on nothing more is sent on that transaction: if your closure catches the error and runs more statements, each returns `Error::SchemaChanged` with nothing run and nothing written, and the transaction returns `Error::SchemaChanged` even if your closure returns `Ok`. A function's error that morm returns as it is inside a savepoint is different: straight to Postgres, when a function fails in a way a stale session can, such as a retired enum label read from stored text, on a connection morm judges fresh, morm decides without reading the schema's state, so you get an ordinary `Error::Postgres` that rolls back only to the savepoint, and you can catch it and go on. Right after a migration, such an error can come from a function the migration left stale, on a connection opened shortly before it, and repeat on that connection inside savepoints, until morm next reads the schema's state outside a transaction or `stale_cooldown` has passed since the migration, whichever is first; after that the same failure gives `Error::SchemaChanged` and morm closes the connection.
>
> **When it's right:** always: it's how morm repairs a stale statement or session without reading an old snapshot. **What you give up:** you can't catch `SchemaChanged` in a savepoint and carry on in the same transaction; the transaction's work is lost and has to run again. And for up to `stale_cooldown` after a migration, a stale function's error inside a savepoint can reach you as `Error::Postgres` rather than as `SchemaChanged`, so `.retry(n)` doesn't run it again. **How to proceed:** give the transaction `.retry(n)`, which runs the whole closure again on fresh statements, `.retry(1)` for a stale statement and, straight to Postgres, `.retry(2)` for a stale statement and a stale session together, and keep work you must not lose out of that transaction. If you catch `Error::Postgres` inside a savepoint and carry on, a stale function's error just after a migration is caught with it: when its SQLSTATE is `22P02`, `42804` or `XX000` and the work matters, let it out of the savepoint so the transaction fails, and run the transaction again yourself; from `stale_cooldown` after the migration at the latest, the same failure gives `SchemaChanged` instead and morm closes that connection, so `.retry(n)` handles it from then on. Every other error inside a savepoint, such as a unique violation, still rolls back only to the savepoint.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside `db.hold()` and `sql_unchecked`:

> **On a held connection, a transaction you open yourself gets no stale-statement repair.** If you run `BEGIN` on a `db.hold()` connection through `sql_unchecked`, morm can't see that transaction: the driver doesn't report it. When a schema change made outside morm leaves a cached statement stale, Postgres fails your transaction at that statement, so morm's usual repair, running the call again on a fresh statement, can't run inside it: you get the statement's own error, as `Error::Postgres` with its SQLSTATE, such as `0A000`, `cached plan must not change result type`, not the fresh run's answer, and your transaction stays failed. morm has dropped the stale statement from that connection, so after your `ROLLBACK` the transaction's next run prepares it fresh. A stale function's error there returns `Error::SchemaChanged`, or, when it's `cache lookup failed for type`, which morm can't tell from a stale statement without a fresh run, its own error; either way the connection is closed when you release it, as every held connection is. A repair morm asks for the whole pool from a held connection never reads the schema's generation, because a transaction you opened would show it an old one; it learns of a migration at the pool's next read elsewhere.
>
> **When it's right:** when you need a transaction on a held connection, beside its session state such as temp tables or `SET`. **What you give up:** the automatic repair there, and one failed transaction per stale statement on that connection. **How to proceed:** use `db.transaction(..)` for transactions where you can, which gets every repair and `.retry(n)`; on a held connection, roll back and run your transaction again on `Error::SchemaChanged`, or on `Error::Postgres` with SQLSTATE `0A000`, `22P02` or `XX000` after a schema change.

**Fault injection:** kill the process and the worker at every point: before commit (no event), after commit (delivered), and after send before recording (delivered twice, same `e.id`).
**Concurrency:** rival workers never hold one event at once while a lease is valid, expired leases return, and keyed events stay in order.

A same-named column on a second table stays on that table. `JOIN ... **`proof`:** on `pg_function!` and `pg_procedure!`, with `file` or inline, each `proof` reaches the manifest byte for byte and in the order written, including several on one declaration, a declaration without one stays valid, and changing, adding or removing only a `proof` opens no migration.

A `language sql` one stops on the proof's boundary row. **What a call may touch:** on Postgres 15–18, an automatic call that reaches `dblink` directly, through another function and through `EXECUTE`, and one using `COPY ... **Same meaning:** on Postgres 15–18, every `USING` and `NATURAL JOIN` shape in T-0190, as a view, a materialized view and a `BEGIN ATOMIC` function, matches the models by text or else by query tree, and after cutover `verify` reports no drift and `makemigrations` proposes nothing, also after `purge` and after a later rename of another column on that table. **Column positions:** on Postgres 15–18, with a `USING` materialized view above the column, an unmanaged column on the live table, in the middle or last, stops `migrate` with exit code `2` before the swap's first step, naming the table, changing nothing, and `--fast` handles the same change. **A cutover gives way:** on Postgres 15–18, under nonstop transactions that touch the table and then read the view, and readers and writers on both, no app transaction gets `40P01` or `55P03`, no read or write fails, and the cutover gets in by retrying, with the three settings at their defaults of `50ms`, `600` and `250ms`. Each setting changes what a run does. Starved by a transaction that holds the table for the whole test, and again by nonstop overlapping transactions each longer than `cutover_lock_timeout`, the cutover stops as `failed` with exit code `2` after `cutover_attempts` attempts. Nothing changes in the catalog, no app transaction is killed, the message gives the attempts and names `--resume`, and writes go on reaching the shadow column. With a `deadlock_timeout` too low for `cutover_lock_timeout` at the cutover's locks, each lock waits `deadlock_timeout / (2 × locks)`, rounded down to a whole millisecond, the output names the three numbers and that wait, and no app transaction is killed. **`EXECUTE`, on Postgres 15–18:** a function that takes no arguments and uses `EXECUTE`, `FOR ... IN EXECUTE`, `OPEN ... **In-comment options, on Postgres 15–18:** a managed plpgsql function with `@plpgsql_check_options` in a comment stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the function, with no file written, whether or not it hides a real break, with no decision to accept, even with a `proof` declared. The text in another case, and in a string, stops it too, and the same function without the text is checked as usual. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

The test builds a sample of what reaches the column, of different kinds, naming neither the table nor the column, and `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3`, with no file written, on one decision listing all of them, until it's accepted, and `meta.json` records it. The sample isn't the rule, and a kind it leaves out is still in scope: it holds a managed plpgsql function with a `numeric(6,2)` variable set by `v := inner_f()`, callers through a chain of two, as `INNER_F()`, as `public.inner_f()`, in another schema and in a `BEGIN ATOMIC` body, a function and a view reading a found view with no cast, a view reading that view, a trigger's `WHEN`, a policy, a rule, an expression index, a partial index, a default and what reads its column, a generated column and what reads it, a table's check and a function that writes to that table, a domain's check and a variable of that domain, an operator used in a plpgsql body as `1 ~~~ 2`, `1~~~2` and `OPERATOR(public.~~~)`, an aggregate, a body using a cast, and an extended statistics object over an expression. In a cycle, `a` calling `b` and `b` calling `a` with one of them calling `inner_f`, and with a function that calls itself, the walk stops at the first round that adds nothing and each is listed once, and so is an object two paths reach. A table, a view, a function, a check and an index nothing reaches aren't listed. A managed function that reads the column through `EXECUTE format('SELECT max(%I) FROM %I', col, tab) INTO v`, naming neither, stops with exit code `2` with no `proof`, asking for one. With one it's on the list until the decision is accepted, even though its `proof` passes, and a function that calls it is found too. A function using `EXECUTE` that names nothing the change touches opens no decision on a retire or a rename. With a function that needs a `proof` and has none, and the list open, the run exits with code `2`. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

**A refusal and an open decision together:** a `makemigrations` run with both a hard refusal, such as a model's `extensions` entry scratch doesn't have, and an open decision exits with code `2`, with no file written, and answering the decision alone still exits `2`. With the refusal fixed and the decision open it exits `3`, and with the decision answered it exits `0`.

A function whose name holds a space and an `=` is answered by pasting the ID morm printed. `meta.json` records the direction of each answer, and a decision open only on `down` is recorded for `down` only.

A decision `meta.json` has answered for `up` opens nothing and adds no row. With two decisions open, a run answering one exits with code `3`, and a later run answering only the other goes through. A run whose first step fails after its answer is recorded keeps the answer, and a rerun with no `--decide` opens nothing. Editing the pending migration's `up.sql` or `meta.json` cancels the answer, and changing the function gives a new ID, and each stops with code `3`. **Live traffic, on Postgres 15–18:** an `integer` identity primary key on 1,000,000 rows, referenced by a `NOT NULL` column with `ON DELETE CASCADE` and a nullable one with `ON DELETE SET NULL`, each on 1,000,000 rows, widens to `bigint` under nonstop clients that insert a parent and two children, insert and then delete a parent, move a child to another parent, update a parent and then read its children, join, and run `SELECT *` on a referencing table, with more clients joining just before the cutover. No app transaction fails, every write count matches the clients' logs, no row is orphaned, no trigger or function is left, each copy stops at its bound, and the catalog equals a fresh build of the target schema, with the foreign keys tied to the new primary key and the sequence `bigint` at its position. The sequence keeps its options, owner, grants and comment, a `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on the old key moves to the new one, and a session open across the cutover gets `55000` from `currval` until its next `nextval`. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options. These tests run in CI's `Migration suite` step, and the PR links that step's log.

**Fault injection, on Postgres 15–18:** under the same traffic, kill the backend at every step boundary, and inside the copy, each concurrent index build, both `VALIDATE`s and the cutover. `--resume` then finishes with no lost write and the catalog of a fresh build, and `rollback --failed` drops every shadow object and leaves the old columns, keys and sequence working. A concurrent index left invalid is built again, a constraint left `NOT VALID` is validated again, and a cutover killed holding every lock changes nothing. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

A foreign key added on the key during the copy stops the cutover with nothing changed. `--fast` with any one table of the group over `max_rewrite_mb` is refused, naming that table and its size, and raising the setting lets it run. `integer` to `uuid` keeps step 39's refusal on a live table, and `--fast` runs it. **Up, down and up, on Postgres 15–18:** under live writers, a widening from `integer` to `bigint`, its `rollback` and the widening again each run online and end on the exact catalog, with the original columns back at their positions after the down and the identity's position carried each way.
